note: Page template (2026-10-20, docs/site-redesign/page-templates.md): optional per project `next` (up to three project slugs shown under What to build next; default the next ones in its outcome that ran); recipe.media may carry `video` and `poster` beside `image`, and is the one hero picture (it never changes with the board picked); a step that changes the program may carry `by_hand` {do, see, say} for the same change made by hand, shown beside its AI prompt under Make it yours; a step whose title starts with Change, Edit or Make it yours moves from Run it to Make it yours. Projects tried on each board, grouped the way beginner guides order them (docs/research/hobbyist-project-list-2026-10-06.md). st: yes, no, partial, untested. radio: which radio the row needs (ble, 154 for Zigbee or Thread, wifi, radio for any), empty for none. Every tried cell names a source file. Yes: the project ran and its pass test was met. Partly: some of it ran, or it ran without the pass test being checked; the line says which part. Each project also carries slug (its page, site/project-<slug>.html), tier (easy, medium, hard; see tiers), what, time, hardware (ids in data/parts.json beyond the board), and optional img (site/media/), demos (ids in demos.json) and experiments (ids in docs/experiments/). q is the end of each project page's H1 after "Can a TI <boards> ...". A no or partly cell may carry why_not (ram, flash, cpu, no-radio, no-software, tools, radio-link, ours, unknown): the reason, so the chip is not blamed for a tool or a weak radio link. Optional per project: hardware_by_board ({board id: [part ids]}, parts only that board needs, such as a debugger an LP-EM board lacks) and variants ([{name, hardware, boards, status, source}], distinct ways the project was run, each with its own parts; status yes means it ran). The hub shows the parts of the demonstrated variant, never a union across variants or boards, and 'not known yet' when nothing ran. Evidence fields on a cell (tools/site_ui.py evidence): proof is how far it got (built, booted, ran, checked, demonstrated; a yes defaults to checked, a partial to ran), checked_by is us (default) or self-report (the agent's own word, never shown as Works), reproduced_by names an independent builder who got the same result (our own repeat runs never count). An outcome with application: true shows Works only when a cell is demonstrated in that application; otherwise Parts work. A project may carry a recipe (the outcome-first page: tools/render_projects.py recipe_html): outcome (the H1), one_line, media ({video, poster, caption, alt, output} under site/), default (variant id), variants ([{id, name, short, boards, status (tested or planned), evidence ([{text, source}]), parts ([{id in data/parts.json or name, qty, role, included (what comes with it), separate (what you need to add)}]), prereqs, wiring ({image under site/, full (a repo path for the full-size file), alt, note, pins ([[display pin, header pin (MCU pin), what it is, required or optional]])}), steps ([{n, app, do, say (optional words to type), see (what you should see), if (recovery, one line)}]), expect, shows, not_shows, limits, technical ([{k, v, source}])}]), compat ({variant id: {board id: {level (tested, expected, adaptation, not-assessed), scope, basis, required ([]), source}}}). Rules checked by tools/site_check.py: a tested entry needs a source and a cell or also entry on that board that ran; expected and adaptation need a basis and the required list; every part id, image, source and board id must exist; a variant's boards and its steps are its own, never inherited from another variant. A variant may also carry total (the priced parts, dated) and why_board (why the recommended board fits, in the reader's terms). card (redesign, 2026-10-12): setup (nodes and link labels, alternating node, link, node), outcome (one sentence, what you end up with) and merit (the one measurement that matters for this project, text plus the source of the project's best cell); rendered on the Projects page by tools/render_projects.py; a project with no card.outcome gets a warning from tools/site_check.py. card.pic (optional): {src, kind photo|screenshot|drawing, alt}; without one the Projects card shows an illustration drawn from card.setup (site/media/illus/<slug>.svg, written by the renderer). Optional per project (site review 2026-10-14): glance ({difficulty, time, parts_cost, works_with}; any absent one is derived: difficulty from tier, time from the default version's step min or the project time, parts_cost from that version's dated prices summed and rounded to $5, status always from the best cell by ui.evidence), system ([{id, name, role, board (true on the board box; id 'board' also counts)}], 3 to 5 boxes, drawn top to bottom, the board in Fox Red) and links ([[from id, to id, optional label]], each joining neighbouring boxes; both directions draw as an up-and-down arrow). A recipe step may carry min (minutes, only when the project's own record states a duration) and title (the one line on its collapsed card; else the first sentence of do). A no cell may carry cant (two or three words for the Other boards list, such as 'no Matter build'); else it is derived from why_not. A compat entry may carry short (the reason shown beside its status word). Checked by validate_recipe. Optional per project page_flags ({long: reason}): the page is allowed more than about 1,000 open words; the check in tools/render_projects.py (layout_problems) needs the reason in words.

prereqs: A Mac with the free tools from step 1: CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login; it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB, 2.2 GB installed), SysConfig 1.26.3 (0.96 GB installed) and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB). Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the helper scripts `sdkmake.sh` and `tools/ocd.sh`.

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free: CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login) (it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon). The helper script `sdkmake.sh` in this repository expects the SDK at `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07`, SysConfig 1.26.3 at `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3` and the compiler under `/Applications/ti/ccs2101`. SysConfig 1.26.3, the version this repo's scripts point at, came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer (10.20.00.39, which you do not need otherwise; you can get SysConfig alone from [TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed) on the test Mac (it put it in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`); CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1, which this repo's scripts do not point at.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `openocd --version` prints 0.12.0.
steps.if: If your tools live elsewhere, set `FRL_MSPM0_SDK`, `FRL_SYSCONFIG` and `FRL_TICLANG` to where they are; `sdkmake.sh` reads them through `tools/frl/toolenv.py`.

steps.do: Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. The board shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. Read your probe's serial number with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` (the text after `usbmodem`, minus the last digit), or with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` from CCStudio.
steps.see: The Mac lists the probe and two serial ports. A new board shows TI's out-of-box demo.
steps.if: If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

steps.do: From the root of this repository, run the whole route with your probe's serial number. It backs the board up, copies TI's blink example, builds it, flashes it and times the LED pin through the debugger. It took 13 to 14 s on this bench with the tools installed. Leave off `--probe` only if one probe is plugged in; with several, it stops with FRL-E002.
steps.see: The run ends with a line that starts `OK:` and the RGB LED on the board cycles.
steps.if: If it stops with FRL-E002, several probes are plugged in: name yours with `--probe`. `python3 tools/frl/frl.py detect` lists them.

steps.do: Or do it by hand, from the `mspm0l1306` folder of this repository. Copy TI's example out of the SDK, build it (3.3 s), then flash it with OpenOCD (0.6 s). The repository's `tools/ocd.sh` picks the probe by serial number and refuses to run if it is missing.
steps.say:
cd <repository folder>/mspm0l1306
cp -R /Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07/examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0L1306/driverlib/gpio_toggle_output .
../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh gpio_toggle_output/ticlang
PROBE=<serial> tools/ocd.sh "reset halt" "program gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out verify" "reset run"
steps.see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **`, and the RGB LED cycles.
steps.if: OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the next line is the real result.

steps.do: Ask for a different pattern: run the same command with `--pattern` and four times in milliseconds (on, off, on, pause).
steps.see: The run ends with `OK:` and says LED2 red (PA26) repeats the pattern you asked for.
steps.if: If the check fails, read the line it prints; the check decides the result, not the LED you see.

variants.expect: The board's RGB LED blinks after a flash that takes about a second, and the one-command run ends with an OK line. Whole run 13 to 14 s with the tools installed.
shows: TI's gpio_toggle_output example builds and flashes on the LP-MSPM0L1306 from one command, with no CCStudio window and no AI step.
The check reads the LED pin through the debugger and passes the pattern you asked for.
not_shows: That an AI assistant can drive this route: no AI step was timed on this board for this route.
A person's first-hour time: the 13 to 14 s is a scripted run with the tools already installed.

steps.do: Copy TI's example out of the SDK and build it, from the `mspm0c1104` folder of this repository. The build took 3.5 s.
steps.see: A build with no errors that leaves `gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out`.
steps.if: On an LP-MSPM0C1104 board older than version E3 the LED does not blink: the red LED moved from PA4 to PA22, and TI's example toggles PA22. Check the version printed on the board (and that jumper J7 is on).

steps.do: Flash it with OpenOCD. Replace `<serial>` with your probe's (0.64 s at a 2.5 MHz adapter speed).
steps.say: openocd -f interface/xds110.cfg -c "adapter serial <serial>" -f target/ti_mspm0.cfg -c init -c "reset halt" -c "program gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out verify" -c "reset run" -c shutdown
steps.see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **`, and the red LED blinks.
steps.if: OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the next line is the real result.

steps.do: Change the delay in `gpio_toggle_output.c`, then rebuild and flash again with the two commands above. The run changed the delay constant from 12,000,000 to 3,000,000.
steps.see: The blink rate changes. On the C1104 the proof was reading the LED pin: the toggle period went from 496 ms to 124 ms. A person did not watch it.
steps.if: If the rate does not change, check the build finished with no errors before flashing; the old image keeps running.

prereqs: A Mac with at least 12 GB free. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9.

Free TI downloads with a free myTI login: CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed) and the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), both the current versions on ti.com on 2026-10-08. The links are in steps 2 and 3.
Claude Code with a Claude subscription, for steps 6, 8 and 9. The blink itself needs no AI; TI's example blinks as shipped.

steps.do: Check you have at least 12 GB free (Apple menu, System Settings, General, Storage). Make a free myTI account on ti.com if you do not have one. Delete each installer file once it has finished installing.
steps.see: At least 12 GB free. CCStudio and the SDK take 10.3 GB once installed.
steps.if: If the Mac runs short during the CCStudio install, the installer file is probably still on disk; delete it.

steps.do: Download CCStudio 21.0.1 for macOS from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB) and install it. It goes to `/Applications/ti/ccs2101`. Open it once when the installer finishes, then delete the installer file.
steps.see: CCStudio opens to its start page. About 19 minutes in all on the test Mac, 7 of them your time.
steps.if: If TI shows a short export approval form before the download, fill it in (about a minute). If CCStudio quits without a window on first launch, open it yourself from Applications.

steps.do: Open [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed) and download the macOS file, `mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07.app.zip` (0.4 GB). On that page it is the macOS `.app.zip` entry for version 2.11.00.07.
steps.see: The zip lands in your downloads folder after about 3 minutes.
steps.if: If nothing seems to download, look in your browser's downloads. The SDK downloads in the browser, not inside CCStudio.

steps.do: Unzip the file, open the installer and click through it. It installs to `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` (2.2 GB). Then delete the zip and the installer.
steps.see: The folder `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` exists. 1 minute of clicks and 2 min 48 s of waiting on the test Mac.
steps.if: If CCStudio lists no SDK afterwards, quit CCStudio and open it again.

steps.do: Choose Help, Get Started with AI. Set Agent to Claude Code and tick Enable. Provider: Anthropic. Scope: pick Workspace. Leave Auth Token and Base URL blank, tick "Enable CCStudio IDE ecosystem MCP servers for Claude Code", click Apply, and log in to Claude in the chat panel if it asks. compilers.text: Where a TI MSPM0 SDK example ships a gcc makefile, GCC builds it as well as TI Arm Clang does. All 224 no-RTOS DriverLib examples that ship one built unchanged for the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0L1306, and 87 of 87 ran on the L1306 with no fault. GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK ran through three small wrapper scripts named `arm-none-eabi-*`; TI names Arm GNU 9-2019-q4. GCC code was a median 15 percent larger. Copy the SDK's example folder somewhere first, go into its `gcc` folder, and put the folder of a GCC install (the one that holds `bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc`) in place of `<GCC folder>`. Details: `portability/toolchains/gcc-mspm0/README.md`.

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free: [MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/ARM-CGT-CLANG), [SysConfig 1.26.3](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), [xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7). steps.do: Plug the board into the Mac with a data cable. The board shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. steps.do: From the root of this repository, run the line for your board with your probe's serial number. It backs the board up, copies TI's example (examples/nortos/<board>/driverlib/gpio_toggle_output), builds it, flashes it and checks the LED. steps.see: The run ends with a line that starts `OK:` and the LED on the board blinks. LED checked: LP-MSPM0G3519: LED2 red (PB26); LP-MSPM0C1104: LED1 red (PA22).
steps.if: If it stops with FRL-E002, several probes are plugged in: name yours with `--probe`. On the LP-MSPM0C1104, jumper J7 must be on or the red LED stays dark, and the route never mass-erases that chip.

steps.do: Ask for a different pattern: run the same command with `--pattern` and four or more times in milliseconds (on, off, on, pause).
steps.see: The run ends with `OK:` and says the LED repeats the pattern you asked for.
steps.if: If the check fails, read the line it prints; the check decides the result, not the LED you see.

compilers.text: Where a TI MSPM0 SDK example ships a gcc makefile, GCC builds it as well as TI Arm Clang does. All 224 no-RTOS DriverLib examples that ship one built unchanged for the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0L1306, and 87 of 87 ran on the L1306 with no fault. GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK ran through three small wrapper scripts named `arm-none-eabi-*`; TI names Arm GNU 9-2019-q4. GCC code was a median 15 percent larger. Copy the SDK's example folder somewhere first, go into its `gcc` folder, and put the folder of a GCC install (the one that holds `bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc`) in place of `<GCC folder>`. Details: `portability/toolchains/gcc-mspm0/README.md`.

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free. Get CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login). It brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. Get the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). Get SysConfig 1.26.3 ([TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed). Get xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon). Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. The helper scripts `sdkmake.sh` and `tools/ocd.sh` are in it. This repo's scripts point at SysConfig 1.26.3. It came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer on the test Mac and sits in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`. CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1. This repo's scripts do not point at it.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1.

steps.do: Leave the jumpers as the board shipped: J16 and J17 on the XDS side, the right-hand position, which carries the chip's UART to the USB cable. Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. Find the probe's serial number: the port names are `/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1` and `...4`.
steps.see: Two ports. The one ending in 1 is the chip's UART0 at 115200 8N1; the one ending in 4 is not used here. With probe serial <probe serial>, the port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1`. Or read the serial with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.
steps.if: If no ports appear, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same. If you moved J16 and J17 to BP for a loop-back test, move them back to XDS or the serial window stays silent.

steps.do: Copy TI's console example out of the SDK, from the `mspm0l1306` folder of this repository, and build it.
steps.see: A build with no errors that leaves `uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma/ticlang/uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma.out`.
steps.if: If the make line cannot find SysConfig or the compiler, the paths in step 1's `sdkmake.sh` do not match your install.

steps.do: Flash it with OpenOCD. `tools/ocd.sh` picks the probe by serial number and refuses to run if it is missing; set `PROBE` to your serial first (`<probe serial>` below stands for it). To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`. Run it from the same folder as the build step.
steps.say:
export PROBE=<probe serial>
tools/ocd.sh "reset halt" "program uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma/ticlang/uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma.out verify" "reset run"
steps.see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **` after about 2 s. In the sweep this example flashed in 2.3 s.
steps.if: OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the line after it is the real result.

steps.do: Open the chip's serial port. To leave `screen`, press Ctrl-A then K. This step is assembled, not recorded: the sweep read the port with a script, and this example's port was read by a script, not opened in `screen`.
steps.see: The line `==== MSPM0 Console Test ====` appears on your Mac, sent by the chip. TI's README says the example writes to the console once a second.
steps.if: If the window stays empty, check the port ends in 1 and the baud is 115200.

variants.expect: A line of text from the chip appears in a terminal window on your Mac every time the example sends it, at 115200 baud, with no extra wires.
shows: The LP-MSPM0L1306 sends text to a terminal on the Mac over the board's own USB cable, using TI's unmodified example.
The same example printed readable text on the LP-MSPM0G3507 in the example sweep.
not_shows: That text typed on the Mac reaches the chip: this example only transmits. The one-wire loop-back tests check both directions and are separate demos. They use J4 pin 34 to pin 33 on the G3507 and J1 pin 4 to pin 3 on the L1306.
That `screen` shows the text as the sweep script did: the sweep read the port with a script, and `screen` is the method this repository's LVGL demo uses. The two were not compared with this example.
A speed or reliability figure: the loop-back demos give those: every byte right from 9.6 kbaud to 4.5 Mbaud.
limits: The route is written for the LP-MSPM0L1306. The G3507 has its own flash command and probe file, and was not run by hand in this form.
TI's example needs the board's shipped jumper settings; the loop-back tests move J16 and J17 and the serial window goes silent until they are put back.

easy.for: Set the computer up once. The guided script finds the board, backs it up, builds TI's example, flashes it and checks the result through the debugger. No prebuilt image: it builds in a few seconds.

compilers.text: Where a TI MSPM0 SDK example ships a gcc makefile, GCC builds it as well as TI Arm Clang does. All 224 no-RTOS DriverLib examples that ship one built unchanged for the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0L1306, and 87 of 87 ran on the L1306 with no fault. GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK ran through three small wrapper scripts named `arm-none-eabi-*`; TI names Arm GNU 9-2019-q4. GCC code was a median 15 percent larger. Copy the SDK's example folder somewhere first, go into its `gcc` folder, and put the folder of a GCC install (the one that holds `bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc`) in place of `<GCC folder>`. Details: `portability/toolchains/gcc-mspm0/README.md`.

prereqs: A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.26.3 and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0. The same tools as the Print a message page; install them there first. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
The code is in this repository. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Run every command from that folder.

steps.do: Leave the jumpers as the board shipped: J16 and J17 on the XDS side. Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. Find the probe's serial number and the port name.
steps.see: Two ports. The one ending in 1 is the chip's serial port at 115200 baud. `frl.py detect` lists the probe serial; use it as `<probe serial>` below.
steps.if: If no ports appear, try another cable. A charge-only cable looks the same.

steps.do: Build the app for the L1306. It reads ADC channel 9 (PA15, the thermistor) every second against the chip's 2.5 V reference.
steps.see: A clean build in about 3 s that leaves `portability/three-ways/driverlib/build-l1306/three_ways.out` and prints its size (2,320 bytes of flash).
steps.if: If SysConfig or the compiler is not found, the install paths at the top of `portability/three-ways/driverlib/build.sh` do not match your install.

steps.do: Flash it with OpenOCD. `ocd.sh` picks the probe by serial number and refuses to run without one. Back up whatever is on the board first; this overwrites main flash.
steps.say:
export PROBE=<probe serial>
mspm0l1306/tools/ocd.sh "reset halt" "program portability/three-ways/driverlib/build-l1306/three_ways.out verify" "reset run"
steps.see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **`. The red LED1 changes state once a second.
steps.if: OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal and the line after it is the real result.

steps.do: Record 12 seconds of the board's serial port and check the lines. Replace the port with yours (the one ending in 1).
steps.see: About 12 lines like `t=5 adc=2645 avg=2645`, one a second, then `PASS`. Expect roughly 2,600 to 2,700 counts at room temperature.
steps.if: If no lines appear, check the port ends in 1 and that J16 and J17 are still on the XDS side. If the checker prints FAIL, it names the first check that failed (t not counting up, avg wrong, gaps off one second).

variants.expect: One line a second on your Mac with the thermistor's raw reading near 2,645 counts at room temperature.
shows: The L1306's onboard thermistor can be read by a small DriverLib program and printed once a second over the board's own USB cable.
In TI's out-of-box demo the same thermistor read 22.8 °C.
not_shows: A temperature in degrees: this app prints raw ADC counts. The 22.8 °C figure came from TI's demo, not from this app.
That the chip's own temperature sensor works: it read -165 °C on this chip with the factory trim (suspected wrong trim).
That warming the thermistor changes the counts: no recorded run does this.
limits: The counts are against the 2.5 V internal reference with a 3.3 V supply assumed; the supply was not measured in this run.
One board was run. No reference thermometer was used, so the counts are not an accuracy test.
The ADC sample window in this app is 125 µs. TI's faster 8-cycle window reads the thermistor 1.7% low.

evidence.text: 2026-10-06: after two fixes (a 10 microsecond chip-select gap and software I2C for the touch chip) the screen filled with color, showed bars, and drew a dot under the finger on each touch. A person at the board saw this. It was not recorded.
Screen ID read back over MISO as 0x7796 (ST7796S); touch chip read as vendor 0x11, chip 0x64 (FT6336U), firmware 0x12 (observed, not saved).

prereqs: A Mac with the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, which comes inside CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login), and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB). Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only; Apple Silicon was not tested. The SysConfig output the program is built from is in the repository (`gen/`). You only need SysConfig 1.26.3 (0.96 GB installed) if you change pins.

OpenOCD needs a connection file for the board. The repository has one, `ports/bitnetmcu/openocd-mspm0.cfg`: the same three lines as Zephyr's `boards/ti/lp_mspm0g3507/support/openocd.cfg`, so Zephyr is not needed.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Take the board folder alone with the sparse-checkout line in its README, or clone the whole repository.

Your LaunchPad kit's debug probe serial number: the text after `usbmodem` in `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`, minus the last digit, or the `Serial Num:` line of `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.

wiring.alt: LP-MSPM0G3507 from above with 12 numbered wires to the Waveshare 3.5 inch touch display
wiring.note: The 40-pin edge is four 10-pin headers. Hold the board with the USB connector at the top: J1 (pins 1 to 10) and J3 (21 to 30) are the two left rows, J4 (31 to 40) and J2 (11 to 20) the two right rows. Pin 1 of J1 and pin 21 of J3 are the top pins of the left rows, nearest the USB connector; J4 and J2 count the other way, so pin 40 and pin 20 are at the top. A diagram drawn on TI's board drawing, checked against the SysConfig pin output this demo is built with (`mspm0g3507/display-test/gen/ti_msp_dl_config.h`). Signal and supply are both 3.3 V: the module's level translator takes the LaunchPad kit's 3V3, and nothing is driven at 5 V. No jumper on the LaunchPad moves.
pins: touch interrupt. The program reads it once at start for a diagnostic value and finds touches by polling the touch chip, so the demo does not need it. Wired in the tested setup.
screen read-back; only to diagnose a dark screen
the module's own 3V3 pin, which stays empty, and its SD card select

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free. Get CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login). It brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. Get the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). Then get xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `...darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon) and unpack it in your home folder. Clone this repository into `<repository folder>`.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and the SDK folder `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` exists.
steps.if: If your tools live somewhere else, change the `SDK` and `CC` lines at the top of `build.sh` in step 3.

steps.do: With the LaunchPad unplugged, run the wires in the table above from the display to the header, power from the 3V3 pin only. Leave the display's own 3V3 and SD_CS pins empty. A 13th wire, MISO, is optional and only for reading the screen's status back.
steps.see: Every wire sits on the header row the picture shows; nothing is plugged into the display's 3V3 or SD_CS.
steps.if: If you are not sure a wire is on the right pin, count from the header's pin 1, the corner nearest the USB connector at J1. Check it against the table before plugging in.

steps.do: From the repository folder, build every variant of the display test into `out/`. Replace `<repository folder>` with the folder you cloned.
steps.see: For each build, a line with the address of its `res` results struct and the program size. The demo, `out/display_8mhz/display_8mhz.out`, is 7,592 bytes of flash and 648 bytes of RAM.
steps.if: If the compiler or SDK is not found, change the `SDK` and `CC` lines at the top of `build.sh`.

steps.do: Flash the 8 MHz demo with OpenOCD. Replace `<probe serial>` with your probe's serial number (read it with `xdsdfu -e`), and `<repository folder>` with your clone. The first command sets `OCD` to the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into.
steps.say:
export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
openocd -s "$OCD/openocd/scripts" -f <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/openocd-mspm0.cfg -c "adapter serial <probe serial>" -c init -c "reset halt" -c "program out/display_8mhz/display_8mhz.out verify" -c "reset run" -c shutdown
steps.see: OpenOCD finishes with the program verified, and the screen starts the demo: it fills red, green, blue, white and black, then draws eight color bars.
steps.if: If OpenOCD reports a CRC mismatch after the program step, see [the OpenOCD CRC mismatch entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#openocd-reports-a-crc-mismatch-after-program-file-verify-but). If the screen stays dark or shows static with every wire right, see [the screen stays dark entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#the-screen-stays-dark-or-shows-static-even-though-every-wire). The chip-select gap or a wire is the usual cause, and LCD_BL on J4 pin 38 is the first wire to check.

steps.do: Touch the screen with a finger and drag it around.
steps.see: A white dot is painted wherever you touch, and the board's red LED toggles on each touch.
steps.if: If nothing follows the finger, touch is not answering: [the touch chip at address 0x38 entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#the-touch-chip-does-not-answer-on-i2c1-at-address-0x38-is-it) has the two checks (software I2C pins, TP_RST).

variants.expect: The screen shows red, green, blue, white and black fills, then eight color bars. Then it paints a white dot under your finger and toggles the red LED on every touch. The whole program is 7.4 kB of flash and 648 bytes of RAM.
shows: A TI LaunchPad kit with 32 kB of RAM drives a 320 x 480 SPI touch screen with 11 jumper wires (12 with the optional touch INT wire) and a small program from this repository. The screen's ID reads back as the ST7796S and the touch chip as the FT6336U.

A full-screen fill of 307,200 bytes takes 364.9 ms at 8 MHz SPI, 182.5 ms at 16 MHz, and 67.2 ms at 40 MHz SPI. The CPU runs at 80 MHz and frames are 16-bit. At every speed 64 pixels of one row were read back and matched.
TI's MSPM0 SDK has no example for this screen or any TFT, so the driver is this repository's own.
not_shows: That the screen is right everywhere. At each speed only 64 pixels of one row were read back. The colors were not checked by eye at 16 MHz or faster.

That 40 MHz SPI is safe in general. The chip's data sheet rates these standard-drive pins to 16 Mbit/s and the panel's allows about 15 MHz. It worked here on short wires; the margin may not hold elsewhere.
The fills, bars and touch dots were seen by a person at the board and not recorded, so no photo or video of this exact program exists in the repository.
A graphics library. LVGL runs on the same wiring, at 7 refreshes a second at 32 MHz and 15 to 19 at 80 MHz, using 25.1 kB of RAM. That is a different program, and its screen was not checked by eye.
limits: Chip select needs a 10 microsecond pause after it goes high between commands. Without it the screen drops the second of two back-to-back commands and never turns on. The program has the pause (`cs_gap()` in `display_test.c`); a rewritten driver must keep it.
The touch chip answered only to software I2C on the same two pins. It did not answer to the chip's I2C block, so the program uses software I2C.
One 320 x 480 frame at 16 bits is 300 kB, 9.4 times the chip's RAM, so drawing goes in strips and stored pictures are cut to 75 kB.
The speed results need the separate `perf` builds and a RAM dump through OpenOCD. The README's read command was assembled from the flash command and not re-run, so this build leaves it out.

technical.v: ST7796S over SPI1 (3-wire, 8 MHz in the demo) and FT6336U touch, software I2C at about 100 kHz, on a Waveshare module with a TXS0108E level translator
364.9 ms at 8 MHz SPI; 182.5 ms at 16 MHz; 168.1 ms with 16-bit frames and DMA at 16 MHz; 134.4 ms at 20 MHz and 67.2 ms at 40 MHz SPI with the CPU at 80 MHz; 84 to 92% of what the SPI clock allows
64 of 64 pixels of one row matched at every speed; no other pixels were checked
7,592 bytes of flash (7.4 kB) and 648 bytes of RAM, from tiarmsize on display_8mhz.out
370 ms from power-up to screen ready with the usual init waits; 12 ms with the shortest waits the data sheet allows
Intel Mac, macOS 15.7; MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07; SysConfig 1.26.3; TI Arm Clang 5.1.1; xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0; 2026-10-06

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free. Get CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login). It brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS. Get the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). Get UniFlash 9.6.0 from [TI's UniFlash page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/UNIFLASH) (0.3 GB download, 1.9 GB installed). Get xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon), as the macOS x64 archive, and unpack it in your home folder. The generated pin and clock setup the build needs is already in the repository, so SysConfig is not needed for this page.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and the folders `mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` and `uniflash_9.6.0` are under `/Applications/ti`.
steps.if: `build.sh` has the SDK and compiler paths written in its first lines (`SDK=` and `CC=`); edit them if yours live elsewhere.

steps.do: Plug the LaunchPad in with a micro-USB data cable and read its XDS110 serial number. No wiring is needed.
steps.see: `Serial Num:` followed by your probe's serial number .
steps.if: If nothing is listed, the cable is charge-only; swap it. With several boards plugged in, unplug the others.

steps.do: Put your serial number where the bench board's is written. Two tracked files name <probe serial>. The probe check in `sdk-common/flash.sh` refuses to run unless that probe is on the USB bus. The two `Value=` lines of the connection file `sdk-common/MSPM0G3507_<probe serial>.ccxml` select the probe by serial number. Replace `YOURSERIAL` in both commands with the number from step 2 (`<probe serial>` below is the bench board's, the text the commands search for). Do not rename the file: `flash.sh` opens it by that name.
steps.see: `grep -n YOURSERIAL` on those two files shows the changed lines, with your real number in place of the word. The filename `MSPM0G3507_<probe serial>.ccxml` is unchanged.
steps.if: If you skip this the flash stops at `Probe <probe serial> missing`; that is the check working. The error text keeps the old number (`Probe <probe serial> missing`) even after the change, so compare the probe your message should name with step 2.
steps.say:
sed -i '' 's/Serial Num: \*<probe serial>/Serial Num: *YOURSERIAL/' mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/flash.sh
sed -i '' 's/Value="<probe serial>"/Value="YOURSERIAL"/g' mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/MSPM0G3507_<probe serial>.ccxml

steps.do: Build the program that runs all four models on the board's 20 stored test windows, with the models compiled at -O3. The program is compiled by TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 at -O2. The model code is the prebuilt archives, built earlier by TI Arm Clang 4.0.4.LTS. It runs at 80 MHz, using the pin and clock setup of TI's `sysctl_mclk_syspll` example.
steps.see: The last lines are the linker map's FLASH and SRAM rows: 0x1dbb0 bytes of flash used, which is 121,776 or 119 kB, and 0x334c of RAM, which is 13,132 bytes. `build-O3/occupancy.out` exists. Use `Os` instead of `O3` to link the smaller, slower -Os libraries, at 97,624 bytes of flash.
steps.if: If a path is wrong the script stops at the first compiler call and names the missing file. The SDK's own makefiles point at folders that do not exist, which this script avoids by not using them.

steps.do: Flash the image and let it run. UniFlash's default erase for this chip is "Erase MAIN memory only", so the board's boot configuration area is not touched.
steps.see: UniFlash loads and then verifies: `Program verification successful for` the `occupancy.out` path. The program starts running.
steps.if: If the script stops at `Probe ... missing`, the serial number in step 3 does not match a probe on the USB bus; compare it with the step 2 output.

steps.do: Wait for the whole run, then read the results table the program leaves in RAM. It is 35 words at `0x202020bc`, the symbol `occ` in `build-O3/occupancy.map`. The read script halts the core after the wait; connecting OpenOCD restarts the program, so the wait must cover the whole run. `OCD` is the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into; `OCD_CFG` is the tracked connection file the digit build uses for this same board; `PROBE` is your serial. This command line is assembled from the saved run's scripts. It was not copied from a log; see the recovery line.
steps.see: Three or four lines starting `0x202020bc:` followed by a list of 35 numbers, the first being 213909505, which is 0x0CC00001: the program finished.
steps.if: If the first number is not 213909505 the program had not finished, or OpenOCD restarted it: raise the wait. A short wait caught the restarted run in its first milliseconds on this bench. The 30,000-weight model at -Os needs about 30 s, and reads with 45 and 70 s waits worked. The default connection file in `ocd.sh` is the one in the Zephyr project folder, and the saved run used it. `ports/bitnetmcu/openocd-mspm0.cfg` has the same three lines. That pairing with this read script was not run as written here.
steps.say:
export PROBE=YOURSERIAL
export OCD=$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7
export OCD_CFG=$PWD/ports/bitnetmcu/openocd-mspm0.cfg
python3 mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/readwords.py 0x202020bc 35 70000

steps.do: Read the numbers. There are three header words: done flag, clock in Hz, and timer read cost in cycles. Each model then has eight words, in the order of the 636, 1,748, 8,484 and 32,836-weight models. They are mismatches and windows with the right class. Then come the smallest and largest of the best-of-5 cycle counts, for the network alone, for the float-to-int8 input step, and for both together. Divide the cycles of the last pair by 80,000,000 for seconds.
steps.see: Header `213909505, 80000000, 8`. Every model reads `0, 20`: no mismatches, 20 of 20. The fastest complete answer, input step plus network, is 320,386 cycles or 4.00 ms, 723,842 or 9.05 ms, 2,821,806 or {{row:mspm0g5187/ai_occ_latency/occ_cnn_8k-c-o3|.2f}} ms, and 10,352,016 cycles or 129.40 ms. The input step alone is about 100,000 cycles, or 1.25 ms, for every model.
steps.if: If a model's first number is not 0 or the second is below 20, an answer differed from the stored one. Reflash, and check you built the same library flavour you are reading. The -Os build is slower: 4.68, 10.87, 39.94 and 199.45 ms.

variants.expect: All four models answer 20 of 20 stored test windows correctly on the board, in 4.00 ms for 636 weights to 129.40 ms for 32,836 weights per answer at -O3 and 80 MHz.
shows: A room-occupancy network runs on a Cortex-M0+ with no FPU and no AI hardware, as plain C, and gives the same class and the same four output values as the quantized model run in onnxruntime. This holds on all 20 stored windows.
Answer time grows with model size: 11,328 to 610,560 multiply-adds took 4.00 to 129.40 ms, about 16 to 20 cycles per multiply-add for the network alone at -O3.
All four models, with their stored test windows, fit one 121,776-byte image in 128 kB of flash and 13,132 bytes of RAM.
not_shows: Anything about live sensing. The windows are stored in the image; no light, sound, CO2 or motion sensor is read.

That the model is accurate in your room. The models score 85.4 to 90.9% on a held-out part of one room's four days of data. Balanced accuracy is 60.5 to 74.7%. They tell empty from occupied on 98.6 to 100% of windows but struggle to tell 2 people from 3. With whole days held out, the 8,484-weight model scored 87.7% overall but 40.2% balanced: 159 of 170 three-person windows came out as empty.
That bigger is better: the 8,484-weight model beat the 32,836-weight one on accuracy.
Stack use, or current. Neither was measured for these programs.
limits: No build steps are given here: Build steps for these models are not published, so the page lists the results only. The numbers come from runs on the boards named in the grid.
The timings are the fastest of five runs on the best of 20 windows, the table's min. They come from one board and one run of the program.
Quantizing the float input costs about 100,000 cycles (1.25 ms) every time, which is 30% of the smallest model's total; feeding int8 directly saves it.
TI's own Neural Network Compiler produced code 6 to 14% slower than this plain C at -Os on the three smaller models and 20% faster on the largest. This page does not run it.
This G3507 has no neural-network accelerator; the TinyEngine accelerator is on the MSPM0G5187.
Checked on an Intel Mac only.

technical.v: 636, 1,748, 8,484 and 32,836 weights and biases (after batch norm is folded in); 11,328, 33,856, 157,824 and 610,560 multiply-adds; int8 weights and activations, int32 accumulators; trained on UCI Room Occupancy Estimation (id 864, CC BY 4.0)
88.4%, 88.5%, 90.9%, 85.4%; empty versus occupied 100.0%, 99.8%, 100.0%, 98.6%; the C code matches the quantized ONNX model exactly on all 1,001 test windows

technical.k: Cycles per answer at -O3, input step plus network (fastest)
technical.v: 320,386; 723,842; 2,821,806; 10,352,016 at 80 MHz (clock read back as 80.85 to 80.90 MHz against the Mac's clock, 1.1% high from OpenOCD latency)

wiring.alt: LP-MSPM0G3507 from above with 12 numbered wires to the Waveshare 3.5 inch touch display
wiring.note: The 40-pin edge is four 10-pin headers. Hold the board with the USB connector at the top: J1 (pins 1 to 10) and J3 (21 to 30) are the two left rows, J4 (31 to 40) and J2 (11 to 20) the two right rows. Pin 1 of J1 and pin 21 of J3 are the top pins of the left rows, nearest the USB connector; J4 and J2 count the other way, so pin 40 and pin 20 are at the top. A diagram drawn on TI's board drawing, checked against the SysConfig pin output the demo is built with (`mspm0g3507/display-test/gen80/ti_msp_dl_config.h`). Signal and supply are both 3.3 V: the module's level translator takes the LaunchPad kit's 3V3, and nothing is driven at 5 V. No jumper on the LaunchPad moves.
pins: touch interrupt. The program reads it once at start for a diagnostic value and finds touches by polling the touch chip, so the demo does not need it. Wired in the tested setup.
screen read-back; only to diagnose a dark screen
the module's own 3V3 pin, which stays empty, and its SD card select

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free. CCStudio 21.0.1 comes from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login); it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. The MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 comes from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 comes from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon); get the macOS x64 archive and unpack it in your home folder. The OpenOCD connection file is in this repository, so nothing else is needed. Checked on an Intel Mac; on Apple Silicon CCStudio runs under Rosetta 2 by TI's own notes. Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. To fetch only the board folder, use the sparse-checkout line in its README. The model and upstream code are already in the tree under `third-party/bitnetmcu`: GPL-3.0, commit 0715bfc, unchanged.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `ls ports/bitnetmcu/touch` shows `digit_touch.c`, `build.sh`, `flash.sh`, `lcd_touch.h`, `prepare.h` and `font5x7.h`.
steps.if: If `third-party/bitnetmcu` is empty, the clone did not bring the third-party folder; it is part of this repository and is not a submodule, so re-clone. If your tools live somewhere else, step 4 and step 6 show how to point the scripts at them.

steps.do: With the LaunchPad unplugged, run the wires in the table above from the display to the header, power from the 3V3 pin only. Leave the display's own 3V3 and SD_CS pins empty. The 13th wire, MISO, is only for diagnosing a dark screen.
steps.see: Every wire sits on the header row the picture shows; nothing is plugged into the display's 3V3 or SD_CS.
steps.if: If you are not sure a wire is on the right pin, count from the header's pin 1 and check it against the table before plugging in. Pin 1 is the corner nearest the USB connector, J1.

steps.do: Tell the build where your SDK and compiler are, check them, and build. The two paths below are the installer defaults on this Mac; change them to where yours are. Keep the quotes: they let a path with spaces work. The build uses the tracked SysConfig output for an 80 MHz CPU and 20 MHz SPI.
steps.say:
# replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/touch
./build.sh --check
./build.sh
steps.see: `check OK: every tool and setting this script needs was found`, then two lines, FLASH and SRAM, then `built .../out/digit_touch.out`. On 2026-10-10 the image was 42.3 kB of flash and 5.0 kB of RAM. The linker map says 43,304 and 5,128 bytes, and 4 kB of that RAM is the stack setting.
steps.if: If the check prints `Not ready` it names each missing item and how to fix it; set `SDK` or `CC` to the folder it says and run it again. Downloads: [MSPM0 SDK](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [CCStudio](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO).

steps.do: Plug the LaunchPad in with a micro-USB data cable and list its serial ports. Your probe id is the text after `usbmodem` without the last digit: `usbmodemAB1234561` and `usbmodemAB1234564` are the two ports of probe `AB123456`. Flashing needs this id and will not guess it, so it can never flash a board that is not yours.
steps.see: Two `cu.usbmodem` lines per board, with the same text and last digits 1 and 4. The backlight may come on but the screen stays dark until step 5.
steps.if: If nothing appears, the cable is charge-only; swap it for a data cable. If several boards are plugged in, unplug the others, or run `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A6 XDS110` and read the `Serial Number` line of the board you mean.

steps.do: Flash and start it. Set `OCD` to the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into, the one that holds `bin/openocd`, and `PROBE` to your id from step 4; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. The check runs first and never opens the probe. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.
steps.say:
export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
export PROBE=<probe serial>
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/touch
./flash.sh --check
./flash.sh
steps.see: `check OK`, then `Verified OK` and `running: the screen should say DRAW A DIGIT`. The script retries up to three times, because on this board OpenOCD's verify fails on about every other load and passes on the next. **Unknown (suspected: Tool or docs).** The retry handles it.
steps.if: If `PROBE: not set` appears, step 4 shows how to read it. If all three tries fail with `Verify Failed`, see [the OpenOCD CRC mismatch entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#openocd-reports-a-crc-mismatch-after-program-file-verify-but); if it says no device, replug and check the probe id against `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`.

steps.do: Look at the screen.
steps.see: "DRAW A DIGIT", a black box and a red CLEAR button, in portrait.
steps.if: If the screen is dark or shows static with every wire right, see [the screen stays dark entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#the-screen-stays-dark-or-shows-static-even-though-every-wire): the chip-select gap or a wire is the usual cause. If the backlight is off, LCD_BL on J4 pin 38 is the first wire to check.

steps.do: Draw one digit, 0 to 9, inside the box with a finger, then lift the finger.
steps.see: About half a second after you lift, the answer and the time it took appear under the box. The inference takes 33 or 34 ms at 80 MHz.
steps.if: If nothing follows the finger, touch is not answering: [the touch chip at address 0x38 entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#the-touch-chip-does-not-answer-on-i2c1-at-address-0x38-is-it) has the two checks: the software I2C pins and TP_RST.

steps.do: Touch the box again or tap CLEAR to try another digit.
steps.see: The box clears and the next digit is read the same way. It reads one digit at a time: "10" came out as 6 and "12" as 4 in the video, because the model knows single digits only.
steps.if: If a digit is read wrong, draw it larger and centered; the drawing is scaled and centered like the MNIST training digits before it is read.

variants.expect: A digit drawn with a finger is answered on screen about half a second after you lift the finger. The inference time, 34 ms at 80 MHz, appears beside it. The demo waits half a second on purpose before it reads the drawing. The 560 ms from lift to answer is computed from the wait, the 25 ms of preparation and the inference. It was not measured end to end.
shows: The 64-wide BitNetMCU model runs on the LP-MSPM0G3507 and reads the ten digits that ship with it, 10 of 10, through the same drawing path a finger uses. The self-test does this at power-up. The author reports 99.55% on MNIST for this model.
Finger-drawn digits were read on camera: counted from the video, seven of the nine drawings were single digits and all seven were read right. No larger count exists.
One inference takes 2.71M cycles on the demo's path, 34 ms at 80 MHz; turning the drawing into the model's 16 x 16 input takes another 25 ms.
not_shows: How often it reads a stranger's handwriting right. The 10 stored digits are a port check and not an accuracy measurement. The only count of finger drawings is the seven in the video.
The 99.55% is the author's figure on the MNIST test set. It is not measured here, and it is not on finger input.

Pen-to-answer time. The demo waits half a second after the finger lifts, then spends 25 ms preparing and 34 ms inferring, so the answer appears about 560 ms after the lift. That figure is computed and was not measured end to end. The 34 ms is the model alone.
Letters or two-digit numbers: the model was trained on single digits.

That 20 MHz SPI is safe everywhere. The data sheet rates SPI1's standard-drive pins to 16 Mbit/s. The panel's allows about 15 MHz. The display test read back only 64 pixels of one row at 20 and 40 MHz. It worked here on 10 to 20 cm wires.
limits: Touch runs over software I2C on PB3 and PB2 because the chip's I2C block did not get an answer from the touch controller through the module. The translator is suspected and was not checked.
Chip select needs a 10 microsecond gap between commands or the screen drops the second one; the driver has it, a rewritten driver must keep it.

SPI runs at 20 MHz, over the 16 Mbit/s the data sheet gives these pins and the 15 MHz the panel allows. If you see wrong colors or noise, change the divider in `digit_touch.c` (`DL_SPI_setBitRateSerialClockDivider(LCD_SPI_INST, 1)`) from 1 to 2 for 13.3 MHz.

1,966,120 cycles, 25 ms at 80 MHz, in software floating point: the digit's larger side scaled to 20 of 28 pixels, center of mass centered, shrunk to 16 x 16, normalized like the training data
80 MHz CPU from the SysPLL (display80.syscfg), SPI1 at 20 MHz, 16-bit frames
TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -O3, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.26.3, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0

prereqs: A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1, the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0, installed in step 1. CCStudio brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, and its `tiarmnm` is the symbol tool the run script uses. Intel Mac, macOS 15.7 only. Python 3 reads the answers back. macOS offers it with the command line tools.

A LaunchPad, either the LP-MSPM0G3507 or, for steps 5 and 6, the LP-MSPM0L1306. You also need a micro-USB data cable and that board's XDS110 serial number. Step 3 shows where to read it. The run script refuses to start without it, on purpose.

The other boards use their own folders and tools: `ports/bitnetmcu/c2000/` with TI C2000 compiler 25.11.1, and `mspm0c1104/`. Each README has its commands. The CC1354P10 row is a stored result. The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

steps.do: Install the tools once, all free. CCStudio 21.0.1 comes from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login); it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. The MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 comes from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 comes from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon); get the macOS x64 archive and unpack it in your home folder. The OpenOCD connection file is in this repository, so nothing else is needed. Checked on an Intel Mac; on Apple Silicon CCStudio runs under Rosetta 2 by TI's own notes. Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. To fetch only the board folder, use the sparse-checkout line in its README.
steps.see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `ls ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0` shows `build.sh`, `run.sh` and `main.c`.
steps.if: If your copies live elsewhere, steps 2 to 6 set `SDK`, `CC` and `OCD` to your paths; each script prints what it could not find.

steps.do: Build the 64-wide model for the LP-MSPM0G3507 at 80 MHz. The two paths are the installer defaults on this Mac; change them to where yours are. Keep the quotes: they let a path with spaces work. The check runs first and builds nothing.
steps.say:
# replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
./build.sh --check g3507 80
./build.sh g3507 cnn_64 O3 80
steps.see: `check OK`, then the FLASH and SRAM lines of the linker map and a new `build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80` folder. The lines read 23.0 kB of flash and 3.3 kB of RAM.
steps.if: If the check prints `Not ready` it names each missing item and how to fix it. Downloads: [MSPM0 SDK](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [CCStudio](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO). Clock 80 exists for the G3507 only; the L1306 uses 32.

steps.do: Plug the LaunchPad in with a micro-USB data cable and list its serial ports. Your probe id is the text after `usbmodem` without the last digit: `usbmodemAB1234561` and `usbmodemAB1234564` are the two ports of probe `AB123456`. Flashing needs this id and will not guess it, so it can never flash a board that is not yours. No wiring is needed: the test digits are in the image.
steps.see: Two `cu.usbmodem` lines per board, with the same text and last digits 1 and 4.
steps.if: If nothing appears, the cable is charge-only; swap it for a data cable. If several boards are plugged in, unplug the others, or run `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A6 XDS110` and read the `Serial Number` line of the board you mean.

steps.do: Run it on the LP-MSPM0G3507. Set `OCD` to the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into, the one that holds `bin/openocd`, and `PROBE` to your id from step 3; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. The script flashes, fills RAM with a pattern, lets the board classify the ten digits for 20 seconds, then reads the answers, cycles and stack depth back over the debugger. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.
steps.say:
export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"   # run.sh finds its symbol tool, tiarmnm, inside this folder
export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
export PROBE=<probe serial>
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
./run.sh --check build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80
./run.sh build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80
steps.see: `check OK`, `magic 0xb17e0001 (done), clock 80000000 Hz, right 10 of 10`, `answers 3209069277`, `cycles 2748503 to 2754797 (mean 2,750,868; 34.39 ms)` and `stack: 3072 bytes reserved, deepest use 2288 bytes`.
steps.if: If `right` is under 10 or the magic says NOT DONE, the image did not run to the end: reflash, and check you built clock 80 for this board. `run.sh` already retries OpenOCD's verify three times; for the known verify failure see [the OpenOCD CRC mismatch entry](board-mspm0g3507.html#openocd-reports-a-crc-mismatch-after-program-file-verify-but). If it prints `PROBE: not set`, step 3 shows how to read it.

steps.do: Only with an LP-MSPM0L1306: build the same model for it at 32 MHz. `STACK=3600` reserves 3,600 bytes of the board's 4 kB of RAM for the stack, as the saved result did. The model's deepest use is 2.2 kB. The default 3,072 also links, so the number only sets the headroom shown in step 6.
steps.say:
# replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
./build.sh --check l1306 32
STACK=3600 ./build.sh l1306 cnn_64 O3 32
steps.see: `check OK`, then the FLASH and SRAM lines and a new `build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32` folder. The lines read 21.4 kB of flash and 3.6 kB of the board's 4 kB of RAM, which leaves 396 bytes.
steps.if: If the link fails with a stack or RAM error, the model is too big for 4 kB: use `cnn_64`, or a smaller model (`cnn_16small`, `12k`, `1k`). `STACK` is the stack size in bytes.

steps.do: Run it on the LP-MSPM0L1306. Use the id of this board, read as in step 3; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. Before OpenOCD starts the script asks TI's `xdsdfu` tool, which is inside CCStudio, whether that probe is plugged in; set `XDSDFU` to its path if yours is elsewhere. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.
steps.say:
export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"   # run.sh finds its symbol tool, tiarmnm, inside this folder
export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
export PROBE=<probe serial>
cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
./run.sh --check build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32
./run.sh build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32
steps.see: `check OK`, `magic 0xb17e0001 (done), clock 32000000 Hz, right 10 of 10`, `answers 3209069277`, `cycles 2646151 to 2653623 (mean 2,649,196; 82.79 ms)` and `stack: 3600 bytes reserved, deepest use 2288 bytes`.
steps.if: If it prints `Probe ... missing`, that id is not on the USB bus: replug, and compare with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`. If `right` is under 10 or the magic says NOT DONE, reflash and check you built clock 32 with `STACK=3600`. Otherwise the stack line reads 3072 bytes reserved.

variants.expect: `right 10 of 10` and the answers `3209069277`, the same ten the Mac gives from `host/host_main.c`.
shows: Every board that ran it gave the same ten answers as the Mac for the model it ran, and the board table says which model. So the port is correct.
Cycle counts per digit are comparable with the author's CH32V002 figure: fewer at 32 MHz on the MSPM0 boards, 0.5% more at 80 MHz with two flash wait states.
not_shows: Nothing about handwriting: no touch input, no finger. Passing ten stored vectors is a functional check of the port and is no accuracy estimate.
A passing stored run on a board does not mean the touch build works there; that needs the screen driver on that board.
limits: On the LP-MSPM0L1306 only the 64-wide model was run, with a 3,600-byte stack leaving 396 bytes of RAM; the SRAM-loop variant does not fit.
The author's cycle counts were not rerun on his chip; the comparison is chip plus compiler.

technical.v: G3507 2,640,383 at 32 MHz and 2,750,868 at 80 MHz; L1306 2,649,196 at 32 MHz; CC1354P10 about 1.13M at 48 MHz; F2800137 2,551,750 from RAM and 2,897,585 from flash at 120 MHz; author's CH32V002 2,736,250
2,288 bytes deepest use on the MSPM0 boards (RAM painted before the run)
64-wide CNN 11.0 kB (99.55%), 16-wide 3.2 kB (98.92%), 12k fully connected 12.3 kB (99.02%), 1k 1.1 kB (94.22%); accuracies are the author's on MNIST
`1L << shift` in ReLUNorm, signed test-data bytes, a 2-word alignment on one shared buffer; the arithmetic is unchanged

variants.total: $20.56 for the board (TI.com, read 2026-10-09); the USB cable extra if your box has none.
variants.why_board: Any of the five boards that ran it is enough for this check. These steps and the build script use the LP-MSPM0G3507: 32 kB of RAM against the model's 2,288 bytes of stack. The LP-MSPM0L1306 at the same price shows the model in 4 kB of RAM.

g3507.scope: the complete application: screen, touch, drawing, inference
g3507.basis: Ran on 2026-10-06 and 2026-10-07; the self-test read 10 of 10 and finger drawings were read on camera.

g3519.basis: Same MSPM0 DriverLib SPI and GPIO calls as the G3507, with 128 kB of RAM and 512 kB of flash against 32 kB and 128 kB. The thermostat screen under LVGL drives this panel from the LP-MSPM0G3519 (40 MHz SPI) with that project's own driver, so the module and chip work together. This demo's driver and pin names have not been built for it.
required: A SysConfig output for the G3519's pins, made by regenerating display80.syscfg for that chip, and the G3519 startup file in place of `startup_mspm0g350x_ticlang.c`
Point `GEN` at the new folder; keep the 10 microsecond chip-select gap and the software I2C pins when the pin names change

l1306.basis: As built, the image reserves 5,128 bytes of RAM, a 4 kB stack setting plus about 1 kB of static data, which is more than the chip's 4 kB. The model's deepest stack on the stored run was 2,288 bytes, so a smaller stack setting might fit. The touch demo's own stack depth has not been measured, and the L1306's pins differ.
required: A SysConfig output for the L1306's pins
A stack setting under about 2.9 kB, with the deepest use measured by painting RAM first

cc1354p10.basis: The model runs there in its stored variant, but the driver is MSPM0 DriverLib; the SimpleLink SDK has a different SPI and GPIO API. A pin map for this display on the LP-CC1354P10-1 exists on paper and has not been built.
required: Rewrite `lcd_touch.h` on TI Drivers SPI and GPIO
Wire by the research page's pin table and keep the 10 microsecond chip-select gap

f2800137.basis: The model runs there with 16-bit-char patches; nobody has looked at the screen driver on the C28x.

cc2340r5.basis: A paper pin map exists for this display on the LP-EM-CC2340R5; neither the model nor the driver has been built for it.

c1104.basis: 1 kB of RAM: the 1k model is the only one that ran there (804 B), and the touch demo as built reserves 5,128 bytes.
required: A different design: host-side drawing, or a far smaller grid and the 1k model

g3507.scope: all four models at 32 MHz; the 64-wide model also at 80 MHz
g3507.basis: 10 of 10 on every model at 32 MHz and on the 64-wide model at 80 MHz.

l1306.basis: 10 of 10 with a 3,600-byte stack.

cc1354p10.scope: the 64-wide model at 48 MHz, in that board's bench folder

f2800137.scope: the 64-wide model from RAM and from flash
f2800137.basis: 10 of 10, 2.55M cycles from RAM, after three source patches for the 16-bit char.

c1104.scope: the 1k model only; the 16-channel model overruns its stack and the 12k model does not link

prereqs: TI's SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0 (DSLite), all free from TI with a myTI login. Checked on an Intel MacBook, macOS 15.7.9.
Python 3 with the `bleak` Bluetooth library: `python3 -m pip install bleak`.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add cc2340r5 cc2755p10 tools`. Below, `<repository folder>` is that clone.

steps.do: Clip the LP-EM-CC2340R5 onto the LP-XDS110ET probe and plug the probe into the Mac with a USB data cable.
steps.see: The Mac lists the probe, and two serial ports appear.
steps.if: If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

steps.do: Copy TI's data_stream example out of the SDK into a working folder and build it with TI Arm Clang. Run it in the example's `freertos/ticlang` folder.
steps.see: The build ends without an error and leaves `data_stream.hex` in that folder.
steps.if: If make cannot find the SDK, SysConfig or the compiler, change the three paths to where yours are installed.

steps.do: Flash the image with DSLite, using the board's CC2340R5.ccxml from the `cc2340r5` folder of the repository. Replace `<home>` with your home folder. The write erases the whole chip first.
steps.see: DSLite prints that the flash finished. In the recorded run it connected and wrote on the first try.
steps.if: If it cannot connect, check that the probe is seated on the board and unplug and replug it. Do not use a mass erase to fix a connection error.

steps.do: Scan for ten seconds from the Mac.
steps.see: A line `Data Stream` with a signal strength in dBm. At 1 to 2 m the recorded runs read about -42 dBm.
steps.if: If the name is missing, press the board's reset button, run the scan again and keep the Mac close. The Mac shows only some of the advertisements, so a short scan can miss it.

steps.do: Connect to it and time the echo. The script writes 20, 64 and 128 bytes, 50 times each, and waits for the board to send the text back with its letter case flipped.
steps.see: `connected + services` in about 0.55 s, then a line per size. The recorded run on this board: 45 ms median for 20 bytes, 105 ms for 64, 135 ms for 128.
steps.if: If it prints `found None`, the scan did not see the board: repeat step 4 first. If bytes come back wrong, the script says so on the size's line.

variants.expect: The Mac sees a device called Data Stream, connects to it in about half a second, and gets 20 bytes echoed back in about 45 ms. The board sends back what the Mac wrote; it does not read a sensor.
shows: TI's own Bluetooth example builds from a terminal, flashes, and is found and connected to by a Mac with no pairing.
