evidence.text: First run 2026-10-05: Zephyr 4.4.2 blinky on an LP-MSPM0G3507, about 9.5 minutes from nothing installed; the blue LED was confirmed blinking by eye.
The script was then run from clean twice: 3 minutes 00 seconds and 3 minutes 06 seconds, exit code 0 both times.

prereqs: A Mac (Intel or Apple silicon) or a Linux machine. Tested on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 (flashed), an M4 Mac on macOS 26.3 (build only, 56 s) and Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 in a container (build only, 93 s). Linux x86_64 is pinned but was not run. Logs: `mspm0g3507/zephyr/logs/setup-*-20261018.txt`.

git, curl and tar (on a Mac: `xcode-select --install`). No Homebrew and no administrator password: if the machine has no Python 3.12 the script installs one into the tools folder with uv, and gets west, CMake and ninja with pip.
About 2 GB of free disk for Zephyr, its four modules, the compiler and OpenOCD.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Take the board folder alone with the sparse-checkout line in its README, or clone the whole repository. The script is `mspm0g3507/zephyr/setup-intel-mac.sh`.
Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 3; it holds the debug probe.

steps.do: Check that git, curl and tar are installed (on a Mac, `xcode-select --install` brings them; 1.8 GB installed). You do not install Python 3.12, ninja, west or CMake: the script fetches them (Python 3.12 through uv) with no administrator password and no Homebrew. It also gets Zephyr 4.4.2 from GitHub, the Arm compiler from Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB), each checked against a SHA-256, about 2 GB in all.
steps.see: `git --version`, `curl --version` and `tar --version` each print a version.
steps.if: If a download fails, rerun the script; it keeps what it already fetched. Apple silicon built the same way in a build-only run on an M4 Mac; it was not flashed.

steps.do: Plug the LP-MSPM0G3507 into the Mac with the micro-USB cable. Plug in exactly one board, or you must name the probe in step 3.
steps.see: The board's green power LED comes on. Its debug probe shows up as an XDS110 with USB id 0451:bef3.
steps.if: If step 3 later reports no debug probe, list the probes it can see as shown in step 3 and check the USB cable is a data cable.

steps.do: Run the script from the folder it lives in (replace `<repository folder>` with your clone). It builds a Python environment and gets Zephyr v4.4.2 and four modules: hal_ti, cmsis, cmsis_6 and picolibc. It downloads the compiler and OpenOCD and checks each against a SHA-256 checksum. It builds `samples/basic/blinky` for `lp_mspm0g3507`, checks the board is there, flashes it with `west flash`, then sends one board-level reset. If two boards are plugged in, set `PROBE_SERIAL` to the one you mean.
steps.say:
cd <repository folder>/mspm0g3507/zephyr
./setup.sh
# two boards plugged in? name the probe:
# PROBE_SERIAL=<your probe serial> ./setup.sh
steps.see: About 3 minutes later, 3:00 and 3:06 in two clean runs, the script prints three things. First a build memory report, FLASH 11,932 B of 128 KB, 9.10%. Then OpenOCD flash output ending `wrote 11932 bytes`. The last line is `The blue LED should now blink once a second.`
steps.if: If it says `Found 2 debug probes` or `Probe ... is not connected`, it built but did not flash (exit code 3): plug in exactly one board, or set PROBE_SERIAL. List probes with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` (CCStudio) or `system_profiler SPUSBDataType`, where the XDS110 is 0451:bef3.

steps.do: Look at the board's blue LED.
steps.see: The blue LED blinks once a second.
steps.if: If the LED stays dark, the chip is probably sitting in Zephyr's NMI handler after the debugger's soft reset. Press the board's reset button; the script's last command does the same thing with OpenOCD's `mspm0_board_reset`.

variants.expect: The blue LED on the LP-MSPM0G3507 blinks once a second, running Zephyr 4.4.2's unmodified blinky sample. It takes about 3 minutes from the start of the script to the blink on a Mac that already had python3.12, git and ninja. The first run, while the workarounds were still being found, took about 9.5 minutes.
shows: Zephyr 4.4.2's upstream blinky for `lp_mspm0g3507` builds and runs from the command line on an Intel Mac. It uses pip and prebuilt downloads instead of Homebrew and a source build of OpenOCD.
The image is small: 11,932 bytes of flash, 9.10% of 128 kB, and 3,976 bytes of RAM.
The install is repeatable: two clean runs from the script took 3 minutes 00 seconds and 3 minutes 06 seconds.
not_shows: That this is Zephyr's officially supported path. Zephyr 4.4.2 asks for Zephyr SDK 1.0.1, which has no Intel macOS build, so the script uses the Arm compiler from SDK 0.17.4 through `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile`. It works here, but it is not an officially supported pairing.
That it works on Apple Silicon, Windows or Linux, or with other Zephyr versions: only v4.4.2 was flashed and run, on macOS 15.7.9; the M4 Mac and the Linux container only built it.
Anything beyond blinking an LED: no serial console, sensor, radio or network sample was run in this build.
limits: After a debugger soft reset the chip sat in Zephyr's NMI handler and did not blink; the record does not say why. The script ends with a board-level reset that clears it, and the reset button does the same.
The script only checks python3.12, git and ninja by using them; if one is missing it stops with that tool's own error.

Two checks were made before flashing a board. Neither is in Zephyr's guide. The December 2025 fix for the "bricked LaunchPad" bug, Zephyr PR 102668, was confirmed present in the source, and the image was confirmed to contain main flash addresses only.

This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Take the board folder alone with the sparse-checkout line in its README, or clone the whole repository.

The board ships with TI's out-of-box demo. Save it first with `python3 tools/frl/frl.py backup --board mspm0l1306 --probe <serial>`, and put it back afterwards with `python3 tools/frl/frl.py restore "<backup folder>" --probe <serial>`.

steps.do: Find your board's debug probe serial number with TI's `xdsdfu` tool from CCStudio. The scripts talk to one probe only and refuse to run without it.
steps.see: A line `Serial Num: <your serial>` for the LaunchPad. Use it as PROBE in steps 4 to 6.
steps.if: If nothing is listed, replug the board with a data cable and run it again; close any serial window open on the board.

steps.do: Plug the LP-MSPM0L1306 into the Mac with the micro-USB cable. No wires and no jumpers move for this build.
steps.see: The board powers up and shows its out-of-box demo.
steps.if: If a script later says `Probe ... missing`, the serial number in step 1 does not match a connected board.

steps.do: Build the one-task blink. `build.sh` compiles the five kernel files from the SDK straight into the image and stops if any part falls outside main flash or the 4 kB of SRAM.
steps.see: `build-blink/sizes.txt` reads `FLASH used 3,784 bytes of 65,528` and `SRAM used 1,008 bytes of 4,096; 3,088 bytes left`. On a lightly loaded Mac each image takes under a minute.
steps.if: If the compiler is not found, change the `SDK` and `CC` lines at the top of `build.sh` to where your installers put them.

steps.do: Flash the blink, paint the chip's RAM with a pattern before any code runs, let it run 5 seconds, read the results, then decode and check them. Replace <serial> with your probe.
steps.say:
PROBE=<serial> ../tools/paintrun.sh build-blink/blink.out build-blink/blink.map fr_blink 6 5000
python3 check.py build-blink
steps.see: LED1 (red) is on half a second and off half a second. `check.py` prints `ok    magic 0xB1E00001`, `ok    ticks = 500 x (toggles - 1): the tick runs at 1,000 per second`, and `ALL OK`. The blink task never used 23 of its 48 stack words.
steps.if: If the flash step prints `flash failed` or `Probe ... missing`, check the serial from step 1. If OpenOCD says it cannot reset the target or find the MEM-AP, see the L1306 FAQ entry on that error (`mspm0l1306/FAQ.md`).

steps.do: Now see how many tasks fit. This image makes 11 minimal tasks with 192-byte stacks and all memory static, one checker task and the idle task.
steps.say:
./build.sh edge-static
PROBE=<serial> ../tools/paintrun.sh build-edge-static/edge-static.out build-edge-static/edge-static.map fr_edge 12 5000
python3 check.py build-edge-static
steps.see: `check.py` prints `made 11 alive 11`, `ok    every minimal task ran in the last second` and `ALL OK`.
steps.if: A twelfth task does not link. The linker stops with `program will not fit into available memory` (see `build-edge-static/search.txt`). That is the answer. It is not a fault.

steps.do: Optional: time what a task costs. This image times a task switch, a semaphore, a notification, a queue round trip and an interrupt waking a task, 1,000 samples each.
steps.say:
./build.sh bench
PROBE=<serial> ../tools/paintrun.sh build-bench/bench.out build-bench/bench.map fr_bench 43 3000
python3 check.py build-bench
steps.see: A table of cycle counts per test and `ALL OK`. A task switch round trip is 499 cycles best case at 32 MHz in this run, about 16 microseconds.
steps.if: If `check.py` does not print ALL OK, it names the check that failed; `magic 0xBE4C0001` means every test finished.

variants.expect: The red LED blinks from one FreeRTOS task using 1,008 bytes of RAM. With 11 minimal tasks the chip's 4,096 bytes of RAM are almost used: 3,956 bytes, with 140 left. Every task runs. A task switch round trip takes 397 to 499 cycles, which is 12 to 16 microseconds at 32 MHz.
shows: FreeRTOS fits and runs on the MSPM0L1306 with static allocation, using TI's own kernel V11.2.0 and Cortex-M0+ port files unchanged. The one-task blink takes 3,784 bytes of flash and 1,008 bytes of RAM.
11 minimal tasks fit with static allocation, and a twelfth does not link. With a heap the figure is 10, as predicted: the 11th task creation failed for lack of heap on the board.
TI's own FreeRTOS settings file for this board needs 5,540 bytes of zero-filled RAM plus the stack and does not link on a 4,096-byte chip.
not_shows: That a useful application fits. 11 tasks is 11 loops that sleep one tick; a real sensor-and-UART task set was not run.
Low-power behavior: tickless idle is off in these settings and sleep current was not measured.
That the timing numbers compare with other RTOS runs one-to-one. The Zephyr thread-yield figure of 431 to 491 cycles used a different timer and build.
Anything about TI's FreeRTOS example makefiles: they were not used. They link a kernel library from a CCStudio workspace, and the SDK's 48 FreeRTOS example makefiles fail from a terminal as shipped.
limits: Task stacks of 48 words come from a stack analysis: the worst case is 44 words for a task that sleeps. High-water marks on the board confirmed it. A task that calls deeper code needs more.
Part of the 256-byte interrupt stack is never given back. The Cortex-M0+ port does not reset the main stack pointer when the scheduler starts, so 100 to 132 bytes stay used.
The settings file changes TI's: static allocation only, 3 priority levels, 4-character task names, no software timers, no tickless idle.

TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS from CCStudio 21.0.1; xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7; Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9
32 MHz SYSOSC, 1,000 Hz tick; cycle counter is TIMG0 at the CPU clock
3,784 bytes of flash, 1,008 bytes of RAM (3,088 left)
11 tasks plus checker and idle; 3,956 bytes of RAM used, 140 left; 12 does not link
499 / 640 / 502.9 cycles best / worst / average with asserts and stack check on; 397 / 537 / 400.6 with them off (`bench-lean`); 1,000 samples
pend to the first line of the task woken by `vTaskNotifyGiveFromISR`: 583 / 724 / 585.7 cycles; by a semaphore from an ISR: 645 / 789 / 651.2
`.bss` of 0x15a4 (5,540 bytes) on 4,096 bytes of RAM: does not link

SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS, a 536 MB macOS installer. CCStudio 21.0.1, for TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 LTS. SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0. Install all of them in `/Applications/ti/`. CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1. This repo's scripts do not point at it.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. The SDK example is already copied into `cc2340r5/src/`, and the connection file is `cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml`.
Your probe's serial number. Get it from `xdsdfu -e`, in CCStudio's `ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/` folder. Put yours in the connection file.

steps.do: Clip the LP-XDS110ET onto the LP-EM-CC2340R5's 20-pin edge, set the TGT VDD jumper to XDS, and plug the probe into the Mac with its USB-C cable.
steps.see: The Mac sees the probe and two serial ports; no driver install was needed.
steps.if: If the next flash fails with `The target failed to see a correctly formatted SWD header` (error -615), unplug the USB cable, pull the probe off the board, press it back on firmly and plug in again. That cleared it here. The likely cause is the seating, but that is not proven.

steps.do: Build TI's example. Change the three paths if your installers put the tools somewhere else. The SDK's own build settings point at folders that do not exist, so pass the paths on the command line.
steps.see: About 22 seconds later, `empty.out` and `empty.hex` are in that folder.
steps.if: If the build cannot find a tool, one of the three paths is wrong.

steps.do: Use the connection file in `cc2340r5/` after putting your probe serial number in it. Do not write one by hand: a hand-written one left SWD off and the errors did not say so. If you need a new one, let CCStudio write it by importing the example, then take it from `targetConfigs/CC2340R5.ccxml` in the imported project.
steps.see: Four seconds later the file `targetConfigs/CC2340R5.ccxml` exists inside the imported project. Replace <any empty folder> with a new empty folder and <SDK> with the SDK folder.
steps.if: If flashing later says `Unable to access the DAP` or `invalid processor ID`, the file has SWD switched off: use CCStudio's file.

steps.do: From `cc2340r5/` flash the hex file and run it. Leave `-v` (verify) off: it reports one mismatch at 0x4E020750 in the boot configuration area and ends with a failure although the program was written and runs.
steps.see: About 7 seconds later the flash finishes. `-e` here is `--verbose`: it prints progress and does not erase.
steps.if: If two probes are plugged in, the tool does not say which it used: put the serial number of the one you mean in the connection file.

steps.do: Look at the board's red LED.
steps.see: The red LED (DIO14) is on for one second and off for one second.
steps.if: If it does not blink, a previous owner's program may still be running; flash again and check that step 4 finished without an error.

variants.expect: The red LED on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 blinks once every two seconds (one second on, one off), running TI's SDK example on its default RTOS, FreeRTOS. The empty FreeRTOS example leaves 23,548 bytes of the chip's 36,864 bytes of RAM free.
shows: On this chip TI's examples run on FreeRTOS by default; the example's folder is `freertos/` and it builds from a terminal with make.
The FreeRTOS example uses 12,022 bytes of flash and 13,316 bytes of RAM, about 6,300 bytes of flash and 3,200 bytes of RAM more than the same example with no RTOS.
not_shows: How many tasks fit, or any task timing: this build only blinks an LED. The task-count and task-switch measurements were made on the LP-MSPM0L1306, and none was made here.
That it works with the probe-less setup: the board needs the separate XDS110 probe.
Other systems than an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7.
limits: Verify (`-v`) reports a mismatch at 0x4E020750 on every image flashed on this board; the program area verified and the program ran each time.
The first run took about 9 minutes of machine time and 3 hands-on, nearly all of it a connection problem that cleared when the probe was reseated.

The 48 FreeRTOS example makefiles in the MSPM0 SDK, for all boards, link the kernel from a CCStudio workspace path that tiarmclang rejects. They fail from a terminal as shipped. steps.do: Install the Zephyr 4.4.2 workspace, the compiler and the `west` environment with the script that builds Zephyr's blinky; `NO_FLASH=1` stops it after the build so it does not touch a board.
steps.see: The script ends with `NO_FLASH set. Built, not flashed.`
steps.if: If a download fails, rerun the script; it keeps what it already fetched.

steps.do: Check out the Arduino core at the pinned commit and put Arduino's API library beside it. The last line is a six-line patch that makes `Serial` wait for room instead of dropping bytes at 9600 baud; skip it if you only run Blink.
steps.say:
git init <ArduinoCore-zephyr folder> && cd <ArduinoCore-zephyr folder> && git remote add origin https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/ArduinoCore-zephyr.git
git fetch --depth 1 origin af5b8610f9be6d7b962e2ba6dd8e6859697c44ff && git checkout FETCH_HEAD
mkdir -p zephyr/blobs && cp -R <repository folder>/third-party/arduino/ArduinoCore-API/api zephyr/blobs/ArduinoCore-API
git apply <repository folder>/portability/arduino/zephyr/serial-blocking-write.patch   # CC2340R5 only
steps.see: The core folder holds `zephyr/blobs/ArduinoCore-API/api`, and `git status` shows the patched file.
steps.if: If the build later cannot find Arduino's API headers, `zephyr/blobs/ArduinoCore-API/api` is missing.

steps.do: Build Blink. The script takes the variables the README lists (`AM` for the core, `ZP`, `TC` and `VENV` for the workspace) and stops with one line naming a missing path. Neither Zephyr tree nor the sketch is edited.
steps.see: About 80 s later the build folder holds `zephyr/zephyr.hex` and `zephyr/zephyr_crc32.hex`. Blink is about 32 kB of flash and 6.1 kB of RAM.
steps.if: If it stops naming a variable, set it: `AM` is the core folder of step 2.

steps.do: Clip the LP-XDS110ET onto the board and plug it into the Mac with its USB-C cable; the board has no USB port of its own (`cc2340r5/AGENTS.md`). Read the probe serial with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.
steps.see: The probe shows up as an XDS110 and `xdsdfu -e` prints its serial number.
steps.if: If `xdsdfu -e` lists nothing, check the clip-on connection and use a data cable.

steps.do: Back up first: read the main flash and the CCFG with DSLite before the first write; the exact backup and restore commands are in `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/README.md`, Flash and run. Then flash the `_crc32` image, which carries the boot checksums, and reset the board.
steps.see: DSLite writes and verifies the image, then the reset starts Blink. The green LED pin (DIO15) is the one Blink toggles; the check read its output register through the probe and saw bit 15 clear, then set. The LED itself was not watched.
steps.if: If the flash fails, close CCStudio or any other program that holds the probe, and rerun it.

steps.do: To see serial output, build AnalogReadSerial the same way (`build-cc2340r5.sh AnalogReadSerial`), flash it as in step 5, and open the probe's serial port at 9600 baud in any serial terminal.
steps.see: A line of a number per read: 10-bit values between about 295 and 400 on a floating A0. The first line may be garbled; ignore it.
steps.if: If bytes are dropped or the numbers run together, the Serial patch of step 2 is missing.

variants.expect: Arduino's own Blink sketch, unchanged, runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 through the Zephyr-based core, and AnalogReadSerial prints readings at 9600 baud on the probe's serial port.
shows: Arduino's two stock examples, Blink and AnalogReadSerial from `arduino/arduino-examples`, build byte-for-byte unchanged for this chip and run.
The port is one devicetree overlay of about 40 lines for the pin map, a CMake file that includes the `.ino` as it is, and an optional six-line Serial patch.
attachInterrupt, analogWrite, SPI and Wire also ran from short test sketches.
not_shows: That the LED blinked to the eye: the check read the pin's output register and the LED was not watched.
That ADC readings are accurate: the values come from a floating pin and show only that the call works.
That PlatformIO works: it was not run, so this page gives no PlatformIO steps.
That it works on Windows or Linux: only an Intel Mac was used.
limits: The core's `Serial` drops bytes at 9600 baud on this chip unless the six-line patch is applied.
The CC2340R5 board file maps the red PWM LED to a timer channel that does not reach the pin; see the board page.

steps.if: If the board stops in the NMI handler, pulse nRST again (`flash.sh` does it after the flash).

steps.do: Check that the Blink pin toggles.
steps.see: The checker prints PASS while PB27 toggles.
steps.if: If it prints FAIL while PB27 toggles, it read the output-enable bit right after its own reset, inside the 0.4 s start-up; read the bit over DSLite without a reset.

steps.do: To see serial output, build AnalogReadSerial the same way, flash it as in step 3, and open the probe's serial port at 9600 baud.
steps.see: A number per read: 10-bit values between about 72 and 400 on a floating A0 (PA25).
steps.if: If the port stays silent, pulse nRST: the G3519 image only starts after one (`flash.sh` does it after the flash).

variants.expect: Arduino's own Blink sketch, unchanged, toggles PB27 on the LP-MSPM0G3519 through the Zephyr-based core, and AnalogReadSerial prints readings at 9600 baud.
shows: Arduino's two stock examples build unchanged for the MSPM0G3519 and run.
With the MSPM0 I2C pull request applied to Zephyr main, Wire, SPI, analogWrite and attachInterrupt also ran from short test sketches.
not_shows: That the LED blinked to the eye: the check read the pin and the LED was not watched.
That ADC readings are accurate: the values come from a floating pin.
That PlatformIO works: it was not run, so this page gives no PlatformIO steps.
That it works on Zephyr 4.4.2: that release has no MSPM0 ADC or I2C driver.
limits: Zephyr sees 64 kB of the chip's 128 kB of RAM.

g3507.why: A minimal 73 kB build with no floating point links; it was not flashed, and the full build does not fit the 128 kB

cc2340r5.why: Prompt at 115200 baud; Pin, ADC, Pin.irq (10 of 10 edges), PWM, SPI and I2C calls run. 174.8 kB of flash, 29.9 kB of RAM

l1306.why: MicroPython's minimal build is 73.8 kB of flash against the chip's 64 kB (8.2 kB over); static RAM plus the stack would leave a 1.1 kB heap

f2800137.why: MicroPython assumes 8-bit bytes and an Arm or x86 host: 132 of 133 core files compile with cl2000 and stub headers, the scheduler stops on an Arm instruction, and no board layer or link exists

g3519.why: A new MicroPython port boots the full build to the banner and prompt: 174 kB of flash with 121,824 bytes of heap free; hardware SPI drives a 3.5 inch touch screen. Measured 2026-10-20.

parts.included: The CC2340R5 board with an RGB LED and two buttons.
parts.separate: It has no debugger of its own: it plugs onto the LP-XDS110ET below.

parts.role: the debugger that programs the board

parts.separate: The board has no debugger of its own: it plugs onto this one.

prereqs: A Mac. Only an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, was tried. Python 3.12 or newer, `ninja`, `cmake`, UniFlash 9.6.0 and `pyserial` (`python3 -m pip install pyserial`) for the REPL helper.
About 5 GB for the Zephyr 4.4.2 workspace, the Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 GCC 12.2.0 cross compiler and a Python 3.12 environment with `west`, plus 62 MB for MicroPython.
Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 5; it holds the debug probe.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

steps.do: Install the Zephyr 4.4.2 workspace, the compiler and the `west` environment; `NO_FLASH=1` stops the script after its build so it does not touch a board. Then clone MicroPython v1.29.0 (commit `0fd6c573e`); nothing in it is edited.
steps.see: The script ends with `NO_FLASH set. Built, not flashed.` and `<MP>` holds MicroPython.
steps.if: If a download fails, rerun the script; it keeps what it already fetched.

steps.do: Copy `prj_cc2340r5.conf` and `lp_em_cc2340r5.overlay` from `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5` into a folder `<proj>`, then build. The conf replaces MicroPython's own `prj.conf`, which overflows the chip's RAM by 46.8 kB; the overlay adds the ADC channels.
steps.say:
. <zephyr workspace>/.venv/bin/activate
export ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile CROSS_COMPILE=<toolchain>/arm-zephyr-eabi/bin/arm-zephyr-eabi-
cd <zephyr workspace>/zephyr
west build -p always -b lp_em_cc2340r5 <MP>/ports/zephyr -d <build> -- -DCONF_FILE=<proj>/prj_cc2340r5.conf -DEXTRA_DTC_OVERLAY_FILE=<proj>/lp_em_cc2340r5.overlay
steps.see: About 3 minutes later the build ends with zero errors: 174.9 kB of flash (34.15 %) and 29.9 kB of RAM (82.99 %). The image is `<build>/zephyr/zephyr_crc32.hex`.
steps.if: If the link stops with ``region `RAM' overflowed by 47888 bytes``, the build used MicroPython's own `prj.conf`: pass `-DCONF_FILE` as shown. If it stops with `relocation truncated to fit: R_ARM_THM_JUMP11 ... nlr_push_tail`, keep `CONFIG_MICROPY_CONFIGFILE="mpconfigport.h"` and do not use the minimal conf.

steps.do: Clip the LP-XDS110ET onto the board and plug it into the Mac with its USB-C cable; the board has no USB port of its own. Read the probe serial with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.
steps.see: The probe shows up as an XDS110 and `xdsdfu -e` prints its serial number.
steps.if: If `xdsdfu -e` lists nothing, check the clip-on connection and use a data cable.

steps.do: Back up the main flash and the CCFG before the first write, then flash the `_crc32` image, which carries the boot checksums. Restore later with the same `flash` command on `restore.hex`.
steps.say:
DSLITE=<UniFlash folder>/deskdb/content/TICloudAgent/osx/ccs_base/DebugServer/bin/DSLite; CCXML=cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml; BK=<backup folder outside the repo>
$DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x0,0x20000 -o $BK/main_flash.bin
$DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x4E020000,0x200 -o $BK/ccfg.bin
python3 cc2340r5/oad/images.py merge $BK/restore.hex $BK/main_flash.bin@0x0 $BK/ccfg.bin@0x4E020000
$DSLITE flash -c $CCXML -e -f -u <build>/zephyr/zephyr_crc32.hex
steps.see: DSLite writes the image and reports success; the restore hex reads back byte for byte against the backup.
steps.if: If the flash fails, close CCStudio or any other program that holds the probe, and rerun it.

steps.do: Open the REPL with the helper that holds the serial port open and sends lines (115200 baud, `/dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1`).
steps.see: `out.log` holds the banner `MicroPython v1.29.0 on 2026-10-24; zephyr-lp_em_cc2340r5 with cc2340r5`, then the line `2`.
steps.if: If nothing appears, check that the port is the probe's second serial port and that no other program holds it.

steps.do: Drive DIO15, the green LED pin, and read an ADC pin from Python. Pins are named by Zephyr devicetree label and number; the ADC number is the channel from the overlay, not the DIO number.
steps.say: python3 ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/repl.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1 out.log -- 'import machine' 'led = machine.Pin(("gpio0", 15), machine.Pin.OUT)' 'led.on(); print(led.value())' 'led.off(); print(led.value())' 'print(machine.ADC(("adc0", 2)).read_u16())'
steps.see: `out.log` shows `1` after led.on(), `0` after led.off(), then an ADC number (about 42,000 to 48,000 on a floating pin). The LED itself was not watched; the state is known from the read-back.
steps.if: If `AttributeError: 'Pin' object has no attribute 'toggle'`, use `led.value(1 - led.value())`. After a Ctrl-D soft reboot a pad you made an output stays one: use `machine.reset()`.

variants.expect: MicroPython 1.29.0 runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5: a prompt at 115200 baud, DIO15 driven from Python, and the ADC read.
shows: MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified on a chip with 36 kB of RAM, once its `prj.conf` is replaced by one file that drops networking, sensors and file systems.
The image is 174.8 kB of flash and 29.9 kB of RAM with a 20 kB Python heap (19.1 kB free after boot).
Pin.irq (10 of 10 edges), PWM with duty_ns, SPI and I2C calls ran from the REPL.
not_shows: That the LED blinked to the eye: the pin read-back changed and the LED was not watched.
That SPI data is right: the loopback wire was not fitted; the HDC2080 read and I2C.scan() did not work.
That the `duty_u16` form of PWM is right in MicroPython 1.29.0: it overflows at 1 kHz; use `duty_ns` or apply the one-cast patch in the folder.
That it works on Windows or Linux: only an Intel Mac was used.
limits: There is no file system, so scripts are typed or pasted at the prompt and re-sent after each reset.
Pin.irq loses its edge when Pin.init() is called on the same pin; call irq() again after init().
An empty Python loop takes 0.63 microseconds a pass at 48 MHz.

174.8 kB of flash (34.2 % of 512 kB), 29.9 kB of RAM (83.0 % of 36 kB), 20 kB heap
19.1 kB of the 20 kB heap

variants.name: MicroPython on the LP-MSPM33C321A
variants.short: MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified on the 160 MHz Cortex-M33 with its stock config, on Zephyr main plus TI's open pull requests.
variants.result_why: REPL, Pin, float and SPI calls run; I2C reads hang and there is no ADC or PWM driver

clocks.install: about 1.5 GB for the Zephyr tree, once
clocks.build: about 10 minutes for the tree, then about 4 minutes

evidence.text: 2026-10-25: the banner `MicroPython v1.29.0 ... zephyr-lp_mspm33c321a with mspm33c321a` appeared and print(1+1) printed 2.
A pin with PULL_UP read 1 and with PULL_DOWN read 0; 2**0.5*1000 printed 1414.2135.
The same steps were run from a scratch copy of only the listed files and produced an image (the image from that build was not flashed).

parts.included: The MSPM33C321A board; its USB debugger programs it and carries the serial port.

parts.name: A Mac to build and flash from
parts.included: Nothing to add if you have one.

prereqs: A Mac or Linux machine; only an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, was tried. git, `cmake` and `ninja` on the path, a Python 3.12 environment with `west`, the Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 GCC 12.2.0 `arm-zephyr-eabi` (`cc2340r5/zephyr/setup-intel-mac.sh` installs both), UniFlash 9.6.0 (DSLite). About 1.5 GB for the Zephyr tree and 0.3 GB for the build.

Zephyr main at `1405adc9a604` plus TI's open pull requests for the UART, clock and GPIO drivers: Zephyr's released board has no serial port, GPIO, I2C or SPI driver. `zephyr-tree.sh` pins each pull request to a commit, and pull requests move.
Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 4; it holds the debug probe.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

steps.do: Clone MicroPython v1.29.0 (commit `0fd6c573e`) from a fresh folder outside this repository; nothing in it is edited.
steps.see: The `mp` folder holds MicroPython.
steps.if: If the clone fails, check the network; the tag is v1.29.0.

steps.do: Build the Zephyr tree this port needs: Zephyr main plus the pinned pull requests, with `picolibc` and `cmsis_6`. Run it from `ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a`. The kinds are `uart`, `i2c` and `spi`; this version uses `uart`.
steps.see: About 10 minutes later the `zw` folder holds the merged Zephyr tree.
steps.if: If a later build stops with ``fatal error: alloca.h: No such file or directory``, the picolibc module is missing: `west update picolibc` (the script does it) and pass the folder as `PICO`.

steps.do: Build MicroPython's `ports/zephyr` for `lp_mspm33c321a` with MicroPython's own `prj.conf` plus `mspm33c321a.conf` (watchdog off, GPIO, I2C, SPI).
steps.see: About 4 minutes later `out/zephyr/zephyr.hex` exists: 292.3 kB of flash (28.5 % of 1 MB) and 83.6 kB of RAM (32.7 % of 256 kB) with the GPIO driver.
steps.if: If the build stops naming a variable, set it. If `machine_wdt.c` stops the build, `CONFIG_WATCHDOG=n` is missing; use `mspm33c321a.conf`.

steps.do: Back up the board, pad the image to a multiple of 16 bytes (DSLite writes 128-bit words), convert it to hex at 0x10000000 and flash it. Restore later with the same `flash` command on a hex made from the saved `main-flash.bin`.
steps.say:
python3 tools/benchmark/backup.py save mspm33c321a --probe <your-probe-serial>
python3 -c "b=open('out/zephyr/zephyr.bin','rb').read(); open('p.bin','wb').write(b+b'\xff'*(-len(b)%16))"
arm-zephyr-eabi-objcopy -I binary -O ihex --change-addresses 0x10000000 p.bin p.hex
DSLite flash -c mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<your-probe-serial>.ccxml -e -f -v p.hex
steps.see: DSLite writes and verifies the 1 MB image in about 20 s.
steps.if: If DSLite says `Error in image size ... should be divisible by 16`, the padding step was skipped. If the next call says `Error initializing emulator (Error -261)`, run `xds110reset -s <your-probe-serial> -a toggle -d 200` and flash again.

steps.do: Open the REPL on the probe's serial port (115200 baud) and read two pins with their pull resistors on: PA12 pulled up, then pulled down.
steps.say: python3 ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a/repl.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1 out.log --reset -- 'print(1+1)' 'import machine' 'print(machine.Pin(("gpioa", 12), machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP).value())' 'print(machine.Pin(("gpioa", 12), machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_DOWN).value())'
steps.see: `out.log` holds the banner `MicroPython v1.29.0 on 2026-10-25; zephyr-lp_mspm33c321a with mspm33c321a`, then `2`, then `1` for the pull-up and `0` for the pull-down.
steps.if: If `ValueError: device gpioc not found` appears, `CONFIG_GPIO` is off: build with `mspm33c321a.conf`. Send one-line statements; a multi-line `def` typed line by line is indented wrongly. If a read of `machine.I2C` hangs the console, press the reset button; use writes only.

variants.expect: MicroPython 1.29.0 prints its banner and a >>> prompt at 115200 baud on the LP-MSPM33C321A, pulled-up and pulled-down inputs read 1 and 0, and float math works.
shows: MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified, with its own `prj.conf` as shipped, on the Cortex-M33 chip.
The image is 292.3 kB of flash and 83.6 kB of RAM with a 48 kB Python heap (47.1 kB free after boot).
machine.Pin and float math run from the REPL on the `KIND=uart` image; machine.SPI calls ran from the `KIND=spi` image.
not_shows: That machine.I2C works: it opens and writes return, but every read hangs until a hardware reset.
That machine.ADC or machine.PWM work: Zephyr has no driver for this chip's ADC or PWM.
That the LED blinked to the eye: the pin state is known from the output register and the LED was not watched.
That the image from the fresh-folder build ran: it produced an image that was not flashed.
limits: Zephyr's released `lp_mspm33c321a` board has no serial port, GPIO, I2C or SPI driver; this port needs Zephyr main plus TI's open pull requests, and pull requests move.
I2C and SPI cannot be in one image: pull requests 110526 and 119347 carry different copies of the UNICOMM driver, so each gets its own build (`KIND=i2c`, `KIND=spi`).
`Pin.value()` reads 0 right after `led.on()`; read the output register instead.
An empty Python loop costs 803 CPU cycles a pass at 160 MHz (5.0 microseconds); the cause is not found.

292.3 kB of flash (28.5 % of 1 MB), 83.6 kB of RAM (32.7 % of 256 kB), 48 kB heap
47.1 of 48 kB after gc.collect()

evidence.text: 2026-10-13, clean virtual environment with ESPHome 2026.9.1 and TI's four tools: esphome compile built the CC2755P10 image in 35 s cold (median of three, 34 to 40) and 27 s warm.

esphome upload flashed it in 15 s (14.6 to 16.1 s over three flashes); Home Assistant listed the entities 5.7 s after the first flash and 6.3 s after the third. The second flash did not rejoin while the old device was still listed.

steps.do: Make a Python 3.12 virtual environment and install ESPHome 2026.9.1 into it. The `cbor2<6` pin is needed on an Intel Mac, where cbor2 6 has no wheel and wants a Rust compiler.
steps.see: pip finishes in about 26 s and the environment holds 222 MB.

steps.do: Install TI's tools once, about 8 GB in all: the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS (it comes with CCStudio 21.0.1), SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0. The downloads need a free myTI login. The platform looks under `/Applications/ti`, `~/ti` and `/opt/ti`.

variants.name: ESPHome Wi-Fi device on the LP-EM-CC35X1
variants.short: ESPHome's own compile and upload put a Wi-Fi device with ESPHome's native API on the CC3551E; Home Assistant adoption has not run.
variants.result_why: Joins Wi-Fi and serves the native API; Home Assistant adoption not run

clocks.install: about 8 GB of TI tools once

evidence.text: 2026-10-13: esphome compile built the CC3551E image in 55.7 s cold and 23.3 s warm; esphome upload took 60 s (a full flash erase, then the signed image).
The board joined Wi-Fi 5.3 s and 5.7 s after a reset on two clean joins, logged through ESPHome's logger on its serial port, and announced itself over mDNS.
An API client on the board itself got 20 of 20 switch commands confirmed, median 120 ms. A 24-hour soak confirmed 5,616 of 5,620 commands.

TI's SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and the SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox 4.3.23, and the LP-EM-CC35X1 activated once with the Toolbox. Override paths with `ESPHOME_TI_WIFI_SDK`, `ESPHOME_TI_CGT`, `ESPHOME_TI_SYSCONFIG_WIFI`, `ESPHOME_TI_TOOLBOX`.
Close any other program that holds the debug probe before step 4.

The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

cp -R <repository folder>/ports/esphome-ti/components <repository folder>/ports/esphome-ti/frl-cc35xx.yaml .
printf 'wifi_ssid: "<your network>"\nwifi_password: "<your password>"\n' > secrets.yaml

steps.if: If compile stops with `KeyError: 'power_save_mode'` (or `max_connections`, `max_send_queue`), keep those three keys in the YAML; they have no platform default on `cc35xx`.

steps.do: Build the firmware.
steps.see: The build ends without errors in 56 s cold, 23 s when repeated.
steps.if: If a tool is missing the build stops with its name and version; install it or set its override variable.

steps.do: Flash the board. This erases the whole flash and writes the signed image.
steps.see: The upload takes about 60 s.
steps.if: If nothing appears on the serial port afterwards, read the port at 115200 baud; programs from the Toolbox start by themselves after a full erase. An image programmed over TI's Wi-Fi CSI image without the erase stays silent (see the CC35X1 FAQ).

steps.do: Read the board's application serial port at 115200 baud, and reset the board.
steps.see: ESPHome's log appears and shows `[I][wifi]: Connected` about 5 s after the reset, then the API waiting for a client.
steps.if: If the log stops after `Starting scan`, use ESPHome 2026.9.1 with this platform's current Wi-Fi backend.

variants.expect: The board prints ESPHome's log on its serial port, joins your Wi-Fi about 5 s after a reset and serves ESPHome's native API on port 6053. Adding it to Home Assistant's ESPHome integration has not been run.
shows: ESPHome 2026.9.1's own `compile` and `upload` commands build and flash a CC3551E through the `cc35xx` platform in this repository.
The board joined Wi-Fi in 5.3 to 5.7 s after a reset and an API client on the board confirmed 20 of 20 switch commands.
Over a 24-hour soak 5,616 of 5,620 commands were confirmed and the board never restarted.
not_shows: That Home Assistant adopts the device: the test network isolates its clients, so port 6053 was not reachable from Home Assistant.
That the API is secure: it runs without encryption until TI's random-number driver is wired in.
That it survives a power cycle with its settings: preferences do not persist.
limits: The API runs without encryption, settings do not survive a reset, the network name and password are built into the image, and there are no over-the-air updates.

projects.q: run a vision model on a TI Linux board
projects.headline: The SK-TDA4VM boots in 24 s and runs TI's zoo models in {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.1f}} to {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.1f}} ms on the C7x; its two A72 cores take 13 to 135 times longer on the same models.

parts.separate: No power supply, camera or Wi-Fi card in the box.

parts.name: USB stick, FAT32, 4 GB or more
parts.role: carries the image to the board when you have no card reader

prereqs: A Mac, checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9. It needs Homebrew (from brew.sh, which needs the Xcode command line tools: 1.8 GB installed here) and Python 3 with pip (the command line tools bring both). Step 1 installs lrzsz 0.13.1 (0.3 MB installed), xz 5.8.4 (2.6 MB installed) and pyserial 3.5 (under 1 MB). The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.
A second computer with 15 GB free for the unpacked image. The 1.1 GB download unpacks to 13.8 GB; a second Mac was used. Not needed if you have a micro-SD card reader and use TI's route.
About an hour: 62 counted minutes from the first console check to the Linux login, 11 of them hands-on and 51 waiting. The serial driver install the evening before is not included.

steps.do: One-time setup before the board: install the CP210x VCP driver on the Mac, a free download from the bridge chip's maker. Then in System Settings, Privacy and Security, click Allow. Then install the helpers the card-writing scripts use with Homebrew and pip. Checked with lrzsz 0.13.1, pyserial 3.5 and xz 5.8.4 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.
steps.see: After step 2 plugs the board in, four serial ports appear: `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`, `...UART1`, `...UART2` and `...UART4`.
steps.if: If System Settings never shows the Allow prompt, scroll to the bottom of Privacy and Security, where a "System software ... was blocked" notice names the driver. **Third-party behavior.**
steps.say:
brew install lrzsz xz
pip install pyserial

steps.do: Check SW1 (BOOT CTL) is all four sliders OFF, the micro-SD card is seated under the board, and plug a micro-B cable from J4 to the Mac. Leave the board unpowered for now. The 20 V USB-C supply goes to J14, the power port at the board's edge. Never plug it into J12, the data port.
steps.see: The four serial ports from step 1 appear on the Mac. The Linux console is `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART1` on the test Mac; the chip's UART-boot port is `...UART2`.
steps.if: If the console later goes silent after you move the cable to another USB port, probe all four ports again: the console can come back under another name. A 5 V charger can reset the board during boot.

steps.do: Open the console first, then power the board: log all four ports with timestamps, one per port, using `python3 tda4/tools/conlog.py <port> <log>`, at 115200 baud, 8N1. Power on the board from the 20 V supply.
steps.see: On a kit whose card carries no image, silence on all four ports before and after a press of SW2 (reset). That was the case on the test kit, so the card in the box was probably blank.
steps.if: If you connect after the board has booted you may see nothing even after Enter: press SW2 with the console open. Silence also looks like a wrong SW1 setting or the wrong port, so check both before writing the card.

steps.do: On a second computer with 15 GB free, download `tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic.xz` from TI's SK-TDA4VM software page. The file is 1.1 GB, from Processor SDK Linux Edge AI 11.00.00.08, and no login is needed. Check it and record your own hash, because the page shows no checksum.
steps.see: `xz -t` prints nothing and exits cleanly. The test file was 1,123,540,588 bytes.
steps.if: With a micro-SD card reader, TI's route is shorter: write the file to the card with balenaEtcher, or from a terminal with `tda4/tools/write-card.sh diskN path/to/image.wic.xz`, then skip to step 8. That route was not run on this kit.

steps.do: No card reader, so the card is written from the board itself. On the second computer, unpack the image and mount the boot partition, using the disk number `hdiutil` prints in place of `diskN`. Then split the image into compressed pieces. Then copy `tiboot3.bin`, `sysfw.itb`, `tispl.bin` and `u-boot.img` from `/tmp/boot` to the folder with `tda4/tools/uart_boot.py`. Keep the pieces that are not all zeros. For this image they are 000 to 030, 032, 040, 041 and 048, 1.95 GB in all. Copy them into a `tda4/` folder on a FAT32 USB stick of 4 GB or more.
steps.see: A 13.8 GB raw image after `xz -dk`; `hdiutil` prints a disk number to use for `diskN`.
steps.if: Edit the console port in the scripts in `tda4/tools/` and the piece list in `write_from_stick.py` for your Mac and image. Skip all-zero pieces: `gzcat f | tr -d '\0' | wc -c` is not 0 for the ones to keep.
steps.say:
xz -dk tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic.xz
hdiutil attach -imagekey diskimage-class=CRawDiskImage -nomount tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic
diskutil mount -mountPoint /tmp/boot /dev/diskNs1
split -b 268435456 -a 3 -d tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic wic.
gzip -1 wic.*

steps.do: Power off. Set SW1: 1 ON, 2 OFF, 3 ON, 4 OFF (UART boot). Put the stick in a USB-A port. Run the script, then power on or press SW2.
steps.see: A stream of `C` on the UART-boot port, then the four boot files go in: xmodem, then ymodem, about 3.5 minutes at 9.7 kB/s. Then `U-Boot 2025.01` and a `=>` prompt on the console port.
steps.if: If it stops at the third file (`spl: ymodem err - Timed out`), press SW2 and run it again. Use the current version of the Python script, and no shell loop. Do not try U-Boot's `ums` command: it crashes U-Boot on this kit and you are back at this step.

steps.do: Write the card from the stick, piece by piece.
steps.see: For each piece, `load usb 0:1`, `unzip` and `mmc write` ending in `blocks written: OK`; 323 seconds for the whole image; at the end `mmc part` lists TI's two partitions.
steps.if: A piece that takes more than a minute is stuck: reset with SW2 and begin again from step 6. If the write was interrupted, run `write_from_stick.py unzip` again from U-Boot: every piece goes to a fixed block address, so a rerun overwrites the same places.

steps.do: Power off. Set all four sliders of SW1 to OFF (SD boot). Make sure the console is being logged, then power on.
steps.see: `U-Boot SPL`, `Starting kernel`, `Welcome to Arago`, then `tda4vm-sk login:` at 27.7 seconds on the first boot. The root file system grows to the card during it. Log in as `root`, no password.
steps.if: The red `Direct firmware load for j7-mcu-r5f0_1-fw failed with error -2` lines and `Failed to start Start psplash boot splash screen` are harmless: three R5F cores have no firmware on the image and there is no display.

steps.do: Push TI's model-timing script to the board over the console after making its folders. The board has no network in this route.
steps.see: The push prints a matching sha256 for the file when it arrives.
steps.if: Push files as 76-column base64 only, which `push_serial.py` does; a single long line hangs the console at a `>` prompt.

steps.do: Run it in the background so the console's Ctrl-C cannot kill it. The script times every precompiled model in `/opt/model_zoo` through its runtime with TI's TIDL delegate on the C7x and its matrix accelerator, 30 timed runs each. Then read the log. These command lines are assembled from the script, its log and the FAQ rule; the recorded run typed them in pieces.
steps.see: One line per model, such as `ONR-KD-7060-human-pose-yolox-s-640x640 | keypoint_detection | onnxrt | tidl-c7x | [1, 3, 640, 640] | median {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms | min 13.72 | max 13.86 | n 30 | rss 284 MB`. The 14 zoo models came out between {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms (MobileNetV1) and {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms (YOLOX-s pose 640). The TVM models need `tda4/bench/zoo/tvm_bench.py` the same way.
steps.if: If a model takes hundreds of milliseconds, it ran on the CPU. Load the model's precompiled `artifacts` folder instead of the bare ONNX file. Then check the runtime log lists every node on the C7x, 274 of 274 for the pose model. Start long jobs with `setsid nohup`; a plain `nohup ... &` died at the next connect.
steps.say:
python3 tda4/tools/lcmd.py "setsid nohup python3 /root/push/zoo_bench.py 30 > /root/night/zoo_tidl.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &"
python3 tda4/tools/lcmd.py "cat /root/night/zoo_tidl.log"

variants.expect: A Linux login prompt 27.7 seconds after power-on, and one timing line per zoo model, each between {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.2f}} and {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms on the C7x. The pose model, the biggest, reads {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms.
shows: TI's Edge AI Linux boots on the SK-TDA4VM from a card written with no card reader, Ethernet or display. That was one kit and one Mac.

All 14 of TI's zoo models run on the C7x and its matrix accelerator in {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.2f}} to {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.2f}} ms each. TI's four published figures are within 10 percent of the measured values.
The same eight ONNX models take 13 to 135 times longer on the two Arm cores with the CPU provider. A model that falls back to the CPU costs that much on this image.
not_shows: No picture was shown to the models: the input is random numbers, and outputs were not compared. These are times only; accuracy was not measured.
The CPU comparison is fp32 on the CPU against int8 on the accelerator. It shows the cost of falling back to the CPU and is no like-for-like comparison of the two cores.
These timings come from one run. No independent builder has repeated them.
Sustained load was not shown to be safe. The board reset about 60 seconds into a two-thread CoreMark plus TIDL loop. A five-minute pose graph took the hottest zone to 91.5 C.
A card reader, an Ethernet link, a display or a camera were never used, so the camera and display paths are untested.
limits: The board had no card reader, Ethernet or display; the whole route is the serial cable at 9.7 kB/s for the boot files. TI's own route, which needs a reader and a display, was not run.
TI's getting-started page assumes a display and Ethernet; the model-zoo layout was learned by listing folders.
The board resets under heavy sustained load; it runs on a 20 V supply of unknown wattage with a passive heatsink and no fan.
The TVM build of ssdLite mobDet 320 is 12.97 ms against 6.40 ms for the TFLite build. **Unknown (suspected: the input conversion inside the graph).**

projects.t: Detect a smoke alarm's beeps with a microphone

g5187.why: Through its own microphone it reported a smoke pattern from a laptop speaker 9.4 s after the sound started. It gave 0 alarms in 3.4 hours of a quiet room. Learning has run only on audio streamed over USB. There it ignored 18 of 18 look-alikes, the same alarm 31 dB quieter and another pitch. A real alarm's horn has not been tried.

projects.what: Try an experimental alarm-pattern detector on the LP-MSPM0G5187. It reported smoke-alarm sounds played through a laptop speaker; learning has run over USB. Detection and learning with a real alarm remain untested.
projects.time: 1 evening; tools need 12 GB free, once
projects.q: learn a smoke or CO alarm by ear and report when it sounds
projects.headline: The LP-MSPM0G5187 reported a smoke alarm pattern from a laptop speaker 9.4 s after it started, through its own microphone, and gave 0 alarms in 3.4 hours of a quiet room. Learning has run only on audio sent over USB; a real alarm's horn is the test still to run.

variants.name: Board on USB, a Mac notification when your alarm sounds

card.outcome: The board detects a smoke-alarm pattern played through a speaker. Learning has run over USB; a real alarm is still to try.

merit.text: Smoke pattern reported 9.4 s after it started; 0 alarms in 3.4 h of a quiet room

pic.alt: A smoke alarm pattern of three beeps reaches a board's own microphone; the terminal prints LEARNED then ALARM smoke from the learned alarm at 3162 Hz

recipe.outcome: Hear a smoke alarm's beep pattern
recipe.one_line: It has heard only recorded alarm sounds from a laptop speaker and over USB; a real alarm was not tested.

output: ALARM smoke from the learned alarm tone=3162 Hz
IGNORED: too quiet to be the alarm beside me

variants.name: Board on USB, notification on the Mac
variants.short: The tested build: one board, its USB cable, a Mac.

evidence.text: On 2026-10-13 a laptop speaker beside the board played 16 look-alike sounds and a smoke alarm pattern through the board's own microphone. The pattern was reported as smoke 9.4 s after it started; 14 of the 16 look-alikes stayed silent with nothing learned. Nothing was learned live in this run.

Audio was streamed over USB onto real room sound, with no sound played. The board learned a smoke alarm, saved it and alarmed on it. It ignored 18 of 18 look-alikes, the same alarm 31 dB quieter, another pitch and a CO pattern.
The two look-alikes that alarmed were CO-like patterns; after a fix to the CO timing check both stay silent, and a CO pattern from the learned horn is reported as CO.

parts.role: the listener: microphone, NPU and buttons on one board
parts.included: The microphone, the audio converter and button S2 are on the board; its USB debugger programs it and carries the serial lines.
parts.separate: The cable in the box is USB-A; a Mac with only USB-C needs an adapter.

parts.name: A smoke or CO alarm with a test button
parts.separate: The one already on your ceiling. This build was not tested with a real alarm; see What this does not establish.

parts.name: A Mac
parts.separate: Checked on an Intel Mac with macOS 15.7 only.

prereqs: CCStudio 21.0.1, which brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 and UniFlash 9.6.0. Install each in its default folder under `/Applications/ti/`, because the build script expects those paths.
Python 3 with pyserial (`python3 -m pip install --user pyserial`).

If you fitted a BP-CC1407P radio BoosterPack and wired it to header J20, take the PB10 and PB11 wires off. Those pins are the microphone's clock lines; with them on, the microphone reads zeros. The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

steps.do: Install the tools in the list above, then get a copy of this repository. To fetch only the board folder, use the sparse-checkout line in its README. The trained model is already compiled for the NPU in `mspm0g5187/alarm/model/nnc_g5187_npu/`, so no training is needed.
steps.see: `ls mspm0g5187/alarm/model/nnc_g5187_npu` lists `mod.a` and `tvmgen_default.h`.
steps.if: If `mod.a` is missing, the clone did not bring the model; it is tracked in the repository, so clone again.

steps.do: Build the listener. The script copies one of TI's SDK examples for its makefile and puts the listener's code in. It links the NPU model and CMSIS-DSP, and builds in a scratch folder under your home folder.
steps.see: A size line with text 80608 and bss 30417, which is 78.7 kB of flash and 29.7 kB of RAM, then `image: mspm0g5187/alarm/out/alarm_detect.out`.
steps.if: If it cannot find `spi_controller_echo_interrupts` or `tiarmclang`, the SDK or CCStudio is not in its default folder; the two paths are at the top of `build.sh`.

steps.do: Plug the board into the Mac and read its probe serial number: it is the text after `usbmodem` without the last digit.
steps.see: Two lines with the same text, ending in 1 and 4, for example `/dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1` and `/dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>4`.
steps.if: Nothing listed: the cable or adapter is charge-only; swap it.

steps.do: Flash it. Make a copy of the connection file with your probe serial number in its name and inside it. The command below does both; replace `<probe serial>` with yours from step 3. Then load the image with UniFlash's command line. This is the board README's tested flash command with the listener's image in place of the blink.
steps.say:
PROBE=<probe serial>
sed "s/<template serial>/$PROBE/g" mspm0g5187/MSPM0G5187_<template serial>.ccxml > mspm0g5187/MSPM0G5187_$PROBE.ccxml
/Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/dslite.sh --mode flash -c mspm0g5187/MSPM0G5187_$PROBE.ccxml -e -f -v -u mspm0g5187/alarm/out/alarm_detect.out
steps.see: The flash ends without an error in about 5 s, and the green LED gives a short blink every 2 seconds, which means the board is listening. The LED lines are in `detect.h`, in the main loop.
steps.if: If DSLite cannot find the probe, the serial number in the `.ccxml` does not match yours.

steps.do: Start the listener's Mac script on the first serial port, the one ending in 1. It logs every line and turns an alarm into a Mac notification. Leave it running.
steps.see: The terminal stays quiet while the room is quiet. `tail -f ~/alarm.log` in a second window shows one `I n=... cls=other` line a second.
steps.if: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'serial'`: install pyserial, as in the list above. No lines in the log: check that the port ends in 1 and not 4.

steps.do: Put the board beside your alarm, where it will stay. Press S2 once and the blue LED blinks fast. Then press and hold the alarm's test button until it has sounded for about 10 seconds. Ear protection helps; smoke alarms are loud up close.
steps.see: `LEARNED cls=smoke f0=... L0=... saved` in the terminal and the blue LED stops; the record is kept through a power cut. Not done with a real alarm: in these runs the learn step used alarm sound sent over USB. The 10 seconds is the expected time: four inferences that hear the pattern. It is not a measured time.
steps.if: `LEARN FAILED: no smoke or CO pattern heard in 45 s`: hold the test button longer, or move the board closer. To start over, hold S2 for 5 s until `FORGOT: generic mode`.

steps.do: Press the alarm's test button again. Then press S2 once to clear the alarm.
steps.see: `ALARM smoke from the learned alarm` and the red LED on. Expected about 10 s after the sound starts; measured 9.4 s with a laptop speaker and nothing learned. The script also raises a Mac notification; these runs did not record one. S2 prints `CLEARED`.
steps.if: `IGNORED ... too quiet` means the board is farther from the alarm than when it learned; learn again in its final place ([FAQ](../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md)).

variants.expect: Expected from the speaker and USB runs, and not seen with a real alarm: your alarm's test sound is reported as smoke, or as CO for a CO alarm, about 10 s after it starts. Beeping from a TV, a kettle, a whistle, a phone or an oven timer is not reported. Neither is the same alarm pattern played quieter or at another pitch.
shows: A 13.8k-parameter model runs on the MSPM0G5187's NPU, on its own microphone, once a second. It takes 20.2 ms per inference in the self-test and 32.4 ms median live, and keeps up in real time.
With nothing learned it reported a smoke alarm pattern from a laptop speaker 9.4 s after it started, and stayed silent through 3.4 hours of a quiet room, 12.1k inferences.

With an alarm learned, on audio streamed over USB and no sound played, it ignored 18 of 18 look-alike sounds. These were oven timers, backup beepers, whistles, a kettle, ringtones, speech and music. It also ignored the same alarm 31 dB quieter, and the same pattern at 3,600 Hz instead of 3,150 Hz.

The learned-alarm rules were applied afterwards to the board's logged answers from the speaker run. They silenced all 16 look-alikes and the same alarm about 22 dB quieter, and still passed the alarm. It was a replay of logged answers; nothing was decided live.
It tells smoke (three beeps) from CO (four short pulses) on the same horn.
not_shows: That it learns a real smoke alarm's horn: every alarm sound was synthetic, from a laptop speaker or sent over USB. A real horn has harmonics and sometimes a warble that the training never heard.
False alarms over weeks in a busy house: 3.4 hours of a quiet room and 2 hours of held-out synthetic scenes are what was measured.
Doorbells: there is no standard doorbell pattern, and none was built.
That it replaces a connected or monitored alarm. It is a demonstration and is not a listed safety device.
limits: On this board PB10 and PB11 are both the microphone's clock lines and the BP-CC1407P radio's reset and interrupt wires. **Setup or handling.** The listener and that radio cannot share J20 as wired here.
The Mac script is the notification path in this version; the board on its own only lights its red LED.
Placement matters: it learns how loud the alarm is where the board sits, and ignores anything more than 10 dB quieter. Move the board and learn again.

technical.v: Five-layer 1-D CNN, 13.8k parameters, 8-bit quantization-aware training, compiled with TI's NNC for the TinyEngine NPU; 16 inputs by 128 frames (8.3 s); answers other, smoke, CO once a second
20.2 ms per inference in the self-test (6 of 6 classes matched onnxruntime); 32.4 ms median over 443 inferences in the live run
Onboard ICS-40720 microphone into the PCM1809, I2S at 47,619 Hz, filtered to 15,873 Hz; 13 features every 64.5 ms from two 512-point FFTs (CMSIS-DSP)
6 of the last 8 answers agree, the NFPA 72 timing check passes, and once learned the tone is within 4 % and the level no more than 10 dB below the learned one
78.7 kB of flash of 128 kB, 29.7 kB of RAM of 32 kB, from tiarmsize on the 2026-10-13 build
MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, UniFlash 9.6.0, Intel Mac, macOS 15.7

projects.what: A three-phase brushless motor with Hall sensors, spun three ways from one LaunchPad and one driver board: six-step on the Halls, field-oriented control (FOC) on the Halls, and FOC with the Halls out of the control loop.
projects.time: 1 evening for six-step; a day for the FOC versions; tools need about 10 GB, once
projects.q: spin a brushless motor with Hall sensors, then without them
projects.headline: Spins on all three: six-step to 3,632 rpm, Hall FOC held at a set speed, and sensorless FOC at 40 Hz on 0.063 A against 0.13 A on the Halls. Unloaded, 12.4 V.

am13e230.why: Ran three ways on this setup (2026-10-15 to 2026-10-17): six-step on the Halls, TI's Hall FOC, and FOC with the observer driving and the Halls only logged. Unloaded, one motor, 12.4 V.

mspm33c321a.why: Six-step on the Halls (about 160 rpm on software PWM, 430 rpm on the timer with dead band), then Hall FOC with the portable motor core and a speed loop that held 300, 600, 450 and 150 rpm within 1 percent. Same driver board and motor, 20 V pack, unloaded. Results are read from RAM over the probe; there is no console or phone remote for this chip, and the driver's current limit is off on this LaunchPad.

prereqs: The code is in this repository. Clone it first: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` (about 300 MB on disk; the sparse clone on the start page is smaller). This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Every command below runs from inside it.

Four free TI tools, each under /Applications/ti on a Mac or named by an environment variable the build script reads: the AM13E230x SDK 26.01.00.03 (https://www.ti.com/tool/LP-AM13E230, myTI login, about 0.4 GB; `FRL_AM13_SDK`), SysConfig 1.28.0 (https://www.ti.com/tool/SYSCONFIG, about 0.15 GB; `FRL_SYSCONFIG`), TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS (https://www.ti.com/tool/ARM-CGT, about 0.3 GB, or the copy inside CCStudio; `FRL_TICLANG`) and, for the flash step, DSLite from UniFlash (https://www.ti.com/tool/UNIFLASH, about 0.5 GB, or the copy inside CCStudio; `FRL_DSLITE`). `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board am13e230` lists what is missing. The build script stops with the tool's name and download page when one is absent. Checked on one Intel Mac only; nothing is installed by the script.

wiring.alt: The DRV8376EVM with the Hall block, motor phase terminals and supply terminals marked
wiring.note: The 40-pin edge is four 10-pin headers. Hold the board with the USB connector at the top: J1 (pins 1 to 10) and J3 (21 to 30) are the two left rows, J4 (31 to 40) and J2 (11 to 20) the two right rows. Pin 1 of J1 and pin 21 of J3 are the top pins of the left rows, nearest the USB connector; J4 and J2 count the other way, so pin 40 and pin 20 are at the top. Nothing needs a jumper wire between the boards: the EVM plugs onto J1 to J4 with its screw terminals pointing away from the USB-C connector. The loose wires are the motor's: phases yellow, red, black to OUT A, B, C (any order), and the Hall leads red, black, blue, green, white to HALL POWER, HALL GROUND, HALL A, B, C. Supply 4.5 to 65 V to VBAT and PGND; 12 V is plenty. The pin table is the one in am13e230/bldc-drv8376/README.md.
pins: Hall inputs; the EVM has 10 k pull-ups to 3.3 V

steps.do: With USB unplugged: set EVM jumper J13 to GVDD, wire the motor and Hall leads as in the table, set LaunchPad switches S6 and S4 to BP, and press the EVM onto J1 to J4 with its screw terminals pointing away from the USB-C connector.
steps.see: The EVM sits flat on all four headers. Nothing is lit.
steps.if: If every Hall line later reads state 7, the J13 jumper is missing or the Hall ground lead is open.

steps.do: Build and flash the six-step program. With one LaunchPad on USB the script finds its probe and writes the connection file it needs; with more than one it lists their serials and asks for `./build.sh --flash <serial>`.
steps.see: About 3 s to build and 5 s to flash over the LaunchPad kit's own probe; 32 kB of flash.
steps.if: If the build cannot find its tools, install the AM13E230x SDK 26.01.00.03, SysConfig 1.28.0 and TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS where the script expects them (the paths are at the top of build.sh); `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board am13e230` lists what is missing with download links.

steps.do: Plug in USB-C, then switch the motor supply on. Open the LaunchPad kit's serial port at 115200 baud and type `v`.
steps.see: The EVM's VM, AVDD and GVDD lights are on and NFAULT is off. `v` shows bus volts near your supply and a Hall state from 1 to 6. The current image boots with the driver off; Check the supply voltage and the driver wiring before the first start.
steps.if: If it says `no bus voltage on VM`, the supply is off or on the wrong terminals.

steps.do: Learn the Hall table once per power-up: type `l`. It takes about 25 s with no hands.
steps.see: The shaft clicks round six steps and a table prints with six different Hall states.
steps.if: If it says `learn failed`, a Hall wire is loose (state 0 or 7), or the rotor did not move: raise the supply voltage.

steps.do: Type `2` then `g`.
steps.see: The motor turns. A line a second shows duty, direction, Hall state, rpm, bus volts and fault. At 20 percent duty it settles near 920 rpm.
steps.if: If it says `DRIVER FAULT`, lower the duty and check the supply can give the current, then type `c` to clear.

steps.do: Type `s`, then `r`, then `g` for the other direction. `b` brakes. `0` then `s` ends.
steps.see: Reverse runs 4 to 10 percent slower than forward at the same duty.
steps.if: If it runs rough or stalls at once, type `a` to trim the commutation advance, then `g` again.

variants.expect: At 10 to 60 percent duty the motor runs from about 400 to about 3,630 rpm forward and 380 to 3,440 rpm in reverse, unloaded, on 12.4 V.
shows: A plug-on driver board and about 350 lines of C turn a Hall-sensor motor, with the Hall table learned by the program in about 25 s.
Unloaded, the motor started from standstill on every try at 10 and at 20 percent duty.
Median speed at 20, 40 and 60 percent duty, forward: 924, 2,312 and 3,632 rpm; reverse: 891, 2,091 and 3,442.
not_shows: Torque or efficiency: nothing was loaded and phase current was not measured in this version.
That the speeds are exact: they come from Hall edge timing, and a tachometer would settle whether they read high.
That the speed sweep repeats: it was run once. The same motor later turned under the FOC image.
limits: Open loop in duty: speed follows the duty you type, with no speed loop in the base program.
One motor, one driver board, 12.4 V from a small adapter, 60 percent duty cap, unloaded.
The Hall sensors sit about 7 electrical degrees off their ideal spacing; the program learns the table rather than assuming it.

Anaheim BLY171S-24V-4000: 24 V, 4,000 rpm, 1.8 A, 4 pole pairs, 2.45 V per 1,000 rpm (label)

steps.do: Wire it as in the six-step version, with the 12 V supply, and make sure J2 (the current-sense reference) is fitted.
steps.see: Same layout. With power on and the motor stopped, the phase-current sense outputs rest near half scale.
steps.if: If the sense outputs read a few millivolts, J2 is missing.

steps.do: Build the normal image, the one with the bench guard: `cd am13e230/foc-drv8376 && OUT=$HOME/frl-build FRL_COMMISSIONING=0 ./build.sh`
steps.see: foc.out and foc.map in $HOME/frl-build/foc-drv8376/ (OUT sets the parent folder). The script builds and never flashes.
steps.if: Without `FRL_COMMISSIONING=0` the script builds the commissioning console instead, which does not run TI's state machine.

steps.do: Flash it over the LaunchPad kit's probe: `python3 am13e230/tools/run_image.py $HOME/frl-build/foc-drv8376/foc.out 3`
steps.see: The flash verifies and the program starts. The script flashes the bench's own probe by default; for yours pass `--serial <probe serial>` and add a matching AM13E23019_<probe serial>.ccxml beside the existing one in am13e230/.
steps.if: If the flash does not return in 90 s the script stops it and tries once more; a probe held by CCStudio or another program is reported as busy.

steps.do: Read the board: `python3 tools/motorlink/link.py poll`
steps.see: State reads stop idle, bus volts near your supply, phase currents under 3 mA.
steps.if: If the fault word reads 8192 (a gate driver fault), the board is not running the guarded image; flash it again.

steps.do: Learn the Hall angle once, under the probe lock: `python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe serial> --op motor-campaign -- python3 tools/motorlink/campaign.py cal` To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.
steps.see: State reports calibration, then idle, with the Hall table marked valid. It took 171 s on the bench; the guard allows up to 700 s.
steps.if: If calibration fails, TI's estimator fault is raised: check the five Hall wires and that the shaft can turn freely.

steps.do: Set the guard's bus window for the supply, then run at 10 Hz electrical: `campaign.py supply adapter12`, then `campaign.py fwd 10 OUTDIR TAG`, each under the same `lock.py exec` line as step 5 (supply takes `adapter12` or `pack20`).
steps.see: The motor aligns, opens loop, reaches closed loop at about 9 s and stops at the 12 s run cap. Speed in rpm is Hz x 15 for four pole pairs. Raw streams land in OUTDIR.
steps.if: If the start is refused with `bus out of range`, the supply is outside the window you set.

steps.do: Or drive it by hand: [Connect to the board and watch the motor live](motor-console.html) in Chrome or Edge, click Connect, set a speed under 40 Hz and click Run. STOP is always on screen.
steps.see: The state lights step Calibrate, Align, Open loop, Closed loop; speed, id, iq, peak current and bus volts update live.
steps.if: If Connect finds no board, it needs the normal image from step 3, not the commissioning build.
img: motor-console-run.png
The Motor console in Chrome after a real run: green Link, Bus, Driver, Calibrated and Hall lights, speed and phase-current graphs, Calibrate and Run buttons, a red STOP button

steps.do: Try the designed speed gains, under the lock: `python3 tools/motorlink/campaign.py gstep 0.0131 0.0157 200 OUTDIR TAG`, then `python3 tools/motorlink/speedloop_analyse.py` on the folder.
steps.see: Settle at 10 Hz, step to 15 Hz at 14 s. Median rise about 50 ms against 91 ms on TI's defaults.
steps.if: If a run ends before the step, the guard's 20 s cap or a fault stopped it: read frlGuard.reason from `link.py poll`.

steps.app: Phone, on the same private network
steps.do: Drive it from a phone. Phones have no Web Serial, so the computer that holds the board's USB port serves the same page with a stand-in serial port. Run the bridge under the probe lock with your own serial port and a private address of the computer; it prints one link with a random token. This is the home network, not Bluetooth. The remote's controls were checked against a simulated board; a run of the phone page on the real motor is not recorded.
steps.say: python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe serial> --op phone-console -- node tools/motorlink/phone_console.mjs --port /dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1 --host <private address of this computer>
steps.see: The page prints a link; opening it on the phone shows the Motor remote with Connect, Forward, Reverse, a speed slider, Start, Slow and stop, and a red STOP button. The board's guard stops the motor within 1 s if the phone goes quiet.
steps.if: If the phone cannot reach the link, check that it is on the same private network as the computer. Details: `tools/motorlink/BRIDGE.md`.

The phone remote running at 552 rpm against a simulated board

steps.do: Optional: TI's own tool. TI publishes the MCU Motor Control GUI, a graphical tool for configuring and tuning motors, on [its public tool page](https://www.ti.com/tool/MCU-MOTOR-CONTROL-GUI) (download `MCU_Motor_Control_GUI.zip`, release notes on the same page). That page lists C2000 boards and reference designs as supported and does not list the LP-AM13E230. The AM13E2x SDK's Hall FOC example sends its variables over a UART at 9.2 Mbaud to MotorVision, the protocol this repository's console speaks. No recorded run connects TI's GUI to this board.
steps.see: Nothing to check here: this step only points to TI's tool.
steps.if: If you try it, note what the GUI says about the board; the console in step 7 is the tested way to see the same variables.

variants.expect: The motor holds a set electrical speed in closed loop on TI's FOC, stops on its own at the cap, and a +5 Hz step settles in about 80 ms with the designed gains.
shows: TI's Hall FOC solution runs on a driver board it was not written for: about 650 lines of change, no fault, peak current 0.57 A in a 12 s run at 10 Hz.

The firmware guard stops every run on its own: a time cap, 1 s after the host goes quiet, a phase-current trip, a speed clamp and a bus voltage window. Host cut-off was tested: the motor stopped 1.0 s after the last packet.
Speed gains designed for the 0.5 ms speed tick halve the step's rise: 50 ms median (41 to 129) against 91 ms (79 to 182) with TI's defaults, five runs against three.
not_shows: Overshoot: one Hall-timed speed sample is only resolved to about 0.7 Hz, 14 percent of the 5 Hz step, so none is reported.
That the designed gains are better everywhere: they hold 10 Hz tighter but hunt more at 15 Hz (13.84 to 15.92 Hz p5 to p95 against 14.47 to 15.92).
That TI's default gains work for reversals: with them, 7 of 7 reversals faulted and 3 of 14 runs at 20 Hz reached a 20 s cap.
limits: The `campaign.py` script these steps call is not in this copy, so the Hall calibration, speed-loop and observer steps cannot be repeated from it; the results are the recorded runs.
Unloaded, one motor, 12.4 V, 10 to 20 Hz electrical; a +5 Hz step only; the 30 Hz design row was not run.
Current polarity and gain rest on the EVM's documented 1 V/A; the gain resistors were not read off the board.

steps.do: Have the guarded FOC image flashed and the Hall table calibrated: steps 2, 3 and 5 of the FOC version. The observer commands need guard version 6; `campaign.py` refuses to run on another version.
steps.see: `link.py poll` reads stop idle, with the Hall table valid.
steps.if: If the campaign stops with `board is not on guard version 6`, rebuild and flash the current am13e230/foc-drv8376.

steps.do: Find where the rotor really is: `campaign.py sweep 2 40 OUTDIR TAG`, under the same `tools/frl/lock.py exec` line as the FOC version's step 5. It steps the FOC angle by -45 to +45 degrees at 40 Hz with the Halls driving.
steps.see: Phase current falls from 0.129 A at 0 degrees to 0.089 A near +49 degrees, and a -45 degree step stalls the motor. The current minimum is the true rotor angle.
steps.if: A stall on the negative steps is expected and the guard stops it; clear faults with the console's Clear faults button before the next run.

steps.do: Shadow run: the Halls drive, FAST runs beside them: `campaign.py obs 2 0 40 40 15 OUTDIR TAG` (observer 2 = FAST, hand-over off, speed ceiling 40 Hz, reference 40 Hz, 15 s cap).
steps.see: FAST reads about 50 degrees from the Hall angle and its speed is within 0.4 Hz of the Halls'.
steps.if: If FAST's speed is far from the Halls' below about 20 Hz, run faster: both observers lock above about 20 Hz electrical here.

steps.do: Run with no Halls in the loop: `campaign.py hallfree 2 0 40 20 OUTDIR TAG` (observer FAST, no trim, 40 Hz reference, 20 s cap).
steps.see: TI's align (5 s at 0.36 A) and open loop to 30 Hz, then FAST takes over at about 8 s. The speed holds at 40.0 Hz and phase current reads about 0.063 A. The Halls are only logged against it.
steps.if: If it faults in start-up, check the Hall-free flag was applied: the campaign prints the config it read back before it starts.

how: Three Hall sensors sit around the rotor and report which of six sectors it is in. In six-step drive the program reads the three Hall bits and turns on the two phases that pull the rotor into the next sector, so the motor steps round. Field-oriented control replaces the table with a current loop that keeps the magnetic field 90 degrees ahead of the rotor; sensorless FOC estimates the rotor angle from the phase currents and voltages and leaves the Halls out of the loop.

The same card drawing plays here at full size: Hall bits change, the lit coil pair steps round, the rotor follows. On the measured run, unloaded at 40 Hz, the sensorless loop ran on 0.063 A of phase current, the calibrated Halls on 0.13 A, and the Halls at their best angle shift on 0.087 A.
