prereqs: A Mac with the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and SysConfig 1.28.0 (`mac-setup/README.md`). The build script copies TI's basic_ble example into a work folder and patches the copy; the SDK is never changed. `rsync` and `patch` are used by the script and ship with macOS.
UniFlash 9.6.0 for `dslite.sh`, and your probe's serial in `cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml` (`xdsdfu -e` lists it).

The code is in this repository: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `cd fox-red-labs` and `git sparse-checkout add ports/esp32-ble-gamepad cc2340r5 mac-setup site/bench`. Every command on this page runs from that folder unless it says otherwise.

steps.title: Build the live gamepad image.
steps.do: Build the image with the two buttons switched on. `LIVE=1` names the board `CC2340R5 Gamepad` and sends BTN-1 and BTN-2 as buttons 1 and 2. Without it the build sends the library's fixed test pattern as `ESP32 BLE Gamepad`. The script only builds; it never flashes.
steps.see: The last line is `built: .../basic_ble.hex (NOT flashed)`.
steps.if: If `make` stops at once with `sysconfig_cli.sh: not found`, name your folders on the same line, for example `SDK=<sdk folder> SYSCFG=<sysconfig_cli.sh> CLANG=<ti-cgt-armllvm folder> LIVE=1 bash ports/esp32-ble-gamepad/boards/cc2340r5/build.sh`.

steps.title: Flash the .hex without verify.
steps.do: Clip the probe onto the board, plug it into the Mac, and flash the `.hex` from the `cc2340r5` folder (`cd cc2340r5`). Leave out `-v`: on CC23xx, verify reads the boot configuration area and reports `Values at address 0x4E020750 do not match`. Do not flash the `.bin`. SWD is the debug connection the probe uses. This command is assembled from the board's flash line and this build's output path.
steps.see: UniFlash reports success and the board restarts as a Bluetooth gamepad (flash time not recorded for this image).
steps.if: If you see `Error -615` or `The target failed to see a correctly formatted SWD header`, press the probe firmly onto the board's debug pins and replug USB. If you see `Values at address 0x4E020750 do not match`, you flashed the `.bin` or used `-v`; flash the `.hex` without `-v`.

steps.title: Pair, and accept the prompt.
steps.do: On a Mac, open System Settings, Bluetooth, and press Connect beside `CC2340R5 Gamepad`. Accept the pairing request when it appears. Then open System Settings, Game Controllers.
steps.see: Bluetooth shows `CC2340R5 Gamepad` as Connected, and Game Controllers lists it with a green Connected status, as in the picture, with no driver or app installed.
steps.if: If the connect hangs about 30 seconds and then drops, the pairing was not accepted: macOS waits out a 30 s timeout and passes no input. Remove the device and connect again, and accept the request this time.

System Settings, Game Controllers on a Mac: CC2340R5 Gamepad listed with a green Connected status

steps.do: In a new terminal at the repository root, serve the site folder and open the reader page (`site/bench/gamepad.html`) in Chrome or Edge. The browser hands a gamepad to a page only after a button press, so press BTN-1 once with the page open. No gamepad? The page's Replay the capture button plays the Mac's recorded run.

steps.do: Press BTN-1, then BTN-2, then both together.
steps.see: Checked by eye: button 1 lit red in the reader while BTN-1 was down, button 2 while BTN-2 was down, and both for both. steps.if: If the Mac still shows button 2, it is running the old image: confirm the flash finished and remove and pair the device again.

prereqs: A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and SysConfig 1.28.0 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders, and CCStudio 21.0.1 for its `DSLite` flasher (`mac-setup/README.md`). Only an Intel Mac with macOS 15.7 was tried.
Your board's probe serial in the target file: copy `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<probe serial>.ccxml` and put your serial in place of `<probe serial>` (`xdsdfu -e` lists it).

The code is in this repository: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `cd fox-red-labs` and `git sparse-checkout add portability/boosterpacks/audio mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from that folder.
The board ships with a demo in its flash. To keep it, back it up first with the command in `mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`.

steps.title: Build the show.
steps.do: Build the 16 kHz show image with the five recordings from `portability/boosterpacks/audio/tracks/`. The script uses TI's SDK makefile and only builds; it never flashes.
steps.see: The last lines are `built build/halloween/gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out` and the flash use from the map, about 913 kB of 1,024 kB.
steps.if: If it stops at once with exit code 2, the script did not find the MSPM33 SDK or TI Arm Clang: install them in the default `/Applications/ti` folders.

steps.title: Check the image, then flash it.
steps.do: Plug the LaunchPad into the Mac by USB-C with no BoosterPack on it. Check the image never puts the chip to sleep, then flash it with DSLite. Copy `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<probe serial>.ccxml` to `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<serial>.ccxml` and put your probe serial in place of `<probe serial>`. The flash line is assembled from the board's flash command and this build's output path.
steps.see: The check prints `SAFE`, DSLite finishes with the verify passing, and a serial terminal at 115200 shows `HALLOWEEN SHOW, BOOSTXL-AUDIO app, ... sample rate 16000 Hz, recorded tracks 5`.
steps.if: If DSLite reports `Device Connection Error ... low power mode`, reset the probe with `xds110reset -s <serial> -a toggle -d 200` (it sits beside `xdsdfu`) and flash again.

steps.title: Unplug, then stack the Audio BoosterPack.
steps.do: Unplug the USB cable first: the swap happens with the board unpowered. Pull off any other BoosterPack. Plug the BOOSTXL-AUDIO onto the same rows, its pin 1 on J1 pin 1 (3V3). Check jumper J5 on the pack sits on SPI DAC, as shipped, and push the pack's volume slider to the top.
steps.see: The pack sits flat on J1 to J4 with its speaker facing up.
steps.if: If the pack does not seat, check both header rows line up; it goes on one way only, pin 1 to 3V3.

steps.title: Plug in the power bank.
steps.do: Plug the power bank into the LaunchPad kit's USB-C socket. Nothing else is connected.
steps.see: The Mountain King recording opens the show and the RGB LED swaps orange and purple on the beat. Songs shuffle and loop, with a scare sound between them.
steps.if: If you hear nothing, check J5 sits on SPI DAC and the slider is up. If nothing happens at all, the bank switched off at low load: use one with an always-on or low-current mode.

steps.title: Use the two buttons.
steps.do: S2 short: next song. S1 short: next light theme (pumpkin, fire, lightning, ghost, heartbeat, witch, music). S2 held 0.7 s: next sound mode (clean, haunted, graveyard, mad lab). S1 held 0.7 s: volume step. Both together, released within 2 s: shuffle on or off. Both held 2 to 5 s: speaker EQ on or off, to compare.
steps.see: Every action beeps, blinks the LED and prints a line on the serial console at 115200. Settings start fresh at each power-up.
steps.if: If the board does not start after you held S1 while plugging in, that button starts the chip's bootloader: unplug and plug in again without touching it.

steps.title: Make it yours: add your own track (no recorded run).
steps.do: Install `ffmpeg` first (`brew install ffmpeg`). The tool cuts, filters and encodes any audio file into the show; then run steps 1 and 2 again. The five shipped recordings use 174 s and leave room for about 22 s more: to add a longer song, delete one of them from `portability/boosterpacks/audio/tracks/` first.
steps.see: The tool prints the track it wrote; after steps 1 and 2, your song joins the shuffle.
steps.if: If the build reports the flash is full, shorten the new track with `--length` or drop another one from the folder.

variants.expect: After flashing and stacking the pack, the LaunchPad plays the show from a power bank with no computer: recordings and synth songs on shuffle, scare sounds between them, and the RGB LED following the music.
shows: One LaunchPad with 1 MB of flash plays recorded orchestra and organ music: five 30 to 40 s cuts at 10 kHz in IMA ADPCM, 849.6 kB together, played back at 16 kHz.
The sample interrupt keeps time with room to spare: 15,999 frames a second, 0 late, with the worst interrupt at 5.8k of its 10k-cycle budget.
A speaker EQ fitted from a measured tone sweep: 300 Hz high-pass, five peaking filters and a bass enhancer for a speaker whose response spreads 15.5 dB from 500 Hz to 4 kHz.
not_shows: The power bank's current draw and run time were not measured.
limits: The pack's microphone gets no power on this LaunchPad (BoosterPack pin 5 is not wired to the chip), so the clap and knock listener is off here.

Loudness stops rising above about volume step 10 of 16: a 1 kHz tone through a laptop microphone rose 8.6 dB from step 4 to 10 and 0.7 dB from 10 to 16. Whether the amplifier, the speaker or the microphone limits it was not separated.
Some power banks switch off under about 50 to 100 mA; the show has no low-power mode, so pick a bank that stays on.
The speaker EQ was fitted from a laptop's built-in microphone, taken as flat.

technical.v: 15,999, 0 late ticks over 480 s
5.8k of 10k cycles at 160 MHz

300 Hz high-pass, five peaking filters and a bass enhancer, fitted to a stepped tone sweep heard by a laptop microphone; the measured spread from 500 Hz to 4 kHz is 15.5 dB, the fit predicts 6.4 dB with the EQ
913.0 kB of 1,024 kB flash; 19.3 kB RAM

variants.name: A. On a microcontroller kit (LP-EM-CC35X1, LP-MSPM33C321A)
variants.short: A Cortex-M33 with 256 to 512 kB of RAM plays the three shareware demos. Build and flash from a Mac.

evidence.text: On the LP-EM-CC35X1 the three demos finish: 1,736, 3,092 and 3,881 frames, the frame checksums equal the emulator's, 39.2 frames a second after frame 400.
On the LP-MSPM33C321A with the Educational BoosterPack screen the game ran in real time at 22.7 frames a second with an 8 kB page cache and 24.5 with 16 kB.
On the same board the three demos finished from the QSPI flash at 19.9 frames a second (8 kB cache) and 21.9 (16 kB cache), with the emulator's frame checksums.
The plain engine needs 593 kB of zone memory at the least, which is why the rp2040-doom design is used here.

parts.included: Probe and cable.
parts.separate: Nothing.

prereqs: A Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39 and the Wi-Fi Toolbox (CC35X1 path), or the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00 with SysConfig 1.28.0 (M33 path). Versions are in `mac-setup/README.md`.
The game data. The shareware DOOM1.WAD is downloaded by `fetch.sh` and checked by SHA-1; this repository never holds it. The engine is GPL-2.0 (`ports/doom/LICENSING.md`).
The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/doom third-party tools mac-setup cc35x1`.
The CC35X1 flash holds the board's demo or another image. Back it up first with the command in `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`; the restore is a full flash erase.

steps.title: Fetch the engine and convert the game data.
steps.do: Fetch the engine at its pinned commit, patch it, download the shareware data file and convert it to the compact WHX format (1,758 kB).
steps.see: `wad-cache/DOOM1.whx` exists. `fetch.sh` checked the data file against its SHA-1.
steps.if: If `fetch.sh` stops on a hash mismatch, delete `wad-cache/` and run it again; do not use a file it refused.

steps.title: Build the LP-EM-CC35X1 image.
steps.do: Build and sign the image. The converted data file is linked into it and read in place from the board's flash.
steps.see: The script prints a build folder and the signed Toolbox files under `ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/`.
steps.if: If the link fails on region size, the build used the dual-image layout; the script switches OTA off, so rerun it from a clean checkout.

steps.title: Program the board.
steps.do: Connect the XDS110 probe and program the signed build with the Wi-Fi Toolbox, then reset the board.
steps.see: The programmer reports success for every region and the board resets.
steps.if: If the programmer fails with error -260 on every call, remove any BoosterPack and replug the probe cable.

steps.title: Read the demos finish.
steps.do: Open the probe's serial port at 921,600 baud. The console prints a checksum line every 100 frames and a line at each demo end.
steps.see: `CRC n xxxxxxxx` lines, then `DEMOEND k frames=` three times (1,736, 3,092 and 3,881 frames), `EXIT`, `FPS after400` near 39 and `DONE`.
steps.if: If the port prints nothing, check the baud rate: the console is 921,600 here, not 115,200.

steps.title: Or build it for the LP-MSPM33C321A screen.
steps.do: The M33 has 1 MB of flash, so the data file goes in the board's QSPI flash first (`ports/doom/m33-whx/E27-qspi-dump-and-load.md`). Then build the real-time screen image with the page cache and flash it with DSLite as in the other M33 pages.
steps.say: EDU=1 BOARD=1 WHXCACHE=8 RT=1 NOCRC=1 WHX_CRC32=0xe9018e36 m33-whx/build.sh 30
steps.see: With the Educational BoosterPack on the LaunchPad the 128 by 128 screen shows the Doom title, then the first demo at about 22 frames a second.
steps.if: If the screen stays blank, the QSPI write did not finish: read the flash back (the dump firmware in `m33-whx/board/`) and compare it with `wad-cache/DOOM1.whx`.

variants.expect: The LP-EM-CC35X1 plays the three shareware demos to the end and prints the rate and frame checksums on its console. The LP-MSPM33C321A draws the game on the BoosterPack screen.
shows: The rp2040-doom design fits a 256 kB chip: 228 kB of static data and zone, against 164 kB static plus 800 kB zone for the plain engine.
The CC35X1 plays three demos at 39.2 frames a second, with frame checksums equal to a Cortex-M33 emulator running the same image.
The MSPM33C321A reads 1.7 MB of game data from its QSPI flash through a software page cache (98 to 99 percent hits) and draws in real time at 22.7 frames a second.
not_shows: It has been played by hand with the BoosterPack's stick and buttons; the frame rate during hand play was not timed.
The 3.5 inch touch panel image for the CC35X1 builds and links; it has not been run on a panel.
Sound, and the other six levels of the shareware episode: only the three demo levels were played.
limits: The CC35X1 rate is on a stepped game clock, about three game tics per frame, so the demo runs faster than real time. It is not the same test as the M33's real-time 22.7.
A 16 kB page cache on the M33 leaves 151 bytes of RAM free.
The LP-MSPM0G3519 (128 kB of RAM) and LP-MSPM0G3507 (32 kB of RAM, 128 kB of flash) stop at static data alone.

technical.v: rp2040-doom: data kept compressed (WHX, 1,758 kB) and read in place; 16-bit pointers into a 256 kB window; a new renderer
39.2 frames a second at 160 MHz, render files at -O2, statics in the 128 kB fast RAM
22.7 (8 kB cache) and 24.5 (16 kB cache), real time, on the screen
256 bytes in 23.8 microseconds

variants.name: B. On the AM62L Linux board, straight to the screen
variants.short: The TMDS62LEVM draws Doom to the HDMI framebuffer with no GPU, 186 to 193 frames a second on the timing run, played with a game pad.

evidence.text: The timing demo runs at 185.8 to 192.7 frames a second at 1280 by 1000 (four runs), 240.6 at 960 by 800 and 412.9 unscaled, on both A53 cores at 1.25 GHz.
Chocolate Doom through Weston and Mesa llvmpipe ran the same demo at 6.54 frames a second, which is why this version writes to the framebuffer itself.
Stick up walks forward on a PS4 pad and the picture reads as 4:3 on the monitor; both were checked by eye on the board.

parts.included: The board.
parts.separate: A power supply, an HDMI monitor and cable, a network connection to the Mac.

parts.name: PS4 DualShock 4 game pad on a USB cable

prereqs: The AM62L booted from TI's SDK 12.01 Linux image with a network connection (`am62l-evm/README.md`). The image has no compiler, so the build runs in a Debian trixie arm64 container on the board.
The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/doom am62l-evm tools`.
The shareware DOOM1.WAD comes from `fetch.sh` on the Mac; the repository never holds it.

steps.title: Fetch the engine and the game data.
steps.do: Fetch the engine at its pinned commit, patch it and download the shareware data file.
steps.see: `src-upstream/doomgeneric/` and `wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD` exist, and the data file's SHA-1 was checked.
steps.if: If it stops on a hash mismatch, delete `wad-cache/` and run it again.

steps.title: Copy the sources to the board.
steps.do: Copy `srclist.sh`, `linux-fb/`, `src-upstream/doomgeneric/` and `wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD` into `/root/doom` on the board, keeping their folder names.
steps.see: `/root/doom` on the board holds the four items.
steps.if: If the board does not answer on the network, check its address on the serial console first.

steps.title: Build the game on the board.
steps.do: Build in the container on the board. It takes about 75 seconds on the two cores.
steps.see: `build/fb/doom_fb` exists.
steps.if: If the container cannot pull its image, the board has no route to the registry: fix the network, then rerun.

steps.title: Run the timing demo.
steps.do: Stop the display demo that owns the screen, then run the timing demo.
steps.see: The monitor shows the game at 4:3 and the last line reports 186 to 193 frames a second.
steps.if: If the screen stays on the display demo, `ti-lvgl-demo` did not stop: run `systemctl stop ti-lvgl-demo` again.
img: am62l/doom.png
Doom drawn on the AM62L's HDMI output

steps.title: Play with a game pad.
steps.do: Plug the pad into the board and start the game. Stick up walks forward; Cross fires, Square uses, Circle runs, Options is the menu.
steps.see: The game takes the pad and prints its frame rate every five seconds.
steps.if: If the buttons do the wrong thing on a DualShock 4, the kernel has `hid-generic` on the pad; the game prints `hid-generic DualShock 4 button table` at start and uses it. Any other pad uses the standard names.

steps.title: Give the screen back.
steps.do: Stop the game and start the display demo again.
steps.see: The monitor shows the board's display demo again.
steps.if: If the screen stays black, start the display demo again.

variants.expect: The AM62L draws Doom on its HDMI output with no GPU, and a game pad plays it.
shows: A frame-buffer port reaches 186 to 193 frames a second at 1280 by 1000; the same engine through Weston and a software GL renderer reaches 6.5.
The picture is 320 by 200 scaled by whole numbers to 1280 by 1000 and reads as 4:3 on the monitor.
not_shows: The timing figure is the engine's own timing run, not the monitor's refresh rate: there is no vsync, so a fast turn can tear.
Sound: the game runs with `-nosound`.
limits: The board reaches 413 frames a second unscaled and 241 at 960 by 800; the scale you pick sets the rate.
320 by 200 shown 4 by 5 times is 1280 by 1000, aspect 1.28 against the 1.33 of a 4:3 screen; it is the nearest whole-number pair that fits 1080 lines.

prereqs: A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and SysConfig 1.28.0 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders, and CCStudio 21.0.1 for its `DSLite` flasher (`mac-setup/README.md`).

The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports portability/boosterpacks mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
The game is Tobu Tobu Girl by Tangram Games (code MIT, art and music CC BY 4.0). `fetch_roms.sh` downloads it and stops on a hash mismatch; no commercial ROM is used or stored.
The board ships with a demo in its flash. To keep it, back it up first with the command in the board's `AGENTS.md`.

steps.title: Fetch the game.
steps.do: Download the two freely licensed test ROMs and check their hashes.
steps.see: `ports/peanut-gb/roms/` holds Tobu Tobu Girl and dmg-acid2.
steps.if: If it stops on a hash mismatch, delete `roms/` and run it again; do not use a file it refused.

steps.title: Build the 160 MHz image.
steps.do: Build the Educational BoosterPack app with the Game Boy emulator at 160 MHz, drawing every second frame.
steps.say:
cd portability/boosterpacks/edumkii
APP=gameboy EDU_CLK160=1 GB_FLAGS=-DPGB_FRAME_SKIP EDU_TAG=skip ./build.sh mspm33c321a
steps.see: The script prints the build folder and the `.out` image.
steps.if: If the SDK is not found, install it as `mac-setup/README.md` says and run the line again.

steps.title: Plug the BoosterPack on and flash.
steps.do: Stack the Educational BoosterPack on the LaunchPad. Copy `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<probe serial>.ccxml` to `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<serial>.ccxml` with your probe serial in place of `<probe serial>` (`xdsdfu -e` lists it), then flash the `.out` the build printed.
steps.see: The logos run first; the Tobu Tobu Girl title appears after about 28 seconds. A and B together press Start, A starts the game.
steps.if: If DSLite reports `Device Connection Error ... low power mode`, reset the probe with `xds110reset -s <serial> -a toggle -d 200` (it sits beside `xdsdfu`) and flash again.

shows: A Game Boy emulator keeps console speed on a Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz with a 128 by 128 screen: 0 late frames in 8,167.
The 160 by 144 picture is scaled to 128 by 128 by a lookup table while the next line renders and the rows stream out by DMA.
not_shows: Nobody has played it by hand: the buttons were driven by script on the Mac and the stick and buttons were not judged by a person on the board.
The screen shows every second frame, about 30 a second.
limits: Aspect ratio: the Game Boy picture is 160 by 144 (10 to 9); the screen shows it at 128 by 128, so it is 20 percent narrower and 11 percent shorter. The true ratio is not kept.

projects.t: Post-quantum on every board

g3507.why: ML-KEM-768 links for this board in 31.4 kB of flash and 28.4 kB of RAM with a 12 kB stack. It was never flashed

cc2340r5.why: Both algorithms with the same code, every step passes NIST's known-answer vectors, in 36 kB of RAM. ML-KEM-768 takes 42.0, 49.9 and 60.8 ms at -Os; ML-DSA-44 key pair 141 ms, verify 164 ms, sign 514 ms (reduced-RAM build, 15 kB of stack at most). Random bytes come from a fixed-seed generator: the chip's RNG driver did not link. No exchange with a Mac was run

f2800137.why: The C28x core has 16-bit chars and the libraries assume 8-bit bytes: both compile once uint8_t is supplied as a 16-bit type, but ML-KEM-768 key generation overruns the largest stack the 36 kB of RAM allows (21.9 kB) and ML-DSA-44 signing lists 44.7 kB of allocations; no known-answer test ran

cc1354p10.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 996,527 cycles (21 ms at 48 MHz) and decapsulation 1.40 million (29 ms); ML-DSA-44 signs in 7.4 million cycles; known-answer vectors pass. Measured 2026-10-08.

cc2755p10.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 961,256 cycles (10 ms at 96 MHz) and ML-DSA-44 signs in 4.77 million cycles (50 ms); known-answer vectors pass. Measured 2026-10-17.

g3519.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 1.97 million cycles (25 ms at 80 MHz) and ML-DSA-44 signs in 25.4 million (317 ms); known-answer vectors pass. Measured 2026-10-17.

mspm33c321a.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 1.29 million cycles (8 ms at 160 MHz) and ML-DSA-44 signs in 9.3 million (58 ms); known-answer vectors pass. Measured 2026-10-17.

g5187.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 1.995 million cycles (25 ms at 80 MHz); ML-DSA-44 key generation (84 ms) and verification (99 ms) run in a low-RAM build, but signing fails its known-answer tests. Measured 2026-11-02.

tda4.why: ML-KEM-768 key generation takes 148,546 cycles (about 74 Âµs at 2 GHz) and ML-DSA-44 signs in 1.18 million, on a Cortex-A72 core under Linux. Measured 2026-10-10.

cc1354p10.why: Both algorithms, and the full key exchange with a Mac over USB serial (the only board where it ran). ML-KEM-768 takes 20.8, 24.0 and 29.1 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 49.5 ms, verify 50.5 ms, sign 154 ms on average; signing needs 50 kB of stack. The board decrypted the Mac's AES-128-GCM line

mspm33c321a.why: Both algorithms with the same code, 6 of 6 steps pass NIST vectors. ML-KEM-768 takes 8.1, 9.2 and 11.3 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 19 ms, verify 19 ms, sign 39 ms. No key exchange with a Mac was run

g3519.why: Both algorithms on a Cortex-M0+ at 80 MHz with no cycle counter. ML-KEM-768 takes 24.6, 29.1 and 35.6 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 82 ms, verify 95 ms, sign 317 ms. No exchange with a Mac was run

g5187.why: ML-KEM-768 only: 24.9, 29.8 and 36.4 ms at -Os in 14 to 18 kB of stack. ML-DSA-44 does not fit its 32 kB of RAM (31 to 52 kB of stack). No exchange with a Mac was run

cc2755p10.why: Both algorithms. ML-KEM-768 takes 10.0, 11.6 and 14.1 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 23.9 ms, verify 24.3 ms, sign 49.7 ms at 96 MHz. The chip's hardware security module signs with ECDSA P-256 in 24 ms against 81 ms in software. No exchange with a Mac was run

am243x.why: Both algorithms in one image, default build, 96 kB stack, pass the known-answer tests in three RAM loads: ML-KEM-768 0.95, 1.08 and 1.34 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 2.4 ms, sign 5.2 ms, verify 2.5 ms. No exchange with a Mac was run

recipe.one_line: A TI board and a Mac agree on a secret key with ML-KEM-768, a method meant to stay safe against quantum computers, then swap one encrypted line. The same code also runs on four more boards.

variants.name: The key exchange with a Mac on the LP-CC1354P10-1
variants.short: Host test, build, then load the board and watch the exchange over USB serial.

evidence.text: On 2026-10-08 the board made its key pair from its hardware random generator, agreed a key with the Mac (key check d01a2f61 on both sides, MATCH) and decrypted the Mac's 76-byte AES-128-GCM line.
Every step passes NIST's known-answer vectors on the board before timing: ACVP key generation, two signing vectors, one valid and one invalid signature.

parts.role: makes the key pair and finishes the key
parts.included: The board with its built-in probe.
parts.separate: A USB cable. The run script power-cycles the board's USB port, so a hub port that `uhubctl` can switch.

prereqs: A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink CC13xx/CC26xx SDK 8.33.00.16 and OpenSSL 3.5 or later (`mac-setup/README.md`). The host test also needs Python with the `cryptography` package.

The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add cc1354p10 portability/pqc-join third-party tools mac-setup`.
This board's debugger connects only just after power-on, so loading needs a USB hub port the Mac can switch with `uhubctl` (`cc1354p10/FAQ.md`).
The run script backs up the board's 1 MB of flash first and writes it back at the end; it prints `READBACK MATCHES BACKUP` when the board is as it was.

steps.title: Run the host test.
steps.do: Build the board code for the Mac, run both sets of known-answer tests and the whole exchange against the Mac side. No board is needed.
steps.see: The last line is `pqc-join host test: OK`.
steps.if: If it stops on the OpenSSL version, install OpenSSL 3.5 or later and put it first on your path.

steps.title: Build the board image.
steps.do: Build at -O3, the timed build. It touches no hardware and takes about 20 seconds once SysConfig has run.
steps.see: The script ends with the path of the `.out` image.
steps.if: If SysConfig is not found, install it as `mac-setup/README.md` says and run the line again.

steps.title: Load the board and run the exchange.
steps.do: Set `UHUB` to your hub and port, and `RESTORE_IMG` to the `.out` you want left on the board afterwards. The run takes about two and a half minutes: 22 s to back up the flash, 18 s on the board, then restore and read-back.
steps.say: UHUB=<your hub>:<port> RESTORE_IMG=<path to the .out to leave running> cc1354p10/pqc-join/run.sh -O3
steps.see: The console shows `board> KAT PASS`, then `key check  Mac d01a2f61  board d01a2f61  MATCH`, then `board> DECRYPTED (76 bytes, tag ok)` and the Mac's line. The script ends with `READBACK MATCHES BACKUP`.
steps.if: If the exchange stops at `join: making an ML-KEM-768 key pair`, the image did not start the random generator; build from this repository's `pqc_board.c`, which calls `TRNG_init()` before `TRNG_open()`.

variants.expect: The board and the Mac end with the same 4-byte key check and the board prints the decrypted line.
shows: ML-KEM-768 takes 20.8, 24.0 and 29.1 ms on a 48 MHz Cortex-M33; ML-DSA-44 verifies in 50.5 ms and signs in 154 ms on average.
The board's own work in the exchange is about 73 ms; the wire at 115,200 baud takes about 420 ms.
The same portable C, unmodified mlkem-native 2.0.0 and mldsa-native 2.0.0, runs on four more boards (the other rows below).
not_shows: The exchange with a Mac ran on this board only. On the other four boards the algorithms ran and passed their vectors; no exchange was run.
No protection against power or fault attacks is claimed. This is a demonstration of the math and its cost. Do not use it for real keys.
limits: Signing needs 50 kB of stack, so a board needs about 64 kB of RAM for ML-DSA-44; the LP-MSPM0G5187 (32 kB) runs ML-KEM-768 only.
Signing time varies from 77 to 361 ms with the message, because a candidate signature is sometimes thrown away and retried.

parts.included: Probe and cable.

prereqs: A Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39 and the Wi-Fi Toolbox (`mac-setup/README.md`), and a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network the board can join.

The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/dns-sinkhole cc35x1 tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
The blocklist is StevenBlack/hosts (MIT). It merges third-party lists: read its README for their terms before redistributing the file. Do not commit it.
The Wi-Fi name and password are compiled into the image. Keep the built image out of git. Back up the board first with the command in `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`.

steps.title: Get a blocklist.
steps.do: Download the hosts file.
steps.see: `hosts.txt` exists and lists tens of thousands of names.
steps.if: If curl fails, check the network and run it again.

steps.title: Make the table.
steps.do: Hash and sort the names: 5 bytes per domain.
steps.see: `blocklist.bin` is about 349 kB.
steps.if: If Python reports a syntax error, use Python 3.12 or newer (`.python-version`).

steps.title: Build and sign.
steps.do: Build the full blocker. The Wi-Fi name comes from the Mac's saved networks and the password from a file you name. It takes about two minutes. `APP=min ./build.sh` builds stage 1, which answers 192.0.2.1 to every name.
steps.see: The script prints the build folder with `ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/tool_settings.json`.
steps.if: If it cannot read the network name, macOS hides it from command-line tools: set it in the file you pass as `WIFI_ENV`.

steps.title: Program the board.
steps.do: Program the signed build with the Wi-Fi Toolbox, then reset the board. Add `-param1 <probe serial>` when more than one probe is connected.
steps.see: The programmer reports success; the console at 115200 baud shows the board's address.
steps.if: If the programmer fails with error -260 on every call, remove any BoosterPack and replug the probe cable.

steps.title: Ask the board.
steps.do: Ask for a listed name and an unlisted one. Your Mac's settings do not change.
steps.say:
dig @<board ip> doubleclick.net
dig @<board ip> www.python.org
steps.see: The first answer is 0.0.0.0. The second is the real address.
steps.if: If dig times out, check the board joined your network: the console prints its address, and a router may hand it a new one, so reserve it.

steps.title: Point one device at it, then undo it.
steps.do: Set one device's DNS server to the board's address in its network settings. To go back, set it to automatic. The board is not inline, so unplugging it only affects devices pointed at it.
steps.see: The counters page shows blocked and forwarded names rising as that device browses.
steps.if: If the device loses the network, set its DNS back to automatic.

variants.expect: The board answers 0.0.0.0 for blocklisted names and the real address for the rest.
shows: A 71,492-name blocklist fits the board as a sorted table of 5-byte hashes searched in place in flash: 349 kB of flash and 0.7 kB of RAM.
A blocked name is answered in a median 6 ms.
not_shows: No DNSSEC: answers are relayed as the upstream gave them, not validated.
Nobody ran it as a household's only resolver for days.
limits: Exact name match only: a listed name does not block its subdomains.
IPv4 and UDP only, no caching, 16 queries in flight, a 2.5 s forward timeout.
A 40-bit hash means an unlisted name matches with a probability of about 7e-8. The largest list the application slot takes is about 304,000 names (link arithmetic, not booted).

technical.v: median 6 ms, 95th percentile 20 ms
median 70 ms, 95th percentile 172 ms (router directly: 52 and 99)
random 16-bit ID from the hardware generator, a fresh random UDP port per query, random upper and lower case in the name

projects.t: A Lisp prompt on a LaunchPad

g3507.why: The same source builds: 98.8 kB of 128 kB flash and 23.1 kB of 32 kB RAM. It was not flashed

cc2340r5.why: The interpreter runs from the board's serial port: 19 of 19 REPL checks pass, the stack-overflow guard fires, (tak 18 12 6) takes 10.8 s and (fib 23) 7.5 s at 48 MHz with the same 2,800-object workspace as the MSPM0 builds; 98.6 kB of flash, 24.6 kB of static RAM. A plain register-variable read of the stack pointer never fired the guard under TI Arm Clang; an explicit move fixed it

l1306.why: The smallest uLisp image is 100.2 kB of flash against the chip's 64 kB (34.7 kB over, even with link-time optimization); RAM would fit with a 24-object workspace

f2800137.why: 19 of 19 REPL checks in three runs from the board's serial port after the sketch's ints were widened to 32 bits for the 16-bit C28x; (tak 18 12 6) takes 8.1 s and (fib 23) 5.3 s at 120 MHz with a 2,000-object workspace; 141.9 kB of flash, 28.7 kB of RAM, written as a raw binary. Faster than the CC2340R5 on the clock, about 2.5 times the clocks per step

g5187.why: A Lisp prompt on the USB serial port passes 19 of 19 REPL checks; (tak 18 12 6) takes 7.5 s at 80 MHz; the image is 98.8 kB of flash. Measured 2026-10-21.

g3519.why: The same source builds: 99.0 kB of 512 kB flash and 71.6 kB of 128 kB RAM. It was not flashed

cc2755p10.why: 19 of 19 REPL checks three times from the board's serial port; (tak 18 12 6) takes 3.1 s and (fib 23) 2.2 s at 96 MHz with the same 2,800-object workspace, 3.4 times the CC2340R5's speed for twice the clock; 96.7 kB of flash, 24.8 kB of static RAM. The stack guard never fired: the workspace fills first

g5187.why: 19 of 19 REPL checks and 5 benchmark runs pass; `(tak 18 12 6)` takes 7.5 s at 80 MHz; the image is 98.8 kB of flash and 23.1 kB of RAM

g3519.why: The same source builds: 99.0 kB of flash and 71.6 kB of RAM with a 9,000-object workspace. It was not flashed

am243x.why: 20 of 20 REPL checks in three RAM loads; (tak 18 12 6) takes 0.91 s and (fib 23) 0.70 s at 800 MHz with the 2,800-object workspace. The LED was read back at the register, not seen

mspm33c321a.why: 19 of 19 REPL checks in three runs and the stack-overflow guard fires; (tak 18 12 6) takes 2.5 to 2.6 s and (fib 23) 1.7 s at 160 MHz with the 2,800-object workspace (two flash wait states at that clock); 87.7 kB of flash, 23.2 kB of static RAM. The UART needs its receive-timeout interrupt on, or the console answers one line late

steps.do: Put an Arm GCC on your path and build. It takes about 20 seconds.

steps.do: Flash the image and read three seconds of the console. The check passes when `uLisp` appears.
steps.see: The tool prints a pass.

steps.title: Type Lisp.
steps.do: Open the board's serial port at 115200 baud. The port name carries your probe serial. Press `~` to stop a running program.

variants.expect: A Lisp prompt on the serial port that evaluates what you type.
shows: An unmodified Lisp interpreter runs on a Cortex-M0+ with 32 kB of RAM, with 2,800 objects of workspace.
`(tak 18 12 6)` takes 7.5 s at 80 MHz; the Arduino Zero (48 MHz) takes 11.4 s and the Raspberry Pi Pico (200 MHz) 2.6 s, from uLisp's published tables.
not_shows: Analog read, sound, SPI and I2C are stubs. The LED path was driven by hand, and the repository's LED check read the pin toggling but printed FAIL for the run because it reads at the instant of reset.
limits: Ran on one board. The LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0G3519 images build and were not flashed.
The workspace is 2,800 objects on the 32 kB parts, 9,000 on the G3519.

evidence.text: On 2026-10-20 the app played a 1 kHz tone and the four-voice tune. The microphone capture read 1000.0 Hz with 99.9 percent of the energy within 50 Hz; the tune's dominant frequency read 1046.5 Hz. Both were heard by ear.
Sending the DAC two 8-bit transfers instead of one 16-bit frame gave silence in every amplifier state.
The tuner, spectrum, DTMF and gate code passes its Mac tests against double-precision references, and the apps image builds for this board.

prereqs: A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (for `DSLite`), TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders (`mac-setup/README.md`).

The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add portability/boosterpacks am13e230 tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
The board ships with empty flash. If it holds your own program, back it up first with the command in `am13e230/AGENTS.md`.

steps.title: Hear the code on the Mac first.
steps.do: Build the DAC and synth code for the Mac. A model of the DAC8311 input stage checks every frame, then the test renders the tone and the tune to WAV files. No board is needed.
steps.see: A `host/out` folder holds `tone_1khz.wav` and `fox_run.wav`.
steps.if: If the compiler is missing, install the Xcode command line tools and run the line again.

steps.title: Build the app for the LP-AM13E230.
steps.do: Build at -O2. Nothing is flashed. The image is 16.9 kB of flash.
steps.see: The script leaves `audio.out` under `out/boosterpack-speedrun/am13-audio-default/`.
steps.if: If the SDK is not found, install it as `mac-setup/README.md` says and run the line again.

steps.title: Plug the pack on and flash.
steps.do: Plug the BOOSTXL-AUDIO onto the LaunchPad. Copy `am13e230/AM13E23019_<probe serial>.ccxml` to `am13e230/AM13E23019_<serial>.ccxml` with your probe serial, then flash.
steps.see: DSLite ends with `System Reset is issued.` and `Running...`.
steps.if: If it then prints `Failed: Target is not halted`, that is the normal end of a flash on this board: the program is running.

steps.title: Play the tone.
steps.do: Open the board's serial port at 115200 baud (`/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1`). Press `a` to drive the amplifier line low, then `1` for the 1 kHz tone. `0` is silence.
steps.see: A clear 1 kHz tone from the pack's speaker.
steps.if: If it stays silent, press `a` first: the amplifier plays only with its line driven low. Key `8` sends the wrong frame on purpose and is silent in every amplifier state.

steps.title: Play the tune and listen back.
steps.do: Press `2` for the four-voice tune "Fox Run", which loops. Press `m` to power the microphone, then `c` to capture 2,048 samples at 8 kHz. Keep the volume at 4 or lower (`v` lowers it) for a level reading. `tools/mic_analyze.py` reads the printed capture and reports its dominant frequency.
steps.see: The tune plays. A capture taken during the tone reads a dominant frequency of 1000.0 Hz.
steps.if: If the capture is pinned at its top values, the microphone clipped: lower the volume. With the speaker beside the microphone it clips from volume 8 up.

steps.title: Check the microphone algorithms on the Mac.
steps.do: Run the tuner, spectrum bars, DTMF decoder and noise gate against double-precision references, on synthetic and recorded signals.
steps.see: The run ends with every check passing; the log is `results/host-algos-20261020.log`.
steps.if: If a check reports a difference larger than the README's table, do not build the apps image until it is understood.

steps.title: Build the apps image.
steps.do: Build the image with the tuner, spectrum, DTMF decoder and gate. It builds and sizes at 29.6 kB of flash and 22.1 kB of RAM; it was not run on the board.
steps.see: The script leaves `audio.out` under `out/boosterpack-speedrun/am13-audio-algos/`.
steps.if: If the build stops on the SDK path, set it as in step 2.

variants.expect: The pack plays a clean 1 kHz tone and a four-voice tune, and its microphone reads the tone back at 1000.0 Hz.
shows: A plain GPIO driver sends 16-bit frames to the pack's DAC8311 from a motor-control chip, with 16 clock pulses and the chip-select held low for the whole frame.
The pack's microphone reads 1000.0 Hz with 99.9 percent of the energy within 50 Hz.

The tuner holds within 0.6 cent on clean tones from 82 to 500 Hz, the 16 spectrum bars within 1.3 pixels of a double-precision DFT above 30 pixels, and the DTMF decoder decodes a 16-digit sequence exactly down to 2 dB signal to noise, all on the Mac.
not_shows: The tuner, spectrum, DTMF and gate code did not run on a board: they were checked on the Mac and built for the LP-AM13E230 and LP-MSPM33C321A.
The gate and echo were not heard on the speaker. The DTMF decoder was tested with white noise only, not speech or music.
limits: The synth runs at 8 kHz, so nothing above 4 kHz plays.
The SPI lines are bit-banged. The DAC is on SPI only: the pack's jumper positions for the LaunchPad DAC and for PWM are not tested.
The LP-MSPM33C321A and LP-MSPM0G3519 build the same app and were not run with the pack on. The pack cannot be driven from the LP-MSPM0G5187 without wires.

within 0.6 cent for clean tones 82 to 500 Hz; no octave errors in 456 tests

evidence.text: liblc3 v1.1.3 encodes 16, 24 and 48 kHz mono 10 ms frames in 12.4, 15.6 and 24.2 percent of real time and decodes them in 4.6, 7.1 and 10.5 percent at 160 MHz. The CRC-32 of every encoded frame and decoded block equals the Mac build in all three configurations.
With the float unit off the same core needs 120 to 262 percent of real time to encode.

parts.role: runs the codec and times it with its cycle counter
parts.included: The board with its built-in probe.
parts.separate: A USB-C cable.

prereqs: A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and CCStudio 21.0.1 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders (`mac-setup/README.md`), and a C compiler for the Mac reference.

The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports portability mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
Run `cd ports/llama2c && PYTHON=python3 ./build.sh O2` once from the repository folder; the codec builds reuse its `gen160` SysConfig output (point `G` at it if a build cannot find it).
The runner flashes the board and leaves the benchmark image on it. To keep what is on the board, back it up first with the command in `mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`.

steps.title: Build the Mac reference.
steps.do: Build the strict and fast-math references with a per-frame CRC for each frame.
steps.see: The Mac references are built under `ports/lc3/results/host`.
steps.if: If the compiler is missing, install the Xcode command line tools and run it again.

steps.title: Build the board image.
steps.do: Build at -O2 with the float unit on and strict arithmetic. Nothing is flashed.
steps.see: The script ends with `built .../lc3.out` and a size line.
steps.if: If it cannot find the SysConfig output, set `G` to the `gen160` folder from the prerequisites.

steps.title: Flash the board and compare.
steps.do: Flash the image, wait for the finished flag, read the results back over the probe and compare every checksum with the Mac reference. It prints cycles, the share of real time and the stack use. It plays no sound and drives no pin.
steps.say:
cd ../..
PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/lc3/run_board.py <path of lc3.out>
steps.see: The CRCs match and the printed shares are about 12, 16 and 24 percent for encoding at 16, 24 and 48 kHz.
steps.if: If the probe is not found, pass the serial of your probe that `xdsdfu -e` lists.

wiring.alt: The BP-CC1407P-9-FE radio board with eight color-coded wires, each tagged with the LP-MSPM0G5187 pin it goes to
wiring.note: Radio pins 1 to 10 run down the left outer row and 11 to 20 up the right outer row (20 at the top). Pins 23 and 36 are in the inner rows: 23 is the third socket down the left inner row, 36 the fifth down the right inner row. J20 is the 2x4 header by the microSD slot, printed PB12 PB10 PB8 PB6 over PB13 PB11 PB9 PB7. PB10 and PB11 also reach the board's audio converter, so the board's microphone cannot be used while the radio is wired.

steps.title: Wire the radio to the LaunchPad.
steps.do: With USB unplugged, screw the 915 MHz antenna onto the radio board's SMA socket and join the radio to the LP-MSPM0G5187's J20 header with the eight wires in the table. Plug the other LaunchPad into the Mac.
steps.see: Each wire's other end is on the pin in the table.
steps.if: If the radio later answers with a checksum error on everything it receives, the inner-row wires (pins 23 and 36) are the usual missing ones.

steps.title: Build the CC1407P side.
steps.do: Build `radio_lab`, which turns the LP-MSPM0G5187 into a radio driven by text commands on its serial port.
steps.see: The script ends with `image: mspm0g5187/radio/out/radio_lab.out`.
steps.if: If the SDK is not found, set the paths the script prints.

steps.title: Build the partner side on the CC1354P10.
steps.do: Follow the Build section of `cc1354p10/radio-rx/README.md` to get the F2 SDK libraries and the `rfPacketRx` example, then build `partner.c` as that README describes, with the Wi-SUN FSK mode 2b setting (`phyType868`, `#define RX_ADV`).
steps.see: The build leaves `rfPacketRx.hex`, about 29 kB.
steps.if: If the make cannot find SysConfig, point `SYSCONFIG_TOOL` at `sysconfig_cli.sh` in the 1.28.0 folder, as the README shows.

steps.title: Flash both boards.
steps.do: Put each probe's serial in its `.ccxml` (`xdsdfu -e` lists them). Flash `radio_lab.out` to the LP-MSPM0G5187 and `rfPacketRx.hex` to the CC1354P10, then start the CC1354P10 with `xds110reset`.
steps.see: Both boards answer on their serial ports.
steps.if: If DSLite fails with `Error -242`, unplug the board's USB for 3 seconds and flash again.

steps.title: Send a voice message.
steps.do: Set the two serial ports and run the demo. It speaks "Hi Mom! This is Fox Red Labs, talking over a nine hundred fifteen megahertz radio. Over.", sends it in 50 ms frames, receives it and writes both recordings. The result is added to `site/data/radio-demos.json`.
steps.say: LAB_G=/dev/cu.usbmodem<G5187 serial>1 LAB_P=/dev/cu.usbmodem<partner probe serial>1 python3 mspm0g5187/radio/demos.py voice
steps.see: The run reports 122 frames received. `site/media/radio-demos/voice-sent.wav` and `voice-received.wav` play the same message.
steps.if: If a frame is cut short, the CC1354P10's serial input dropped characters while it was sending; run it again.

Range was not measured: both boards were on one desk.

projects.t: Button, knob and dimmer
projects.what: Read the board's own S2 button, read a knob with the analog-to-digital converter, and dim an LED with PWM, in one short build on a breadboard.
projects.time: One sitting, not yet timed
projects.q: read a button and a knob and dim an LED with them
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: Press S2 to toggle an LED, turn a knob to dim it.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Easy. Five wires and one resistor on a breadboard; the button is on the board.
glance.time: One sitting, not yet timed

how: S2 on the board pulls its pin to ground when you press it, and the chip's internal pull-up holds the pin high otherwise, so the program reads a low level for a press. It waits 20 ms after an edge before it believes the next one. The knob is a voltage divider: its middle pin sits between 0 V and 3.3 V, and the analog-to-digital converter turns that voltage into a number from 0 to 4095.

PWM switches the LED on and off 1,000 times a second. The share of each cycle that the LED is on sets how bright it looks, so the program turns the knob's number into that share. The program also prints the number, the LED state and the duty on the serial port twice a second.

steps.title: Build and flash the program

steps.do: Press S2, the button on the board.
steps.see: The LED toggles on each press.
steps.if: If nothing happens, check that the LED's resistor leg is on J3 pin 28 and its other leg on ground. The pins are listed in `portability/hobby/button-knob-dim/PINS.md`.
steps.title: Press S2

steps.do: Turn the knob slowly from one end to the other.
steps.see: The LED gets brighter as you turn one way and dimmer the other way. The serial port (115200 baud) prints a line like `adc=914 led=on duty=22` twice a second.
steps.if: If it only jumps between off and full, the middle pin is on a digital pin or the outer pins are swapped; check the pin table.
steps.title: Turn the knob

steps.do: Open `portability/hobby/button-knob-dim/app.c` in a text editor. Change `PWM_PERIOD_US`, stop the knob at half brightness, or make S2 hold the LED on for two seconds. Run the command from step 2 after each change.
steps.see: The change shows within seconds of the flash.
steps.if: If the old behavior is still there, the flash did not finish: run the command from the build step again and wait for done.

projects.t: Traffic light, police strobe and a buzzer tune
projects.what: Three LEDs run a traffic light, a two-button reaction game times your press, and a passive buzzer plays a 14-note melody, in a loop.
projects.time: One sitting, not yet timed
projects.q: run a traffic light, a police strobe and a buzzer tune
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: A traffic light, a reaction game and a melody run in a loop.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Easy. Three LEDs with resistors, a buzzer and a second button on a breadboard.
glance.time: One sitting, not yet timed

how: Each LED is a simple output: a high level lights it, a low level turns it off. The traffic light is a list of which LEDs are on and for how long (red 3 s, green 3 s, yellow 1 s), and the program walks down the list. Every step prints a line on the serial port.

In the reaction game the red LED lights, the program waits a random 2 to 5 s, then lights green, and the first button pressed wins; its time in milliseconds prints. Pressing early is a foul. A passive buzzer makes sound only when its pin switches on and off at the pitch you want, so the melody changes the PWM rate for each of its 14 notes.

projects.t: Parking sensor
projects.what: An ultrasonic distance sensor measures how far away your hand or a wall is, and a buzzer beeps faster as the distance shrinks.
projects.time: One sitting, not yet timed
projects.q: measure distance and beep faster as something gets closer
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: The buzzer beeps faster as you move your hand toward the sensor.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. One sensor, one buzzer, and a 3.3 V sensor on purpose.
glance.time: One sitting, not yet timed

how: The program sends a short pulse on the trigger pin. The sensor sends out a burst of ultrasound and raises the echo pin until the sound comes back. The time the echo pin stays high is the round trip, so the distance is that time halved and multiplied by the speed of sound.

A counter that runs freely at the CPU clock stamps the rising and falling edges of the echo pin, so the program does not need a hardware capture. The distance sets the beep: 40 ms beeps, with a gap of 60 ms plus 5 ms for each centimeter, and silence beyond 100 cm.

recipe.outcome: Parking sensor that beeps faster as you get close
recipe.one_line: An RCWL-1601 ultrasonic sensor and a buzzer; the closer you get, the faster it beeps and the serial port prints the distance.
recipe.learn: Timing an echo pulse with a timer capture, and turning distance into beep rate.

projects.t: Room weather station
projects.what: A DHT11 sensor reads temperature and humidity and a 0.96 inch OLED shows them; the Sensors BoosterPack's own humidity sensor can sit beside it.
projects.time: One evening, not yet timed
projects.q: show room temperature and humidity on a small screen
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: The OLED shows the room's temperature and humidity every 2 seconds.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. Two parts on the breadboard, one on a one-wire pin and one on I2C.
glance.time: One evening, not yet timed

how: The DHT11 sends its reading as 40 bits on one wire. A short pulse from the board wakes it, and then the length of each pulse it sends back says whether the bit is a 0 or a 1. The program times those pulses with a timer.
The OLED is an I2C device. The program sends it drawing commands over two wires, and the u8g2 library turns letters and numbers into the right dots.

how: A hobby servo has a small motor and a position sensor inside. Every 20 ms the program sends it a pulse, and the width of the pulse, about 1 ms to 2 ms, tells the servo which angle to hold. A timer makes the pulse in hardware, so the program only changes the width.

projects.t: Motion alarm with a counter
projects.what: A PIR motion sensor sets off a buzzer, and a four-digit display counts each time something moves in front of it.
projects.time: One sitting, not yet timed
projects.q: sound an alarm and count motion with a PIR sensor
projects.headline: Not run.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. A 5 V sensor with a 3.3 V output, plus a display on two wires.
glance.time: One sitting, not yet timed

how: The PIR module watches for a change in infrared from a warm body crossing its field. When it sees one it raises its output pin and holds it for a time you set with a trim pot. The program watches that pin and counts each rising edge.
The TM1637 chip on the display module scans four digits on its own. The program sends it the digits over a two-wire protocol of its own, a clock and a data line.

projects.t: Motor speed from a knob
projects.what: A rotary knob sets the speed and direction of a small DC motor through a DRV8833 motor driver, with the speed shown on a four-digit display.
projects.time: One evening, not yet timed
projects.q: set a motor's speed and direction with a rotary knob
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: Turn the knob and the motor speeds up or slows down; press it to reverse.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. Solder four header pins first, then 12 wires.
glance.time: One evening, not yet timed

how: The DRV8833 is an H-bridge: four switches that connect the motor to power one way or the other. The program drives two inputs with PWM. A PWM signal on AIN1 with AIN2 low spins the motor one way at a speed set by the share of time AIN1 is high; the other way around spins it backward.
The KY-040 knob has two switches that open and close in sequence as you turn it. Which one changes first tells the program the direction, and each step changes the speed by one notch.

projects.t: Addressable LED ring and strip
projects.what: An 8-LED ring from the Freenove kit runs a rainbow and a few effects, then a 60-LED strip runs the same effects.
projects.time: One evening, not yet timed
projects.q: light an addressable LED ring and strip with effects
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: A rainbow runs round the ring and along the strip.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. One data wire, and a separate power supply for the strip.
glance.time: One evening, not yet timed

how: Each WS2812 LED reads 24 bits of color from the wire, keeps its own, and passes the rest on to the next LED. A 0 and a 1 differ only in how long the signal stays high within a fixed time slot.

The program turns each bit into a short pattern of SPI bits so that the SPI clock makes the right slot timing. Sending the pattern in the SPI hardware keeps the timing exact without the program counting cycles.

projects.t: Relay lamp from a button
projects.what: A push button switches a 12 V lamp through a relay, the first step toward a lamp that a phone or Home Assistant can switch.
projects.time: One evening, not yet timed
projects.q: switch a low-voltage lamp through a relay
projects.headline: Not run.

card.outcome: Press a button and a 12 V lamp switches on and off.

merit.text: not run

glance.difficulty: Medium. A relay coil, a diode and a low-voltage lamp. Never mains.
glance.time: One evening, not yet timed

how: A relay is a switch moved by a magnet. A pin cannot drive the coil directly, so a transistor does it: the pin turns the transistor on, current flows through the coil, and the contacts close. The lamp's supply is only ever connected to the contacts, never to the board.

When the coil switches off, it pushes a voltage spike backward. The diode across the coil gives that spike somewhere to go so the transistor survives. The program reads the button and flips the relay's state on each press.

recipe.one_line: A button, a relay and a low-voltage lamp: the board switches something real.

system.role: records, wakes, encodes Opus and plays the reply

system.name: xiaozhi server
system.role: speech to text, the language model, text to speech

how: The pack's microphone is sampled at 16 kHz, packed as Opus in 60 ms packets and sent over a WebSocket to a xiaozhi server on your network. The server transcribes it, asks a language model, speaks the reply with a text-to-speech service and sends Opus back, which the board decodes into the pack's DAC and speaker.

The screen is optional. It draws one of four looks (Core, HUD, Visor, Kid) for each state: asleep, waiting, listening, thinking, talking. A swipe changes the look and it is remembered across resets; a long press opens volume, brightness, look and wake settings, and the Kid look opens offline games that run entirely on the chip. The pictures on this page are drawn by the same renderer the board runs.
This is a port of the open-source xiaozhi project (the device side and protocol of xiaozhi-esp32 and the xiaozhi-esp32-server, both MIT-licensed) to a TI chip.

recipe.outcome: A voice assistant on a LaunchPad
recipe.one_line: A LaunchPad with the Audio BoosterPack hears you, asks a language model through a server on your network and speaks the answer. Add the 3.5 inch touch panel for four animated looks and offline kids' games.

variants.name: Voice assistant, with or without the screen
variants.short: Run a xiaozhi server, build and program the image, join Wi-Fi over Bluetooth, press a key and ask.

evidence.text: Three questions spoken by a Mac about 30 cm from the pack were each transcribed word for word; the first reply audio started 2.28 to 2.67 s (median 2.47 s) after the question ended, with Claude Haiku as the language model. Measured on 2026-10-29. The speaker's sound quality was not judged by ear; the counters say every decoded sample played.
Five boots from reset to the ready line with Wi-Fi joined took 5.9 to 6.7 s (median 6.5 s).
The first voice build is 1,577 kB of flash (of a 2,696 kB slot) and 190 kB of static RAM, plus a 319 kB task heap.

prereqs: The code is in this repository. Clone it first: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Every command below runs from inside it.

TI's free tools: the CC35X1 SDK, SysConfig, TI Arm Clang and the SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox, each from ti.com; `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board cc35x1` lists which are missing and where to get them. Opus, TFLite Micro and the other libraries are in the repository.

A language model the server can call. This build used Claude Haiku through the relay in `ports/xiaozhi/host/`, which caps calls at 8 a minute and 150 a day; a local model through the server's own config works the same way.

wiring.note: Only for the optional screen. Header pins are the LP-EM-CC35X1's (SDK board file and the user's guide). LCD_DC and LCD_RST avoid header pins 25 and 26, which reach the chip through ADC buffers on this LaunchPad. Pin 30 also runs to the audio pack's J5 jumper: keep J5 on SPI DAC. None of these pins is used by the audio pack.
pins: reads the panel ID back at start
low while a finger is down

steps.title: Start a xiaozhi voice server.
steps.do: The board does the listening and the speaking; a server on your network turns speech into text, asks the language model and speaks the answer. Run the open-source xiaozhi-esp32-server (MIT license) in Docker on a computer on the same Wi-Fi, with a speech-to-text and a text-to-speech provider in its config. This build used FunASR, Edge TTS and Claude Haiku through a small rate-limited relay (`ports/xiaozhi/host/claude_relay.py`, which keeps the API key out of the server's config). Note the computer's IPv4 address.
steps.see: The server listens on port 8000, path `/xiaozhi/v1/`.
steps.if: If the board later says No server, check that the computer's firewall allows port 8000 from the Wi-Fi.

steps.title: Stack the audio pack, and the screen if you have one.
steps.do: Press the BOOSTXL-AUDIO onto the LaunchPad headers. For the screen, wire the 3.5 inch touch panel as in the wiring picture and the wire table above; keep the pack's J5 jumper on its default SPI DAC position.
steps.see: The pack sits flat on the headers. No wire is needed for voice alone.
steps.if: If you skip the screen, nothing else changes: the image runs the same without a panel attached.

steps.title: Build the firmware.
steps.do: Clone the repository, put your Wi-Fi name and password in a small file (`HOME_SSID=...` and `WIFI_PASSWORD=...`) outside the repository, and build with the server's address. The values go into the firmware copy under `out/`, never into the repository. `XZ_WAKE=0` builds push-to-talk (see the limits for the wake word). The build needs 1.5 GB of free disk and flashes nothing.
steps.say: XZ_WAKE=0 XZ_HOST=<server IPv4> WIFI_ENV=<your wifi file> ports/xiaozhi/target-cc35x1/build.sh
steps.see: `out/xiaozhi-cc35x1/b/xiaozhi.out` and a `b/toolbox/` folder of signed images. The image is about 1.6 MB of the board's 2.7 MB application slot.
steps.if: If a tool is missing the script names it and its download page; `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board cc35x1` lists what is missing.

steps.title: Program the board with the Wi-Fi Toolbox.
steps.do: From TI's SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox folder, program the image over the board's debug probe, then reset it with `xds110reset` (the Toolbox does not reset afterwards). Programming takes under a minute. If the board ran another program before, erase it first with `full_flash_erase` as `cc35x1/AGENTS.md` says.
steps.say:
./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> programming --tool_settings <repository folder>/out/xiaozhi-cc35x1/b/toolbox/tool_settings.json
xds110reset -s <probe serial>
steps.see: The console on the probe's serial port (115200 baud) prints a ready line about 6.5 s after reset, once the board has joined Wi-Fi.
steps.if: If the board does not answer, it may be in the other flash slot after an over-the-air update: erase, then program again (the FAQ for the board has the exact commands).

steps.title: Give it your Wi-Fi over Bluetooth.
steps.do: If you built without a network, or it cannot join, the blue LED lights and the board advertises as `TI CC3xxx`. Send the network name and password with TI's SimpleLink Connect phone app, or from a computer with `ports/wifi-provisioning-ble/provision.py`. The board saves the network and joins it at every start. Holding S2 for 5 seconds (or typing `W` on the console) forgets it.
steps.see: The board joins and prints its IPv4 address.
steps.if: If it never advertises, wait: it tries the saved or built-in network three times first.

steps.title: Ask it something.
steps.do: Press S2, or type `s` on the console, and ask a question about 30 cm from the pack. The microphone stops while the answer plays, so wait for it to finish; one turn per press.
steps.see: Your words are transcribed on the server and the first reply audio starts about 2.5 s after you stop (median 2.47 s, three questions, Claude Haiku).
steps.if: If the reply is quiet or distorted, `v` and `V` set the volume (0 to 16, starts at 6); the microphone clips beside the speaker from about 8.

steps.title: With a model of your own: say Hey Sparky.
steps.do: Build without `XZ_WAKE=0` and with `XZ_WAKE_MODEL=<your microWakeWord .tflite>` (its `.json` beside it). The board listens by itself, opens the connection only when it hears the phrase, runs one turn, closes it and listens again, with a 2 s deaf period after each reply.
steps.see: The console prints `[wake] ready`; on the screen the word line reads Say "Hey Sparky".
steps.if: The Hey Sparky model itself is not published (see the limits), so this step is for your own phrase.

steps.title: Look A, Core (the default).
steps.do: Swipe left or right anywhere, or press LOOK in the settings strip (hold a finger still for 1 s to open it), to step Core, HUD, Visor, Kid.
steps.see: An energy orb in a ring: the ring lights with the voice, comets circle while it thinks, a crown of rays rises while it talks.
img: sparky/sparky-look-core-listening.png
Look A, Core: a green orb in a lit ring with the word Listening and a status strip of chip temperature, Wi-Fi and motion
steps.if: If nothing happens on a swipe, check the panel wiring and that the image was built with the screen (the default).

steps.title: Look B, HUD.
steps.do: Swipe to the next look.
steps.see: A thin-line instrument in cyan on black with one amber accent: a mic level while listening, SPEAKING with a level bar while it talks, mode and wake word at the sides.
img: sparky/sparky-look-hud-listening.png
Look B, HUD: a cyan 270 degree dial reading MIC LEVEL 50 and LISTENING on a dark grid
steps.if: If the look does not change, the swipe was too short or began on a button; swipe across the face.

steps.title: Look C, Visor.
steps.do: Swipe to the next look.
steps.see: A glass band with two glowing capsule eyes that blink and glance, a voice line under them and a scanline every few seconds.
img: sparky/sparky-look-visor-listening.png
Look C, Visor: two green capsule eyes in a glass band with the word Listening
steps.if: If the look does not change, the swipe was too short or began on a button; swipe across the face.

steps.title: Look Kid.
steps.do: Swipe to the next look. Kid raises the wake sensitivity while it is on, and puts a GAMES chip in the top right corner.
steps.see: Core in candy colors with a face on the orb: blinking eyes, a smile, an o while listening and a mouth that opens with the reply, and friendlier words (I'm listening).
img: sparky/sparky-look-kid-listening.png
Look Kid: a purple screen with a green orb that has a face with round eyes and a small mouth, and the words I'm listening
steps.if: If the look does not change, the swipe was too short or began on a button; swipe across the face.

variants.expect: A press of S2 or the `s` key and a spoken question give a spoken answer, first audio about 2.5 s after you stop. With the screen, a face that listens, thinks and talks in one of four looks.
shows: A Wi-Fi LaunchPad with a BoosterPack can be a complete voice terminal: microphone to Opus to a server and back, with the Opus encoder and decoder running on the Cortex-M33 in 24 kB and 17.5 kB of RAM.
Median 2.47 s from the end of a spoken question to the first reply audio (2.28 to 2.67 s, three questions, Claude Haiku).
Joined Wi-Fi 6.5 s after reset (5.9 to 6.7 s, five boots).
The four looks, touch navigation, the settings strip, a Wi-Fi motion score and offline kids' games run in the same image over the air-updatable slot.
not_shows: That the speaker sounds clean: it was not judged by ear.
That S2 works by hand: the press was sent from the console.
Power use: the radio is kept always on and power was not measured.
A real room: the questions came from a Mac speaker 30 cm away, in a quiet room.
limits: The server is a separate computer on your network; the board does not run the speech recognition or the language model.
Half duplex: the microphone stops while the answer plays, so there is no talking over it, and one turn per connection.

The Hey Sparky wake word model is not in the repository: its training clips are available for non-commercial use only. Build with `XZ_WAKE=0` for push-to-talk, or train a model of your own for the board's detector (microWakeWord on TFLite Micro).
Sound is the audio pack's small speaker: it has almost nothing below 500 Hz.
Plain `ws://` to a computer on the same network; the WebSocket client does not check the server's accept hash.

outcomes.name: Post-quantum key exchange and signatures
outcomes.one_line: The board and a Mac agree on a secret key with ML-KEM-768, a method meant to stay safe against quantum computers, then swap one encrypted line.
outcomes.why: Each ML-KEM-768 step takes 21 to 29 ms at 48 MHz on the CC1354P10.

lines: board> KAT PASS
key check  Mac d01a2f61  board d01a2f61  MATCH
board> DECRYPTED (76 bytes, tag ok): Hello from the Mac: this line was encrypted with a key agreed by ML-KEM-768.

outcomes.name: Time a motor-control loop
outcomes.one_line: A timer starts an ADC reading, one field-oriented control step runs in the interrupt, and the PWM output updates. The timing runs from trigger to new PWM value.
outcomes.why: The F2800137's math unit makes the loop 1.5 times faster than software math on the same chip (2.4 against 3.7 µs).

lines: Trigger to new PWM value: {{row:f2800137/control_loop/hw|.1f}} µs on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 at 120 MHz with its math unit; {{row:mspm0g3507/control_loop/hw|.1f}} µs on the LP-MSPM0G3507 at 80 MHz with its math accelerator
The control step alone takes 0.585 µs on the LP-AM13E230 (117 cycles at 200 MHz); its trigger-to-PWM loop is not measured

outcomes.one_line: Read a board's running current through the debug probe, even on a board with no EnergyTrace of its own.
outcomes.why: Running current grows 263 µA per MHz between 60 and 120 MHz.

lines: 35.4 mA running CoreMark at 120 MHz and 2.59 mA in STANDBY (LAUNCHXL-F2800137, read through an LP-MSPM0L1306 EnergyTrace probe). Coin-cell life is not measured.

lines: CoreMark runs from {{row:mspm0l1306/coremark/ticlang-bare-o3|.0f}} on the LP-MSPM0L1306 (2.45 per MHz at 32 MHz) to {{row:am13e230/coremark/ticlang-bare-o3|.0f}} on the LP-AM13E230 (4.36 per MHz at 200 MHz), both at -O3

outcomes.name: A touch screen on a LaunchPad
outcomes.one_line: A 3.5 inch touch screen on 11 jumper wires (12 with the optional INT), drawing shapes and reading touches.
outcomes.why: A full frame is 300 kB, 9.4 times the chip's RAM, so drawing goes in strips.

lines: Fills, bars and touch dots; a full-screen fill takes 67 ms at 40 MHz SPI (LP-MSPM0G3507)
proof.alt: Wiring diagram: 11 jumper wires (12 with the optional INT) from the LaunchPad to the 3.5 inch screen

outcomes.name: Play music and light from a BoosterPack
outcomes.one_line: The Audio BoosterPack plays recorded music and synth songs while the board's RGB LED follows the beat.

lines: Five orchestral recordings and four synth songs at 16,000 samples a second, 0 bad frames over 480 s (LP-MSPM33C321A with the BOOSTXL-AUDIO)
proof.alt: A carved jack-o'-lantern glowing orange and purple from the LaunchPad inside it

outcomes.name: A USB device
outcomes.one_line: The board shows up on the Mac as a USB device, such as a keyboard or a serial port of its own.

lines: Nothing has run.

outcomes.missing: No USB demo has run on any of these boards.

outcomes.name: Blink an LED, box to blinking in minutes
outcomes.one_line: Plug the board in, build TI's blink example, then change the pattern.

lines: 2 min 29 s from board in hand to a changed blink (LP-MSPM0G3507, tools already installed)
proof.alt: An LP-MSPM0G3507 board on a desk, plugged in by USB

outcomes.name: Run Zephyr or FreeRTOS
outcomes.one_line: A real-time operating system runs on the board, from the command line.
outcomes.why: TI's own FreeRTOS settings file for the L1306 needs 5.4 kB of RAM and does not link in 4 kB.

lines: Zephyr's blinky runs on the LP-MSPM0G3507
11 FreeRTOS tasks fit in 4 kB of RAM on the LP-MSPM0L1306

outcomes.name: Run example code written for another chip
outcomes.one_line: Take example programs written for another chip, or for another TI chip, and run them on the board.
outcomes.why: 21 of the 34 ported variants had their behavior checked on the board.

lines: 34 of 53 example variants ran on the LP-MSPM0L1306 (a port of Cmsemicon's public CMS32F04x examples to a LaunchPad development kit)

outcomes.name: Use Arduino, MicroPython or ESPHome
outcomes.one_line: Write for the board with a tool you already know.

lines: Arduino's Blink and AnalogReadSerial run unchanged on two boards. MicroPython runs on two boards. ESPHome compile and upload put a Zigbee device in Home Assistant from two boards.

outcomes.name: Run a vision model on a TI Linux board
outcomes.one_line: TI's SK-TDA4VM runs its model zoo on a deep-learning accelerator while two Arm cores run Linux; video goes from the hardware decoder into the model with no CPU copy.
outcomes.why: The first board here that is a computer, not a microcontroller: 24 s to a Linux prompt, {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.1f}} to {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.1f}} ms per model on the C7x, about 500 frames a second of hardware H.264 decode.

lines: Warm boot {{row:tda4/linux_boot_time/warm|.1f}} s to the login prompt; every zoo model (14) runs on the C7x in {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/mobilenetv1-mlperf-224-tflitert-tidl-c7x|.1f}} to {{row:tda4/dl_inference_ms/yolox-s-pose-640-onnxrt-tidl-c7x|.1f}} ms, the two A72 cores take 13 to 135 times longer on the same models
Decode into a model with TI's zero-copy settings: 110.8 fps for a third of one core; without them 56.2 fps for two thirds

outcomes.name: Hear the smoke alarm you already have
outcomes.one_line: A board beside your smoke or CO alarm learns it by ear and tells you when it goes off.
outcomes.why: No new alarm to buy: the board listens to the one you own.

lines: A smoke alarm pattern from a laptop speaker reported 9.4 s after it started, and 0 alarms in 3.4 hours of a quiet room (LP-MSPM0G5187); a real horn is still to test, and the Mac notification was not recorded

outcomes.name: Sense a room with radar
outcomes.one_line: A 60 GHz radar board says whether a room is occupied and where.

lines: A seated person at 2 m and 4 m was held in 100 percent of frames (IWRL6432BOOST, one pass per cell)
0 false alarms in 87,602 empty-room frames, 6.08 h
