line_plain.E1: The CC2340R5 has too little RAM for a Thread node. The same builds link on the larger CC2340R53 but have not run.
line_plain.E2: Bluetooth and an 802.15.4 radio at once do not fit in the CC2340R5's RAM. They link on the CC2340R53 but have not run.
line_plain.E3: Zephyr's Bluetooth runs on the CC2340R5 with one heap setting, and TI's own beacon sample crashes.
line_plain.E4: Updating a CC2340R5 Zigbee device over the air from Home Assistant reached 89% of a 200 kB image at best, and none of twelve transfers finished.
line_plain.E5: Most CC2340R5 radio settings can be changed as text without SysConfig. One was silently ignored and needed C code.
line_plain.E6: Zephyr runs on the 4 kB MSPM0L1306 with an out-of-tree board file and a small heap. CoreMark fits with 16 bytes of RAM to spare.
line_plain.E7: The 8k-parameter occupancy model runs on the MSPM0L1306 in 84 to 100 ms in 4 kB of RAM. The 32,836-weight model does not fit.
line_plain.E8: FreeRTOS runs on the MSPM0L1306 with static allocation and small stacks, 11 tasks in 4 kB of RAM. TI's own settings file needs 5.4 kB and does not link.
line_plain.E9: A 3.5 inch touch screen works on the MSPM0G3507 over 11 jumper wires (12 with the optional INT). A full frame is 9.4 times the chip's RAM, so drawing goes in strips.
line_plain.E11: EnergyTrace does not work on a Mac as shipped. Patched copies of TI's libraries load but have not run against a board.
line_plain.E12: All four BitNetMCU handwriting models read 10 of 10 test digits on the MSPM0G3507, and one runs on the MSPM0L1306 in 4 kB of RAM.
line_plain.E13: The F2800137 has no EnergyTrace, but two wires to an MSPM0L1306's probe make it the meter. Its own debugger will not connect on borrowed power.
line_plain.E14: BitNetMCU's smallest model reads all 10 test digits on the MSPM0C1104 in 804 bytes of RAM. The larger CNN overruns the stack.
line_plain.E15: None of the four room-occupancy models fits in the MSPM0C1104's 1 kB of RAM. The smallest needs 1.2 kB.
line_plain.E17: Standard CoreMark does not link on the MSPM0C1104. Reduced versions link, then crash.
line_plain.E19: Zephyr's blinky for the MSPM0G3519 builds and flashes from a Mac, then stops right after reset on an SRAM error, so the LED never blinks.
line_plain.E32: One control step takes 0.585 µs on the AM13E230, 3.1 times faster than the F2800137. Its trigger-to-PWM loop is not measured.
line_plain.E52: The u8g2 display library compiles for the C2000 only when uint8_t is an unsigned char. It has not run on a display.
line_plain.E73: TI's CC1407P radio driver does not compile for the C2000 as shipped. With two changes it compiles, but most message structures come out the wrong size.
line_plain.E109: A Mac terminal does everything the CC35X1 needs, with no Windows step. Edit to blinking LED took 60 s.
line_plain.E127: ST's AES example runs as shipped on the NUCLEO-U083RC and passes its own checks. Its README promises 192-bit keys that the chip does not have.
line_plain.E128: All 40 kB of the STM32U083's RAM works as one block, though ST's linker scripts and Zephyr give programs only 32 kB.
line_plain.E129: On the NUCLEO-U083RC, one flash wait state at 48 MHz costs at most 1.3 percent of CoreMark.
line_plain.E113: Wi-Fi setup over Bluetooth works on the CC35X1 without TI's phone app. A Mac script took it from reset to a Wi-Fi address in 16.5 to 17.8 s.
line_plain.E130: The MSPM0G5187's neural-network engine runs all four occupancy models with matching answers, 1.9 to 16.7 times faster than the best CPU build.
line_plain.E33: TI's compiler runs all four occupancy models on the AM13E230's neural-network engine with matching answers, 2.4 to 8.8 times faster than its own CPU build. The CDE build halts.
line_plain.E37: A minimal ESPHome device takes 816 kB of flash and leaves 305 kB of heap on the ESP32-C6. On the test board the Wi-Fi-only image found no network, and over-the-air updates stalled.
line_plain.E38: ESPHome's Zigbee end device on the ESP32-C6 joined Home Assistant in 6 s and sent 31 of 31 reports; it takes 492 kB of flash and 83 kB of RAM. It offers sensors, not switches.
line_plain.E39: Zigbee and Thread in one ESP32-C6 image compile but do not link: both stacks define the same seven radio callbacks.
line_plain.E40: The shared BTHome header runs on the ESP32-C6 with 40 lines of glue, against 58 on the TI chip, and a Mac decodes the packets.
line_plain.E41: An ESPHome Thread device on the ESP32-C6 joins the house network in about a second and answers pings from the MacBook; the Home Assistant computer has no route to it.
line_plain.E42: The ESP32-C6's low-power core runs the 8,484-weight occupancy network (20 of 20) in 214 ms; the float input step does not fit its 16 kB, so the main core does it.
line_plain.E43: One ESPHome image can be a Bluetooth proxy and a Zigbee end device, but the Zigbee side never joined; the proxy loses about 10 percent of its advertisements.
line_plain.E105: ESPHome's Zigbee router, a switch and a temperature sensor run on the CC2755P10 on TI's Zigbee libraries: 263 kB of flash and 37.6 kB of RAM, 124.4 kB of RAM left. Joined the house Zigbee network in under 8 s and switched the LED 20 of 20 times.
line_plain.E191: ESPHome's Zigbee end device runs on the CC2340R5 with 4.0 kB of its 36 kB of RAM left and answers 93 of 100 commands; as a router it needs the heap cut by 2 kB and then has none left.
line_plain.E192: ESPHome's own commands build and flash it: with an external platform in the YAML, esphome compile takes 35 s and esphome upload 15 s, the CC2755P10 joins Home Assistant's Zigbee network 5.7 to 6.3 s later and switches its LED 32 of 32 times. The CC2340R5 end device builds, flashes and joins the same way (4.0 kB of RAM left).
line_plain.E193: The Wi-Fi board too: esphome compile and esphome upload build and flash the LP-EM-CC35X1 (56 s, 60 s); it joins Wi-Fi 5.3 s after a reset, logs through ESPHome, announces itself over mDNS and its native API answered 20 of 20 switch commands from a client on the board; Home Assistant adoption over Wi-Fi is the next run.
line_plain.E289: Seven models in the files their training tools wrote (float CNNs from torch, scikit-learn trees, XGBoost) ran on the AM13E230 through a plain Python-to-C step with matching answers; float as trained takes 0.8 to 1.2 times the int8 C build, the neural-network engine stays 2.4 to 8.9 times faster, and the XGBoost model is the most accurate and runs in 80 Âµs.
